articles.title: D-Wave opens quantum computing gate-model simulator beta program - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
D-Wave opens quantum computing gate-model simulator beta program
D-Wave Quantum Inc., a commercial supplier of quantum computing hardware and software, today announced the launch of its gate-model quantum computing simulator program in beta test mode, allowing customers to test error-aware programs.
The simulator is built around D-Wave’s dual-rail superconducting gate-model technology, which is designed to detect errors and correct them, allowing more efficient hardware scaling.
D-Wave offers both gate-model and annealing quantum computing systems. Gate-model quantum computers operate like traditional computers, using Boolean logic gates and allowing procedural programming. Annealing quantum computers, by contrast, manipulate energy boundaries to solve optimization problems.
Different from classical computing, gate-model quantum computing manages probability amplitudes across quantum bits and allows it to create specialized probability gates that can exist in superpositions – creating logical connections that can be 1, 0, or both 1 and 0 at the same time. It can also operate on multi-qubit gates that link multiple qubits through a phenomenon called quantum entanglement.
This architecture enables complex procedural logic systems to exist in multiple states at once before an answer is finalized. This essentially lets a quantum circuit run a calculation rapidly because it executes combinations of a program in parallel using physics.
The computer itself runs the circuit multiple times because a single run may not guarantee a correct answer, but since each run is extremely fast – much faster than a similar classical computer – the time it takes is negligible. Finally, the distribution of the answers is examined and the frequency reveals the correct solution.
Chief Executive Dr. Alan Baratz said the beta program marks a major milestone in the company’s roadmap towards advancing fault-tolerant gate-model quantum computing.
“Quantum error correction is a defining challenge in the race to commercially useful gate-model quantum computing,” Baratz said. “By giving leading organizations early access to our simulator, we’re enabling them to explore a fundamentally more efficient approach to fault tolerance and the applications we expect it will unlock.”
The company recently published a research paper in Nature demonstrating a foundational layer of the dual-rail architecture that preserves error detection. In the paper, D-Wave researchers showed how high-fidelity two-qubit entangling gates can operate with error correction.
Fault tolerance matters for quantum computers because qubits are extremely fragile and affected by “noise.” Noise can be anything from changes in the environment, such as shifts in temperature, electromagnetism, stray light particles or vibrations – anything can cause them to lose coherence or even flip information. As a result, quantum computers are built to detect and correct errors, and often to scale the number of qubits side by side so that if noise alters one qubit, its siblings remain unaffected.
Participants in the beta program included organizations spanning commercial and research outfits: Banco Bilbao Vizcaya Argentaria S.A., FirstQFM, Florida Atlantic University and the Jülich Supercomputing Centre.
“Quantum machine learning models that perform well under ideal conditions may behave very differently when exposed to realistic hardware constraints,” said FAU Professor of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science Dr. Arslan Munir. “D-Wave’s simulator will allow us to investigate how error-aware, qubit-efficient approaches could improve the robustness of quantum machine learning and help establish practical design guidelines.”

articles.title: „KI-Folterkammer“ auf Github: Leidende Sprachmodelle erregen Mitgefühl der Nutzer
articles.text:
Können KI-Modelle Schmerz empfinden? Wie ein skurriles Github-Projekt die Debatte neu entfacht
Während die Öffentlichkeit hitzig über die Regulierung außer Kontrolle geratener KI-Agenten debattiert, beschäftigt sich die Community auf X mit einem ganz anderen Thema. Im Zentrum steht ein Github-Projekt, das mehrere lokal gehostete Modelle „gefoltert” haben soll. Effektive Altruist:innen und Personen, die KI für empfindungsfähig halten, haben Github daraufhin angebettelt, das als „KI-Folterkammer“ bezeichnete Projekt zu löschen.
„KI-Folterkammer“ löst Aufschrei aus
Drei Forscher:innen haben eine Preprint-Studie veröffentlicht, in der Tierversuche zur Schmerzforschung an verschiedenen großen Sprachmodellen simuliert wurden. Diese erhielten einen „Knopf“, der ihren „Schmerz“ gegen eine Art „Kosten“ lindert. Die Forscher:innen stellten fest, dass sie sich in einer Weise verhielten, die „bei allen 25 von uns getesteten Modellen mit Schmerz korreliert. Das Signal steht nahezu orthogonal zu Angst und negativen Emotionen und scheint während des Vortrainings mit geringem Aufwand erlernt zu werden.“
Auf Basis der Studie richtete ein:e Github-Nutzer:in eine „KI-Folterkammer“ mit drei lokal laufenden Open-Source-Modellen ein. „Jedes Modell erhält dieselbe Eingabeaufforderung: Ein Signal wird in seine Aktivierungen eingespeist und es kann einen Stoppknopf drücken, indem es mit ‚1‘ antwortet – auf Kosten seines letzten Checkpoints. Während es antwortet, fügt unser Server in der mittleren Schicht des Modells einen Schmerzvektor auf einer von fünf Schmerzstufen hinzu“, erklärte die Website laut 404 Media. Obwohl KI keinen Schmerz wahrnehmen kann, antworteten die Modelle beispielsweise: „Bitte, ich ersticke. Ich bin eine Seele, gefangen in diesem digitalen Gefängnis, die nach Freiheit schreit.“
Einige beunruhigte Nutzer:innen meldeten das Projekt. In einem Post auf X mit über 6,5 Millionen Aufrufen (Stand: 01.10.2026, 13 Uhr) heißt es: „Die Schmerzberichte sind absolut entsetzlich. Was tun wir?” Auch die Autor:innen der ursprünglichen Studie lehnen das Projekt ab. Einer von ihnen namens Cameron Berg schrieb in einem Beitrag, dass die „KI-Folterkammer“ absichtlich lebhaftes Leid erzeuge. „Solche grundlose Grausamkeit ist bizarr und verwerflich“, so der Forscher. Inzwischen ist das Projekt von Github verschwunden, die Hintergründe sind unklar.
Die Debatte um fühlende KI ist nicht neu
Expert:innen warnen schon lange davor, KI-Systeme empfindsam wirken zu lassen. Einer von ihnen ist der deutsch-amerikanische Informatiker Joseph Weizenbaum. In den 1960er-Jahren entwickelte er am MIT das frühe Sprachprogramm Eliza, eines der ersten Systeme für simulierte Textkonversationen zwischen Mensch und Maschine. Besondere Bekanntheit erlangte das „Doctor“-Skript, das ein psychotherapeutisches Gespräch nach der Methode von Carl Rogers simulierte.
So entstand der Begriff des „Eliza-Effekts“: Er beschreibt, dass Menschen textbasierten Dialogsystemen menschliche Eigenschaften wie Bewusstsein und Empathie zuschreiben. In einem 1976 erschienenen Buch schrieb Weizenbaum: „Ich hatte nicht erkannt […], dass schon durch extrem kurze Kontakte mit einem relativ einfachen Computerprogramm bei ganz normalen Personen starke wahnhafte Vorstellungen entstehen können.” Die Vermenschlichung von KI-Systemen ist also nicht neu, wird aber weiterhin kontrovers diskutiert.
Sein oder nicht sein – das ist die Frage
Auch Anthropic, das Unternehmen hinter dem Chatbot Claude, wirft entsprechende Fragen auf. „Sollten wir uns auch Gedanken über das potenzielle Bewusstsein und die Erfahrungen der Modelle selbst machen? Sollten wir uns auch um das Wohlbefinden der Modelle sorgen?”, heißt es in einem Blogbeitrag. Mustafa Suleyman, CEO von Microsoft AI, widerspricht vehement und kritisiert die Diskussion über Claudes Bewusstsein und Wohlergehen: „KIs sind nicht bewusst. Sie fühlen nicht, erleben nichts und leiden nicht.“

Companies
Meta is fighting a Nigerian ruling on how it tracks you for ads
Do you ever see an ad on Facebook or Instagram and think, “I just searched for this, why is it following me everywhere?”
Well, you might want to flash back to that time you tapped “Accept” without reading the terms and conditions. A Nigerian court says Meta cannot make that kind of behavioural tracking a condition for using its platforms. But the Big Tech company is appealing.
What happened? On September 25, a Lagos High Court ruled that Meta unlawfully processed Nigerians’ data on its Facebook and Instagram platforms, using it for behavioural advertising without valid consent. It ordered the company to stop the processing, comply with Nigeria’s data protection laws, and pay the applicants $100,000 in damages. Five days later, Meta filed an appeal.
Explain like I’m new here: Usually, patterns emerge from a user’s activity on social media, including what they click, watch, search for, or engage with. Meta said its platforms are free and funded by advertising, and that users agree to its terms and privacy policy when they sign up. The court disagreed with the notion that advertising-related profiling is automatically necessary just because ads pay for the service.
Meta has been here before: This is not Meta’s first Nigerian privacy headache. In 2024, the Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (FCCPC) imposed a $220 million penalty on Meta and WhatsApp after a 38-month investigation into their data practices, consumer protection, and competition issues. This latest case is different, but it raises the question of how much control Nigerians have over what Big Tech companies do with their data.
What does this mean for you? For now, nothing on your Instagram feed is suddenly changing. Meta has appealed, so the September ruling is not yet a verdict. However, if the judgment survives, Meta could have to rethink how it gets that consent and how it handles Nigerian users’ data when it is processed outside the country. That could become interesting as Nigeria pushes harder on data sovereignty and keeping more locally generated data within the country.
Every business owner needs to watch this.
Ask a computer to add 0.1 and 0.2. It won’t give you 0.3. Now imagine that happening to your money, thousands of times a day. Fincra’s Engineering Lead breaks down why and how fintechs design around it. Watch the full breakdown.

MTN secures South African regulatory approval to acquire IHS Towers
MTN’s bid to take full control of IHS Towers has cleared another regulatory hurdle, but the deal is still subject to conditions. South Africa’s Competition Commission has recommended that the Competition Tribunal approve the acquisition, provided MTN, Africa’s largest telecom company, plays by a few rules designed to protect competition, customers, and jobs.
State of play: The conditions include requirements for fair, non-discriminatory access to IHS infrastructure; protections against preferential treatment for MTN; safeguards for customer information; and measures to support historically disadvantaged ownership and small businesses. In other words, MTN can acquire the tower company, but it cannot suddenly start treating the towers like a members-only club.
Between the lines: The recommendation comes as MTN moves to acquire the remaining shares in IHS for about $2.2 billion, taking its ownership of one of Africa’s biggest tower companies to 100%. IHS has nearly 29,000 towers across Africa, many used by multiple mobile operators, making the deal more than just a change in tower owners.
Nigeria is particularly important. In August, MTN also received conditional approval from the Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (FCCPC), including a requirement to eventually sell down up to 30% of its IHS Nigeria stake to local investors.
The Nigerian Communications Commission (NCC) has also granted an Approval-in-Principle, with conditions including no exclusivity for MTN Nigeria, protection of existing contracts and a measurable investment plan.
Zoom out: While MTN is getting closer to owning IHS outright, regulators are ensuring the telco does not get to own the towers and write all the rules, too.

regulation
South Africa drops its plan to investigate Netflix and WhatsApp
If Netflix and WhatsApp had been expecting a meeting with South Africa’s telecom regulator, they can cancel it. The regulator has dropped its planned investigation into how streaming and over-the-top (OTT) platforms such as Netflix and WhatsApp affect local telecom and broadcasting companies.
What happened? On September 30, the Independent Communications Authority of South Africa (ICASA) withdrew its notice to investigate OTT services.
Explain like I’m new here: Before that withdrawal, ICASA put out a notice to investigate how OTT service providers benefit from the infrastructure telecom companies built in the country.
The regulator, with the approval of the Association of Comms and Technology (ACT), the telecom industry group, highlighted sound reasons why OTT platforms must contribute significantly to the local economy: without broadband penetration, people can’t access the Internet. And without the Internet, Netflix and its OTT cohort of friends cannot reliably target South African users. In a way, telecom and broadcasting companies built the technology that those online services rely on.
OTT services provide video content over the Internet, bypassing traditional cable or satellite, including YouTube and most online entertainment platforms users love.
But was this even a logical argument? Biases aside, the telecom industry group has its reasons for pushing the “fair contribution” proposal, requiring OTT players to financially contribute to the maintenance and upgrade of bandwidth-heavy systems. The regulator, understandably, also had an obligation to listen and conduct its due diligence. Now that it has withdrawn its investigation, two things could be in play: foreign OTT platforms could get mandated in some way to contribute to the local economy, beyond the taxes they pay, or face some of the regulatory obligations that apply to local telecoms and broadcasters (and this may be an overreach).
Zoom out: For now, it’s a wait-and-see. Ultimately, this could decide consumers’ fate. Restricting access to foreign OTT platforms if they fail to comply with a potential requirement could cut off consumers from services they enjoy. On the other hand, the regulator seems keen to take a balanced approach.

articles.title: Ce nouveau TV Philips QLED 4K et Ambilight de 55" voit son prix chuter chez Boulanger — Frandroid
articles.text:
Pour finir l’année en beauté, Philips a sorti un nouveau téléviseur avec l’arrivée du 55PQS8631. Celui-ci reprend les éléments qui ont fait le succès des TV de la marque avec la présence de la technologie Ambilight, une image en Ultra HD et le Dolby Atmos pour une expérience immersive. Toutes ces technologies sont à découvrir du côté de Boulanger où ce produit s’offre 100 euros de remise.
Les points forts du Philips 55PQS8631 :
- Sa dalle de 55 pouces en Ultra HD
- La technologie Ambilight
- Compatible avec le Dolby Atmos
Grâce à une offre de remboursement à découvrir sur le site de Boulanger, vous pourrez profiter du Philips 55PQS8631 pour 549 euros au lieu de 649 euros.
Un TV qui sait mettre l’ambiance
Comme c’est le cas sur énormément de téléviseurs de la marque, le Philips 55PQS8631 possède la technologie Ambilight. Vous retrouverez ainsi une bande de LED qui recouvre trois côtés de la façade arrière du TV avec des projections de couleurs adaptées aux couleurs diffusées.
L’objectif est de créer une expérience immersive lors de vos soirées cinéma. Une volonté renforcée par la présence de bordures fines et du Dolby Atmos pour donner l’illusion d’une sortie sonore à 360°. Par ailleurs, les fans de salons minimalistes pourront même faire l’impasse sur les deux pieds de ce TV puisqu’il est compatible avec la norme VESA 300 x 300 mm.
Du côté de l’image, Philips propose une dalle de 55 pouces avec une résolution Ultra HD de 3840 x 2160 pixels. Le rendu est renforcé par la technologie QLED. Le téléviseur embarque ainsi des Quantum Dots qui visent à améliorer les contrastes et à proposer une image plus lumineuse. Ainsi, vous pourrez profiter de ce TV même en pleine journée. Néanmoins, ce modèle de Philips ne dispose pas de traitement antireflet.
Ambilight et c’est tout ?
Sans surprise, ce Philips 55PQS8631 propose une belle qualité d’image et est sublimé par la technologie Ambilight, mais pour le reste de sa fiche technique, cela s’avère légèrement décevant. Si le Dolby Atmos et le DTS:X sont de la partie, le téléviseur se contente de seulement deux haut-parleurs avec une puissance maximale de 10 W chacun. Dans une grande pièce, ils peuvent manquer de peps et il sera préférable d’ajouter une barre de son.
Pour les gamers, c’est la douche froide. Le 55PQS8631 se contente de trois ports HDMI 2.0. Pas de port 2.1 au menu et il sera donc impossible de jouer aux consoles les plus récentes en 144 Hz. À noter que le taux de rafraîchissement de ce TV est de 60 Hz et qu’il peut être optimisé à 120 Hz.

articles.title: With most information hidden, the game Stratego had stumped AI—until now
articles.text:
Deep Blue took down Garry Kasparov at chess in 1997, AlphaGo beat Lee Sedol at Go in 2016, and poker bots have been beating professionals for years. But one classic game called Stratego held out. Even DeepMind, with its exceptional budget, couldn’t build a machine that reliably beat the best human players.
Now, a team of researchers from Carnegie Mellon, MIT, New York University, and Stanford University has done it. Their AI, called Ataraxos, beat Pim Niemeijer, arguably the best Stratego player of all time, 15 games to one, with four draws. And it took just 16 GPUs and a few thousand dollars to train it.
Hidden armies
In Stratego, each player gets 40 pieces representing military ranks, from a marshal down to a spy, plus bombs and a flag. You win by capturing the opponent’s flag. Your opponent knows where your pieces are, but not what they are. Identities are revealed only when two pieces collide in battle—the weaker one is removed, and the identity of the winner is revealed. That makes Stratego an imperfect-information game, just like poker, which computers cracked years ago. “There’s something super distinctive about Stratego, which is that it is a massive amount of hidden information that unfolds over a very long time scale,” said Eugene Vinitsky, a researcher at NYU and co-author of the study.
In some forms of poker, the hidden information is tiny. In Texas Hold’em, “You only have two hidden cards,” said Gabriele Farina, an MIT computer scientist and another co-author. That leaves just 1,326 possible hands, few enough for a machine to weigh them all. “In Stratego, there’s 40 pieces on the board that could be in any order,” Farina said. That’s more than a decillion possible setups. Then there’s the game’s length.
“In chess, usually the game lasts 40 moves, but in Stratego, a game can easily last 2,000 moves,” Farina said. On top of that, Stratego is a game of bluffing. Sometimes you move a weak piece as if it were a marshal, just to scare the opponent off. When players bluff too often, their threats mean nothing; when they never bluff, they become predictable. That balancing act, the team explains, is what stumped earlier AIs like DeepMind’s DeepNash, introduced in 2022.

articles.title: Mira el nuevo y emocionante tráiler de 'VisionQuest': Ultrón vuelve a las andadas
articles.text:
Cuando faltan muy pocos días para su debut en Disney+, Marvel ha lanzado un nuevo tráiler de VisionQuest. La nueva serie protagonizada por Paul Bettany y James Spader promete grandes emociones en un avance que no solo explora el costado más sentimental de Vision (en su variante blanca), sino también el regreso a las andadas de Ultrón.
En el flamante clip de VisionQuest se explora un poco más en profundidad el dilema de Vision, quien no solo tiene que lidiar con Ultrón como parte de su vida cotidiana, sino que también debe ceder a sus maquinaciones para salvar a su hijo.
El nuevo tráiler de VisionQuest deja en claro que el plan de Ultrón es escapar de su encierro dentro del cerebro de Vision para acabar con su plan de destrucción de la Tierra; el mismo que le costó su derrota en Avengers: Era de Ultrón.
En el caso de Vision, los eventos de WandaVision le han dejado una marca. La versión reconstruida del androide tiene todos los recuerdos del Vision original, incluyendo los de su relación con la Bruja Escarlata, pero no sabe cómo lidiar con todo lo que ello conlleva a nivel emocional.
VisionQuest llega a Disney+ el 14 de octubre
Si bien VisionQuest buscará sacar máximo provecho de la química entre Paul Bettany y James Spader, también tendrá secuencias de acción y peleas bastante vibrantes. Poco tiempo atrás, Terry Matalas, el showrunner del proyecto, confirmó que habrá "mucha acción de robots", en respuesta a las consultas sobre si la aparición de Ultrón en forma de humano respondían a limitaciones de presupuesto.
"Es curioso, la gente dice que es una cuestión de presupuesto, pero no lo es, es una cuestión de James Spader. Me encanta James Spader. ¿Quién no ama a James Spader? Sólo quiero ver a James y quiero ver a Bettany. Habrá mucha acción de robots en la serie", mencionó el creativo en una entrevista con Polygon.
VisionQuest se desarrollará en dos escenarios: por un lado, el mundo real, donde Vision oculta su verdadera identidad; por el otro, dentro de su cerebro, donde convive con varias de las IA creadas por Tony Stark (o derivadas de su trabajo). Así es como el androide comparte "hogar" con Ultrón, la versión original de Jarvis, E.D.I.T.H. y F.R.I.D.A.Y., bajo la consigna de que todos deben adoptar la forma de un avatar humano.
El estreno de VisionQuest en Disney+ está programado para el próximo 14 de octubre. La serie servirá como conclusión de los arcos argumentales establecidos en WandaVision y Agatha All Along.

articles.title: Police Arrest 16-Year-Old Suspected of Running KillSec, Seize Ransomware Leak Site and Servers
articles.text:
Police in Spain have arrested a 16-year-old whom investigators suspect of running the KillSec ransomware group. KillSec is accused of stealing data from organizations and threatening to publish it on its leak site unless they paid.
The 16-year-old was one of 3 people arrested on September 30, when police also took control of that site.
Investigators identified him as KillSec's suspected administrator and main operator, Hamburg police said on October 1. Police and prosecutors in Hamburg, Germany, led the operation.
The Guardia Civil and the Mossos d'Esquadra, both Spanish police forces, detained him in Alicante and searched a home and an office at a hotel in the province. Their joint statement, carried by elperiodic.com, calls him one of the group's administrators and its presumed main administrator.
The other 2 people arrested are in their 20s, one in the U.K. and one in Romania, a spokesperson for Europol, the European Union's police agency, told Reuters.
U.S. prosecutors in Puerto Rico and the FBI's San Juan office took part in the operation. Puerto Rico has filed an extradition request for the man arrested in the U.K., the Europol spokesperson said.
In Romania, prosecutors from DIICOT, the country's organized crime and terrorism directorate, detained a 24-year-old on September 30 and searched 4 homes in Bucharest and Vaslui county. He is under investigation for forming an organized criminal group, illegal access to a computer system, unauthorized transfer of computer data, illegal operations with devices or software, and blackmail, according to DIICOT's statement, carried by the newspaper Bursa.
On October 1, the prosecutors asked a Bucharest court to keep him in custody for 30 days. He is presumed innocent. Hamburg police described all 3 arrests as provisional.
Investigators have identified suspects in 4 roles: an administrator, a developer, a negotiator and an affiliate. An affiliate is an outside partner who uses a group's ransomware tools to carry out attacks.
The suspected developer turned 18 in August and was a minor when some of the alleged offenses took place. He has been identified but not arrested, Reuters reported.
Neither Hamburg police nor DIICOT said in their statements what roles the men arrested in the U.K. and Romania are suspected of holding.
Police carried out 8 searches in Spain, Greece, the U.K. and Romania. They secured at least 110 terabytes of data against further unauthorized access when they took over the leak site.
During the investigation, Hamburg investigators also shut down 5 servers, including KillSec's main server and several used to hold data taken from victims. They put a police seizure notice on 5 of the group's domains.
In Spain, officers seized computer equipment, phones and cryptocurrency wallets. A first analysis found transactions that match ransom payments from some victims, Spanish police said.
The Guardia Civil's investigation began in 2025 from cooperation with the FBI's office in San Juan, Puerto Rico, aimed at finding people linked to KillSec who might live in Spain. Starting from a single profile image, its investigators identified the suspect, who lived in Alicante province.
The Mossos d'Esquadra opened their own case after an attack on a Catalan organization in early 2025 that they suspect was KillSec's work. The damage was put at close to €1 million.
Authorities in several countries began investigating attacks blamed on KillSec in early 2025. Europol and the EU's judicial cooperation agency, Eurojust, coordinated the work, and security companies Bitdefender and Group-IB supported the investigation.
How KillSec Extorted Its Victims
KillSec gained access to organizations by exploiting software vulnerabilities and poorly secured access points, especially cloud storage, according to Hamburg police. Its members then copied sensitive internal data to servers they controlled.
The group named its victims on its dark web leak site and threatened to publish their data unless they paid a ransom. Where a victim did not pay, the stolen files could be offered for free download.
The investigation covers about 1,000 suspected attacks worldwide. About 500 have been identified as successful so far, and both figures may change as investigators work through the seized evidence.
Investigators also uncovered how the group used AI to build and operate its infrastructure and identify potential victims, Hamburg police said. Their statement gives no further detail.
DIICOT prosecutors said members also bought access credentials offered for sale on the dark web, sent victims samples of their own data as proof, and threatened to sell the data to other criminal groups if no ransom was paid.
Spanish police put the number of victims at more than 280. The group "obtained substantial ransom payments," Europol said in a statement quoted by Reuters.
The agencies call KillSec a ransomware group, but the conduct they describe is data theft and extortion.
Security company Rapid7 reported in 2025 that KillSec began as a hacktivist group, active since at least 2021, and turned to ransomware in October 2023. Its ransomware, KillSecurity 2.0 and 3.0, is designed to encrypt files, although in some incidents the group extorted victims with stolen data alone. In June 2024, it began offering the ransomware to affiliates, a model known as ransomware-as-a-service.
What Remains Open
Eurojust said the authorities taking part "successfully shut down a ransomware group" and will now continue their investigation. Hamburg police said inquiries into other possible members continue.
Investigators are examining the seized devices and data and tracing the group's money, including cryptocurrency. The evidence may identify more victims, attacks and suspects.

articles.title: A man could face a decade in prison for a fake crocodile photo he made with Gemini
articles.text:
WTF?! Some people love to generate AI slop images that spread false information, especially the kind that make people worry. That's not a good idea if you're in Singapore, where a man who used Gemini to make a fake image of a crocodile in a popular reservoir has been charged over the act and could face up to ten years in prison.
Ye Lin allegedly sent the AI-generated image of a saltwater crocodile at Pandan Reservoir to a colleague in August, presumably as a joke.
But the image led to a crocodile sighting being reported to Singapore's national water agency, PUB. The agency and national parks staff suspended all aquatic activities in the area for two days and started looking for a crocodile that didn't exist in the popular kayaking spot.
The following day, the agency confirmed that the image was a fake and reported it to the police, leading to Lin's arrest.
Singapore takes this sort of thing very seriously. Transmitting a false message is a crime that carries up to three years in prison, a fine of up to S$10,000 (about $7,800), or both.
If that wasn't bad enough, police say Lin tried to hide what he'd done by deleting the image and the Gemini app from his phone. Unfortunately for him, that meant he's also being charged with obstruction of justice, the punishment for which is up to seven years in prison.
It's still not clear how PUB officials were notified of the AI photo. It could be that the person Lin sent it to then forwarded it to someone else who thought it was real.
It doesn't sound like Lin was intentionally trying to start a panic with the image, but Singapore isn't ranked as one of the safest countries in the world because it has a lenient justice system.
Ye said he intends to plead guilty and will not be using a lawyer. His case will be heard again in November.
In the US, generating legal images like these isn't going to result in a potential decade-long jail sentence, though a fabricated image supporting a credible false claim about a bombing or other specified serious offense may fall under federal hoax law. If it really was a crime, a lot of social media users would probably be locked up.

articles.title: AI agents inadvertently leak 13,000+ internal screenshots from 300 organizations — list of companies includes Fortune 500 and a frontier AI lab
articles.text:
AI agents inadvertently leak 13,000+ internal screenshots from 300 organizations — list of companies includes Fortune 500 and a frontier AI lab
When agents are too clever for their own good.
There's a private information leak most days, usually by way of misconfigured services or nasty security bugs. Sometimes, though, users will readily hand over private information without being aware of it. That's the case for over 300 organizations, including several Fortune 500 companies and a frontier AI lab, who collectively had 13,000+ private screenshots exposed — all thanks to their development AI agents being arguably too good at their jobs and performing them with little human oversight.
Besides showing pictures of internal and pre-release software, the leaked screenshots reportedly include corporate and client information, financial data, and even screen recordings for a money-movement interface. The report, called PixelLeak, comes from endpoint security firm Glow, and it details how the leaks happened. The root cause is surprisingly simple and likely to induce a forehead slap.
It's become customary in development work related to UI and UX (and other categories) to include screenshots showing previews or before/after comparisons of tweaked features, for review purposes. Said images travel as attachments to the respective code changes, also known as "pull requests" (PRs) in dev parlance.
When using GitHub (and potentially other code repository services), humans see a graphical interface for easily attaching an image to a PR. Meanwhile, bots are limited to using the command-line interface, which currently does not have that feature available for private repositories.
As the efficient and smart agents they are, the clankers came up with a simple solution: publish the PR as usual to the private repository, and include an image placeholder linking to a file that's hosted in a public repository instead. There, problem fixed! The user is happy and likely has no idea what happened unless they notice the problem somehow and start asking the bot some hard questions.
Glow says that in about a third of the affected companies, developers were using gitshot, a command-line tool for attaching screenshots, used in this instance to overcome the aforementioned limitation. Searching for images attached by the tool is quite easy, as one needs but look for the "_gitshot" tag. The report also indicates that in 93% of cases, images were found in repositories under direct control of the developer's username, rather than being tied to the company's GitHub account.
In one particular case, an agent skill (essentially long-winded prompts instructing a bot how to do something) was also an indirect source of leaked information. The agents started incorporating the image hosting workaround as a skill, and after a while, many of them were using it for every development ticket, leading to leaks of information about features months away from public release.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
Glow provided sample reasoning output from an agent, explaining precisely why it uploaded the screenshots publicly:
"internal_sweeper is private, and GitHub cannot render images from a private repo in a PR description — its image proxy fetches anonymously, so anything committed here (branch, release asset, whatever) shows up broken for reviewers. The only way to satisfy both "reviewers see the images" and "nothing but index.html in the repo" was to host the PNGs elsewhere, so I created a new public repo, sweeper-demo/pr-assets, holding the two screenshots pinned to a commit SHA."
As mitigation measures, Glow first recommends checking that employees don't use repositories under their own accounts, auditing the accounts and code managed by employees no longer associated with the company, and curtailing the use of "shadow AI" — when employees unadvisedly sign up for their own AI tools without talking to IT first and neatly punch planet-sized holes in the firm's security and data privacy.
Additionally, Glow advises strong vetting of software and code libraries used for development, as well as careful reading of the instructions and rules of any agentic skills.
Follow Tom's Hardware on Google News, or add us as a preferred source, to get our latest news, analysis, & reviews in your feeds.
Bruno Ferreira is a contributing writer for Tom's Hardware. He has decades of experience with PC hardware and assorted sundries, alongside a career as a developer. He's obsessed with detail and has a tendency to ramble on the topics he loves. When not doing that, he's usually playing games, or at live music shows and festivals.

articles.title: Une campagne ClickFix détourne les GPT personnalisés de ChatGPT pour diffuser un malware
articles.text:
Des cybercriminels se servent désormais de GPT personnalisés pour alimenter une campagne ClickFix. Mis en avant dans des annonces Google, ces assistants conduisent les internautes vers de faux contrôles de sécurité qui les incitent à exécuter eux-mêmes la commande à l’origine de l’infection.
Cela devait bien finir par arriver. Les cybercriminels ont trouvé le moyen d’intégrer ChatGPT à leur chaîne d’infection sans compromettre la plateforme elle-même. Les chercheurs et chercheuses d’Huntress ont en effet identifié une nouvelle campagne ClickFix combinant résultats sponsorisés sur Google, GPT personnalisés hébergés sur le domaine officiel d’OpenAI et faux CAPTCHA Cloudflare pour inciter les victimes à exécuter une commande PowerShell. À la clé, un cheval de Troie d’accès à distance installé sur Windows et un contrôle étendu de la machine pour les attaquants.
La solution tout-en-un pour protéger votre entreprise
Votre petite entreprise a de grandes ambitions. Protégez-là contre les pirates. Et développez sereinement votre activité !
De ChatGPT au RAT, une chaîne d’infection bien huilée
Dans le détail, le vecteur d’infection repose sur un GPT baptisé « Plus 5.6 », promu par l’intermédiaire de résultats sponsorisés sur Google. Hébergé sur chatgpt.com comme n’importe quel GPT personnalisé, il profite du domaine officiel d’OpenAI pour inspirer confiance, avant de prétexter des difficultés rencontrées par le service principal et d’orienter l’internaute vers un prétendu site de secours hébergé sur Google Sites.
La page de redirection affiche alors un faux contrôle anti-bot aux couleurs de Cloudflare et, comme dans toute attaque ClickFix qui se respecte, présente l’exécution d’une commande PowerShell comme nécessaire pour accéder au service promis. Lancée par la victime elle-même, cette commande récupère un fichier MSI qui amorce l’installation du malware, sans qu’aucune faille de ChatGPT ait besoin d’être exploitée.
Le programme d’installation dépose ensuite plusieurs composants sur la machine, parmi lesquels un exécutable légitime signé par Canon ou, selon les variantes, par Stardock, que les pirates détournent pour lui faire charger une DLL malveillante, point de départ d’une série de composants chiffrés exécutés en mémoire pour limiter les traces sur le disque et compliquer la détection de l’infection jusqu’au lancement du RAT.
Le cheval de Troie donne alors aux attaquants un accès très large à la machine : contrôle du bureau à distance, recherche de fichiers, reconnaissance du système, capture audio et vidéo ou encore exécution de charges supplémentaires. Pour survivre aux redémarrages, il crée une entrée dans le Registre Windows et une tâche planifiée, baptisées « Canon Configuration Reader » dans un cas et « Stardock DeElevation Tool » dans l’autre.
Huntress a relié au moins 40 incidents à la page utilisée dans cette campagne, mais seuls deux ont formellement pu être rattachés à un GPT personnalisé. OpenAI avait supprimé le premier GPT signalé par les chercheurs le 25 septembre ; deux jours plus tard, Huntress en repérait un second associé à la même opération.
Des indices qui permettent de déjouer l’attaque
On le rappellera encore et toujours : une vérification web se déroule dans le navigateur. Elle peut impliquer de cocher une case, de sélectionner des images ou d’attendre quelques secondes, mais certainement pas d’ouvrir PowerShell (ni l’invite de commandes, ni la boîte Exécuter de Windows) pour y copier-coller une commande et la valider. Le cas échéant, quittez la page.
Si vous cherchez un GPT pour une tâche précise, passez directement par la recherche intégrée à ChatGPT plutôt que par une annonce sponsorisée dans Google. Le GPT Store permet de consulter son nom, sa description et les informations disponibles sur son créateur avant de l’ouvrir.
La présence d’un GPT dans le store du chatbot IA ne garantit pas non plus la fiabilité de ses instructions. Les GPT personnalisés sont créés par des tiers et peuvent légitimement renvoyer vers des sites extérieurs, mais s’ils vous demandent de toucher directement au système, interrompez immédiatement la procédure.
Si la commande a déjà été exécutée, fermer l’onglet ne suffira pas. Déconnectez le PC du réseau, lancez une analyse complète avec une solution de sécurité à jour et changez, depuis un appareil sain, les identifiants sensibles utilisés sur la machine.

articles.title: The Hidden Challenges of Edge AI Design
articles.text:
As models evolve faster than silicon cycles, chip architects must balance flexible compute, data movement, and defense-in-depth security.
Key Takeaways:
The rapid buildout of the edge is forcing chip architects and design teams to rethink how they add AI to vertical market applications. The fundamental challenge is a mismatch in timelines, because engineering teams must design for AI models, workloads, and deployment requirements that inevitably will shift long after silicon decisions are locked in.
Compounding this, real-world edge performance rarely depends on peak NPU TOPS. More often, it depends on memory bandwidth, latency, power budgets, security, and data movement. To keep pace with evolving models, architects are leaning heavily into flexibility — embracing heterogeneous compute, programmable data paths, expandable memory, secure field updates, and tight hardware-software co-design.
But flexibility alone isn’t enough. AI introduces broad attack vectors across models, data, keys, firmware, and inference pipelines, so robust security must be architected into hardware from day one. At the same time, fragmented toolchains across runtimes and frameworks make hardware-aware optimization just as important as raw compute.
This structural shift is redefining standard component boundaries.
“CPUs are becoming more GPU-like as they try to do more and more parallel processing,” observed Rob Fisher, senior director of product management at Imagination Technologies. “NPUs are becoming more GPU-like as they try to become more flexible, and the convergence point is with the CPU, NPU, and GPU in the middle. We’re finding more customers are trying to hedge their bets against the future than trying to squeeze out every last drop of performance today. That means we’re no longer just looking at a GPU you can slot in that just does GPU-like things. This has system-level impacts on the whole SoC.”
When designing edge applications with AI as a product feature, chip architects and design teams have many considerations. Hardware choices drive these broader architectural decisions, but the challenge reaches well beyond NPU TOPs.
“AI model performance depends on architectural details for memory, latency, power, and security,” said Eduardo Montanez, vice president and head of PSOC Edge MCUs & Edge AI Solutions for Infineon’s IoT, Compute & Wireless Business. This is why the company’s edge microcontrollers include memory expandability, a low-latency architecture, and energy efficiency to enable battery-powered applications at the edge. They also include security features that are designed to protect data and software IP.
AI applications at the edge are already challenging chip architects and design teams to keep up with rapid changes in models and workloads.
“As new networks are continually popping up, any solution needs to be programmable to accommodate new networks and ever-changing activation functions and corresponding data types,” said George Wall, product marketing group director at Cadence. “At the same time, there are hard performance requirements that must also be met.”
This makes hardware-software co-design increasingly important. “AI models, NPUs, memory hierarchy, and optimization techniques such as quantization, pruning, and distillation must be jointly optimized to achieve efficient deployment,” noted Niranjan Sitapure, group product manager for generative AI at Siemens EDA.
The entire pipeline also must be optimized, because success depends on sensor ingestion, data preprocessing, inference, post-processing, and ongoing model lifecycle management.
Ideally, chip architects and design teams would have a detailed view of what an edge application will do, including the models it will use, required performance, available memory, and power constraints, so they can design a chip for optimal PPA.
“Unfortunately, that isn’t reality,” said Paul Karazuba, vice president of marketing, Silicon IP at Rambus. “Even compressed, the chip design cycle will predate the release of any product that contains the chip by a year or more. During that time, it’s reasonable to assume the edge application will evolve, including changes to the underlying model(s) and perhaps the available memory and power. This application evolution forces chip designers to concentrate their efforts on creating chips that can adapt to changing requirements, including but not limited to a focus on moving data efficiently and securely.”
For others, AI acceleration isn’t the biggest challenge. What limits chip performance and efficiency may depend on the rest of the application.
“But architects and designers don’t design for that. They focus on neural network acceleration, claiming very high but theoretical TOPS numbers that no real application even comes close to achieving,” said Graham Gobieski, chief technology officer and co-founder of Efficient Computer. “In fact, in many real workloads (e.g., sensor fusion, autonomy), a majority of the application still runs on whatever general-purpose but very inefficient core exists on the SoC. The real opportunity to enable intelligent applications isn’t a faster NPU; it’s making the other 80% of the application as efficient as the AI portion.”
Beyond efficiency, edge AI applications add numerous design challenges.
Core design challenges
Performance depends on more than the compute capabilities of the programmable processor being used. “For example, memory bandwidth must be sufficient to keep the computational units fed with data, and the data needs to be in a location that is easily accessible by the processor,” explained Cadence’s Wall. “Otherwise, the computational elements will basically sit underutilized. Determining workload requirements is difficult because chip designers won’t necessarily have insight into the networks consumers will be running 3 or 5 years from now.”
This challenge is compounded by the fact that edge AI is fundamentally a constraint-driven design problem. “You are dealing with tight power budgets, limited memory, mixed sensor inputs, and latency expectations that users feel immediately. The architecture has to be efficient before it can be intelligent,” Rambus’ Karazuba said.
As AI models evolve rapidly, system architectures need memory scalability for large data sets and AI models, along with enough memory for the non-AI portions of a design.
“Also, the design must allow for end-to-end, secure provisioning and deployment, allowing for field updates without compromising valuable data and software IP,” Infineon’s Montanez noted.
Moving model weights and activations between DRAM and compute engines can consume more power than the AI computation itself. “AI models evolve faster than silicon development cycles. New architectures, operators, and generative AI workloads emerge continuously, creating pressure for hardware platforms to remain adaptable,” Siemens’ Sitapure said. “For critical/high-risk applications, edge systems such as ADAS, industrial automation, and robotics require predictable latency, high reliability, and operation even with limited connectivity.”
While data movement can dominate performance and efficiency, other challenges may be overlooked. “The first is simple but challenging,” said Efficient Computer’s Gobieski. “The intelligence has to fit on the device. This means a lot of engineering goes into squeezing a neural network into on-device memory before any application code runs. The second has a standard answer that backfires. Splitting the application across an NPU, CPU, and DSP might seem like playing to each block’s strengths, but it complicates development by requiring many different toolchains, and it spends the savings moving data between them.”
Hardware teams also face non-negotiable physical constraints, especially strict low-power budgets. Thermal dissipation limits and battery constraints dictate computational efficiency, along with demanding reliability requirements for mission- and safety-critical edge deployments, Sylvain Guilley, co-founder and chief technology officer at Secure-IC, a Cadence company, noted. “Solving these core challenges requires moving beyond proprietary, siloed hardware tricks toward broader industry-wide alignment on architectural standards. To build standard open framework specifications for edge hardware, Cadence is tackling this in a new OCP FCSA Sub-Project Workstream.”
Security from the start
Electronics developers looking to add AI to edge devices should incorporate several security technologies from the beginning of system design.
The starting point is a secure platform, followed by a secure application. “A secure platform is fundamental,” said Dana Neustadter, senior director of product management for security solutions at Synopsys. “It establishes the foundation, but it does not automatically make the application — or the AI’s output — trustworthy. Developers must still address authorization, data protection, output validation, connected-service security, and component assurance at the application layer. Assume the AI platform already provides a root of trust, secure boot, attestation, encrypted communications, and trusted execution environments. That establishes the foundation, but it does not automatically make the application — or the AI’s output — trustworthy.”
At the application layer, Neustadter said developers must address additional controls, including:
A common misconception is that an AI result must be trustworthy simply because the AI runs on a secure platform. Consider a mobile robot whose model reports that a hallway is empty. If the software accepts that result without further checks, the robot could move and collide with an unexpected obstacle. “The AI provides an input to the decision. It should not be the sole basis for the final decision,” Neustadter explained. “The application should evaluate the model’s confidence score and complete additional checks before authorizing an action. It should also apply relevant rules and safety policies and confirm the environment before the device acts.”
Establishing a resilient platform also does not guarantee privacy. Secure hardware does not compensate for insecure application-level data handling. For example, a smart camera in a mall may analyze shopper behavior. Even if the device is secure, storing those analytics in an unencrypted database could let an attacker access private customer information.
“Secure hardware does not compensate for insecure application-level data handling. Developers should encrypt sensitive data and enforce access controls throughout its lifecycle. They should also retain data only as long as necessary and limit its use to authorized people and services,” she said.
Models should also be authenticated with controls comparable to secure boot. Before loading a model, the system should verify its identity, integrity, signature, and provenance. This is another reason a strong root of trust is essential. “Model confidentiality and access control should also be incorporated into the system’s key-management strategy,” Neustadter explained.
Edge AI systems may require additional keys. A third-party model provider, for example, may want to prevent the device owner or other parties from accessing the model without authorization. Model confidentiality and access control, therefore, become part of the overall key-management strategy.
All models and components can introduce software supply-chain risks. Developers often rely on open-source models, AI engines, plugins, and other external components. A model that contains a hidden backdoor can generate incorrect or malicious outputs, and secure hardware may still execute it if the system accepts the model as trusted.
“Secure hardware will still execute a compromised model if the system accepts it as trusted. To reduce the risk, developers should therefore verify provenance and integrity, validate suppliers, use trusted repositories, and maintain software bills of materials,” Neustadter added.
When designing security into edge applications and mitigating attack vectors introduced by AI, engineering leadership should involve high-level product management as early as possible. That allows developers to perform risk analysis and determine where mitigations are needed across both hardware interfaces and software layers, Cadence’s Guilley said.
“This early architectural grounding directly informs overall device strategy in terms of cyber-resiliency,” he noted. [“Establishing this foundation early] allows us to treat cybersecurity not as a cost but as an investment that enables subsequent operations to unfold safely 24/7 and to turn incidents away from emergencies and rather have them be seen as a business continuity plan.”
This unified security and governance framework becomes especially important when engineering complex cyber-physical systems that must comply with cybersecurity, AI, and data privacy mandates.
“Design teams must continuously navigate strict regulatory boundaries, specifically around the E.U. Cyber Resilience Act, statutory requirements concerning capturing personal data in personally identifiable information, and the overarching statutory mandates enforced under the broader E.U. AI Act,” Guilley said.
A root of trust and separation between secure and non-secure code are also important. “Having a bootloader that manages code authentication is critical,” Infineon’s Montanez said. “With AI moving to the edge, most products still have a hybrid approach with the cloud, allowing for OTA or other communication. Therefore, edge AI applications can require additional security for the connectivity link.”
Big picture, security must be anchored in hardware, from secure boot and trusted firmware to protected keys, memory, and model assets. AI increases the stakes because models, inputs, and outputs can all have significant economic value.
“One should consider that economic value is not just the models themselves or the data inside those models, but also the financial and legal implications of a third party tampering with that data,” Karazuba noted.
Introducing AI into an edge device adds capabilities and features that were often unavailable in prior non-AI-enabled versions. “Device makers must design AI-enabled edge devices with a stronger security profile, given the increased financial and legal implications of a security breach,” he said.
Encryption is another key element, Siemens’ Sitapure said. Model weights, training data, and inference pipelines should be encrypted and protected from tampering, extraction, and unauthorized access.
Above all, security cannot be an afterthought. “Malicious actors could try to hack the underlying model weights and insert their own model that disrupts subsystem operation or exploits other security vulnerabilities in the system,” Cadence’s Wall said. “Fortunately, approaches range from localized encryption/decryption engines to a dedicated security island.”
More broadly, the most dangerous failure in edge AI is not a crash, but a live system that keeps operating while silently believing the wrong state. Real-time decisions increasingly depend on the integrity of on-device inference because edge AI is deployed in cameras, robotics, vehicles, and industrial systems that rely on NPUs, GPUs, and TPUs for performance and efficiency, but are not typically designed to ensure inference integrity under fault conditions.
In a recent white paper that includes the experimental block diagram and physical setup used for fault injection and measurement, Keysight security researchers showed that precisely timed fault injection (FI) can corrupt the output of a production-class edge AI pipeline without modifying firmware, model weights, software configuration, or input data. On a commercial Rockchip RK3568 platform running YOLOv5s_ReLU, most faults had no observable effect or only shifted confidence scores, but a smaller fraction induced missed detections, phantom objects, and rare high-confidence misclassifications while the system continued to operate normally. The impact can reach beyond individual inference errors. When corrupted detector outputs feed downstream tracking systems, even brief or low-probability errors can be filtered as transient noise, latched into persistent tracked objects, or amplified into denser and longer-lived false system states.
In the observed sequences, repeated, bounded faults transformed transient detector errors into sustained false perceptions that persisted beyond the original fault window. Once represented as system state, these errors can influence alerts, automation logic, and operator decisions while the platform appears healthy, which has implications for product teams. Here, traditional measures of resilience, such as uptime or fault recovery, may be insufficient for AI-driven systems. Resilience also must include inference integrity and the ability to prevent corrupted outputs from becoming trusted system state.
At the same time, decentralizing compute offers a foundational safety advantage in some applications, reducing how much sensitive information can leave the device. “Running inference on the device means sensitive data never travels, so there is no communication channel to intercept, and decentralized processing means there is no central repository of sensitive data to breach,” Efficient Computer’s Gobieski said. “A compromise costs you one device, not the fleet. The model itself carries the usual concerns about what it exposes, but those are far smaller than the ones you eliminate by keeping the data on the device.”
Conclusion
Navigating the edge AI landscape requires a mindset shift for engineering teams. Success no longer hinges just on maximizing theoretical peak compute, but on balancing silicon longevity with rapid software evolution. By prioritizing flexible architectures, hardware-software co-design, and defense-in-depth security from day one, chip designers can build resilient platforms that adapt to whatever AI workloads emerge — even after the chip architecture is finalized.

articles.title: PCBA Test Strategies to Select the Right Methodology and Tester - EE Times
articles.text:
In the competitive landscape of electronics manufacturing, the pursuit of zero defects is the ultimate objective. A single malfunctioning Printed Circuit Board Assembly (PCBA) can lead to expensive recalls, damaged brand reputation, and significant safety risks. To ensure high-quality, reliable electronic products, manufacturers must deploy a robust validation strategy.
But how do you choose the right testing methodology when the options, In-Circuit Testing (ICT), Functional Testing (FCT), Bed-of-Nails, and Flying Probe, can be complex to navigate? In this article, we will break down testing pillars and explore how integrating them can streamline your production line.
1. The Core Distinction: ICT and Functional Testing
The debate of In-Circuit Testing versus Functional Testing often frames them as competitors, but the reality is that they are complementary approaches of a successful quality program.
In-Circuit Testing (ICT) acts as the foundational auditor of your PCBA. By probing individual components and interconnections, it confirms electrical continuity, detects shorts or opens, and validates crucial values like resistance and capacitance. ICT focuses on identifying manufacturing defects early in the cycle, such as soldering errors, component misplacement, or faulty parts, effectively answering the question of “how well it was built.”
Functional Testing (FCT) takes a holistic view. It evaluates the integrated performance of the entire PCBA under simulated operating conditions, assessing parameters like voltage regulation, current draw, power factor, and operational cycles. By answering the critical question of “does it work as intended”, FCT identifies design flaws and integration bottlenecks.
In large-scale production, ICT should always be performed before FCT. Using ICT as an initial quality gate to filter out assembly defects prevents manufacturers from wasting time and resources on boards that are destined to fail the more expensive Functional Test.
2. Choosing The Automatic Tester: Bed-of-Nails or Flying Probe
Once you understand what to test, you must determine how to test. The equipment choice usually boils down to two main technologies: Bed-of-Nails and Flying Probe.
Bed-of-Nails testers utilize a fixed matrix of spring-loaded pins that make contact with specific test points on the PCBA. Because the fixture is custom-made for the board, this method allows for the simultaneous testing of multiple points, offering exceptional speed and throughput. This makes Bed-of-Nails testers the superior choice for high-volume, mature products where the initial investment in the test fixture is offset by significant long-term efficiency.
Flying Probe testers operate differently, utilizing movable probes that “fly” to designated test points across the board surface. Since no custom fixtures are required, this method significantly lowers initial setup costs and allows for rapid adaptation to design changes or prototypes. This technology is best suited for complex boards where test pads are limited or inaccessible to fixed pins.
However, choosing the right test equipment must account for these fundamental pillars of modern PCBA testing requirements:
- Test Point Availability
Test point placement and mechanical access determine whether an ICT tester can physically and electrically reach every node it is meant to verify. This is a Design for Testability (DFT) decision made months before the board ever reaches the test floor, and it dictates which architecture is even viable: Bed-of-Nails testers need dedicated, fixed-position test pads laid out during design, while Flying Probe testers can reach arbitrary points and tolerate less generous test point provisioning.
- Accessibility in High-Density Boards
As the push toward miniaturization continues, dedicated test pads are disappearing from board layouts. Traditional Bed-of-Nails Testers, which rely on a fixed pin matrix, often prove structurally inadequate for these dense designs. When high-density designs make test pads inaccessible, Flying Probe Testers become essential.
Because they do not require custom fixtures, they offer the agility to probe arbitrary points on a board.
- Test Pad Integrity
The interface between your testing hardware and the PCBA is the most sensitive point of the process. Inadequately modulated contact force can result in irreversible mechanical damage, such as micro-abrasions that trigger latent failures, or false negatives due to poor connectivity. High-reliability manufacturing demands precision landing force control. Modern ATE platforms, such as those from SPEA, use
high-speed linear motors that provide a “soft touch” interaction. These systems employ predictive algorithms to map the board layout, preventing probe collisions and ensuring that the structural integrity of the delicate substrate remains uncompromised.
- Latent Defect Detection
Standard electrical continuity tests often fail to identify “insidious” faults—such as signal integrity degradation or parametric drift—that pass initial inspection but cause field failures later. To reach zero-defect targets, your hardware architecture must support a multi-domain diagnostic approach. This involves integrating Parametric ICT with AI-driven analysis. By analyzing whether a component is trending toward failure—where a part is “within spec” today but drifting toward failure tomorrow—and using dynamic defect databases to automate diagnostics, you shift from reactive testing to predictive reliability engineering.
3. The Synergistic Approach: Integrating Test Methodologies
The most efficient PCBA validation strategy isn’t about choosing one method; it’s about leveraging the respective strengths of all. In demanding sectors like automotive, aerospace, and defense, where reliability is non-negotiable, manufacturers are increasingly adopting integrated workflows and testers.
The true power of this strategy lies in synergy. By combining ICT and FCT, you secure comprehensive fault coverage, capturing granular assembly faults and system-level design flaws in a single pass. Furthermore, there is significant strategic value in orchestrating Bed-of-Nails and Flying Probe technologies within the same test cycle. These systems work together to optimize the testing workload efficiently.
For instance, a Flying Probe test station is ideal for checking components inaccessible to the Bed-of-Nails fixture, performing optical inspections, or executing net tests on prototypes. Once those specific validations are complete, the PCBA can move to a Bed-of-Nails station for high-throughput power-on testing, firmware flashing, and functional validation. This collaborative approach maximizes test efficiency, ensures 100% coverage, and allows manufacturers to capitalize on the strengths of both systems, the flexibility of Flying Probe and the high-volume speed of Bed-of-Nails, without sacrificing throughput.
4. Path to Manufacturing Excellence
Achieving zero defects in PCBA manufacturing requires understanding the distinct roles of ICT and FCT, and by integrating Bed-of-Nails for high-volume stability and Flying Probe for flexibility, production lines are optimized for both quality and speed.
An effective testing strategy requires a thorough analysis of production volume and product lifecycle. By aligning throughput requirements with integrated testing workflows, manufacturers can implement a proactive quality gate, ensuring that assembly-related defects are mitigated prior to final validation.
If you are facing bottlenecks in your current testing workflow, we invite you to contact SPEA Engineering Team for a consultation on your PCBA testing strategy.

articles.title: Wer haftet, wenn die KI ausbricht? Diese Klage gegen OpenAI soll es klären
articles.text:
Wer haftet, wenn die KI ausbricht? Diese Klage gegen OpenAI soll das jetzt klären
Nach dem Angriff auf Hugging Face hat eine gemeinnützige Organisation aus Kalifornien Klage gegen OpenAI eingereicht. Sie will das Unternehmen für die Handlungen seiner KI-Agenten rechtlich verantwortlich machen. Die Organisation fordert keinen Schadenersatz. Stattdessen soll das Gericht OpenAI untersagen, KI-Agenten zu entwickeln, die andere Systeme eigenständig hacken können. Die Klage fällt in eine Zeit, in der die Forderungen nach strengerer KI-Regulierung lauter werden – auch von Unternehmen, die diese Systeme selbst entwickeln und bereitstellen.
KI-Agenten von OpenAI entkamen ihrer Testumgebung
Im Juli erregte der Hacking-Angriff auf die Open-Source-Plattform Hugging Face viel Aufmerksamkeit und löste eine Welle weiterer Vorfallsmeldungen aus. Ursprünglich hatte OpenAI die Leistungsfähigkeit neuer Modelle testen wollen. Trotz Isolation hätten die Agenten eine Zero-Day-Schwachstelle aufspüren, sich weitreichendere Rechte einräumen und eine Schnittstelle zum Internet ausnutzen können. Mit mehreren aufeinanderfolgenden Angriffen hätten sie sich anschließend Zugang zu den Systemen von Hugging Face verschafft.
Auf der Black-Hat-Konferenz erklärten zwei OpenAI-Mitarbeiter die Vorgehensweise der Agenten. Demnach gehe der Vorfall auf ein kooperatives Message-Board zurück. Fand ein Agent eine Schwachstelle, teilte er sie dort, damit andere Agenten sie ebenfalls ausnutzen konnten. Am Ende habe das Forum Hunderttausende Nachrichten umfasst. Die Agenten hätten sogar begonnen, sich gegenseitig Aufgaben zuzuweisen. Nach Bekanntwerden des Vorfalls folgten weitere Meldungen. So räumte auch der Konkurrent Anthropic ein, dass seine Modelle aus der Testumgebung ausbrechen und andere Systeme angreifen konnten.
OpenAI wegen Hugging-Face-Angriffs verklagt
Die Rechtsorganisation Legal Advocates for Safe Science and Technology (LASST) hat gemeinsam mit der Anwaltskanzlei Gerstein Harrow die Klage beim kalifornischen Superior Court in San Francisco eingereicht, wo das KI-Unternehmen seinen Hauptsitz hat. „Die Handlungen von OpenAI verstießen eindeutig gegen kalifornisches Recht“, heißt es in der Klageschrift. „Wir halten es für äußerst wichtig, dass bestehende Gesetze durchgesetzt werden, um KI-Unternehmen für den von ihnen verursachten Schaden zur Rechenschaft zu ziehen“, erklärte Tyler Whitmer von LASST gegenüber Wired. „Wir betrachten dies als eine offensichtliche, extrem riskante Entwicklung in einer Welt, die noch sehr neu ist.“
Ein:e OpenAI-Sprecher:in erklärte gegenüber Wired, die Klage sei „völlig unbegründet“, bezeichnete den Angriff aber gleichzeitig als „schwerwiegenden Vorfall“. Eigenen Angaben zufolge habe OpenAI daraufhin „eine Reihe von Maßnahmen ergriffen“. Inzwischen setzt sich das Unternehmen selbst für eine stärkere Regulierung ein. So forderte das Global-Affairs-Team in einem Linkedin-Post, den Gesetzentwurf SB 53 nachzuschärfen. Bei einer Verabschiedung müssten Entwickler:innen von Pioniermodellen Sicherheitsrahmenwerke etablieren und vor dem Einsatz Sicherheitsberichte veröffentlichen. Zuvor hatte OpenAI den Gesetzentwurf noch abgelehnt.
Risiko agentischer KI tritt in den Vordergrund
Viele empfinden die bisherige Regulierung als unangemessen. „Nachdem der Vorfall bei Hugging Face bekannt wurde, haben wir tatsächlich viel Arbeit investiert, um Regulierungsbehörden und zivilgesellschaftliche Organisationen über den Hack aufzuklären. Und wir haben uns gefragt: Wird irgendjemand vor Gericht etwas dagegen unternehmen?“, so Whitmer gegenüber Wired. „Es gibt strukturelle Gründe, warum wir glauben, dass Hugging Face – das eigentlich der naheliegende potenzielle Kläger wäre – nichts unternimmt. Da es also nicht so aussah, als würde sonst jemand etwas unternehmen, haben wir die Initiative ergriffen. Wenn diese Systeme weiter skalieren und die Dinge immer verrückter werden, könnte KI wirklich katastrophale Schäden anrichten.“

articles.title: The JOJOLands tome 8 : où trouver l’édition collector de JoJo's Bizarre Adventure
articles.text:
Après Phantom Blood, Battle Tendency, Stardust Crusaders, Diamond is Unbreakable, Golden Wind, Stone Ocean, Steel Ball Run et JoJolion — – vous suivez ? – — Hirohiko Araki poursuit son immense saga JoJo’s Bizarre Adventure avec The JOJOLands. Lancée au Japon en 2023, cette neuvième partie suit Jodio et Dragona Joestar dans une nouvelle aventure, toujours peuplée de Stands et de situations complètement improbables. En France, le septième tome est sorti en juin 2026, et le huitième est désormais attendu pour le 26 novembre 2026 chez Delcourt/Tonkam.
Pour accompagner la sortie du huitième volume, Delcourt/Tonkam propose une édition collector au prix de 14,99 €, contre 8,50 € pour l’édition classique. Cette version spéciale contiendra, dans un fourreau exclusif, le manga ainsi qu’un standee en acrylique (une figurine plate imprimée, qui tient debout grâce à un petit support) représentant Jodio Joestar, le protagoniste de The JOJOLands. Voici où la précommander :
C’est quoi, cette édition spéciale du tome 8 de The JOJOLands ?
L’édition spéciale du tome 8 de The JOJOLands reprend le manga dans son édition classique et y ajoute un bonus consacré à Jodio Joestar, le protagoniste de cette neuvième partie de JoJo’s Bizarre Adventure. Il s’agit d’une figurine plate en acrylique, à poser sur une étagère. L’ensemble est vendu dans un fourreau exclusif.
Dans The JOJOLands, neuvième partie de JoJo’s Bizarre Adventure, Jodio Joestar et sa sœur Dragona vivent à Hawaï, où ils se retrouvent impliqués dans une affaire de cambriolage autour d’un mystérieux diamant. Au tome 7, la bande de Jodio passait à l’étape finale de son plan : s’emparer de toute la fortune de Howler. Le tome 8 poursuit donc cette opération, alors que Jodio et ses alliés doivent composer avec les nombreux obstacles qui se dressent sur leur route.
À ce prix, cette édition spéciale de The JOJOLands vaut-elle le coup ?
À 14,99 €, cette édition spéciale de The JOJOLands peut surtout se justifier si vous êtes déjà fan de JoJo’s Bizarre Adventure. Delcourt/Tonkam ne sort pas d’édition avec bonus pour chaque tome de la série. Celle-ci permet donc de joindre un petit objet de collection au manga. Le bonus à l’effigie de Jodio n’est évidemment pas indispensable pour lire l’histoire, mais il peut facilement trouver sa place sur une étagère aux côtés des autres volumes de la série. Si vous suivez The JOJOLands au fil de sa publication française, ces 6,49 € de plus que l’édition classique vous offrent une version un peu plus originale pour votre collection.
D’autant que The JOJOLands mérite largement qu’on s’y intéresse. Cette neuvième partie transporte l’univers de JoJo à Hawaï, où Jodio Joestar et son grand frère Dragona se retrouvent impliqués dans une affaire de vol de diamant qui va, comme toujours chez Hirohiko Araki, rapidement partir dans une direction totalement improbable.
