articles.title: Amazon releases its own Jev clone as decision models flood the web | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Amazon Web Services released an open source decision model inspired by TypeSafe’s Jev, with AI developers increasingly seeking intelligence that is more suited to computer automation than frontier LLMs.
Amazon’s Strands Decider 2B, released the same week OpenAI announced a similar offering, is a high-speed, low-cost way to sort between pre-decided options and deliver a measure of how confident it is in its choice. The model is fully open sourced, available now, and small enough to run locally.
Amazon distinguished engineer Marc Brooker came up with the project after seeing Jev and trying to build his own take on such a model. The homebrew project was successful enough — it briefly reached the top spot on the Jevbench ranking for models of its size — that Amazon engineers cleaned it up and released it as an offering from their Strands Labs, an organization developing new tools and protocols for deploying AI agents.
Brooker says the need for a tool like this emerged in conversations with AWS customers, whose agentic workflows didn’t always require the capability or cost of a fully featured LLM all the time.
“What originally piqued my interest in this class of models was that they make a perfect decider for a workflow step — ‘what is the next thing for me to do here, based on where I am?’” Brooker told TechCrunch. He said it offers customers “a workflow step that can be structured in a way that is more reliable, thanks to the confidence scores, thanks to the closed domain of answers, [and is] lower latency, potentially lower cost.”
Like other decision models, Strands Decider is built on the “torso” of an LLM, in this case Qwen3.5-2B, but instead of generating text, it delivers calibrated choices. TypeSafe named their model Jev after the economist William Stanley Jevons, with hopes of invoking his theory that the falling cost of something — like computer intelligence — can, in fact, increase its demand.
The fact that dozens of similar models have been produced by researchers since TypeSafe debuted its idea shows the wide interest, but also raises the question of how valuable they can be. Brooker suggests that the challenge will be in optimizing the model’s speedy decision-making without compromising its intelligence.
“There is a very careful balance to be found where you want to push its performance on accuracy and calibration on these kinds of tasks, without degrading its performance on understanding different languages, on having the kind of knowledge it has, which is what makes it general purpose and interesting and useful,” he told TechCrunch.
Still, he doesn’t necessarily expect the frontier labs to dominate the space, especially since, with smaller markets, the cost to build something interesting is in the hundreds or thousands of dollars.
For their part, TypeSafe executives say they are keeping their heads down and improving future models.
“I get that people think it’s a gold rush, but they might be underestimating the difficulty of making the models actually smart,” CEO and founder Diogo Almeida told TechCrunch, saying that for now, he didn’t see real competition for his company emerging yet.
“The current batch seems more like ML people wanting to implement a cool architecture than a team deeply dedicated to making intelligence useful.”

Veja os destaques do Olhar Digital News desta quinta-feira (01/10).
Aconteceu de novo: agentes de IA tentaram invadir site do governo do Canadá
A empresa de pesquisa em inteligência artificial Transluce revelou que agentes de IA tentaram acessar um site ligado ao governo do Canadá. As investidas ocorreram em 28 de maio e 9 de junho, sem indicação de que os sistemas públicos tenham sido comprometidos.
Redes sociais são vistas como ameaça à democracia, revela pesquisa
Um número crescente de pessoas acredita que as redes sociais manipulam e dividem a população. É o que revela uma pesquisa do Pew Research Center divulgada nesta quinta-feira (01). Segundo o levantamento, cidadãos de países mais ricos tendem a ter uma percepção pior das plataformas.
SpaceX lança chips de IA do Google em teste para futuros data centers espaciais
A SpaceX lançou, nesta quinta-feira (01), um protótipo de satélite equipado com chips de inteligência artificial do Google. O dispositivo foi enviado à órbita a bordo de um foguete Falcon 9 durante a missão Transporter-18, realizada a partir da Base da Força Espacial de Vandenberg, na Califórnia.
NASA e SpaceX lançam astronautas à Estação Espacial Internacional
A NASA e a SpaceX lançaram nesta quinta-feira (01) a missão Crew-13. Com destino à Estação Espacial Internacional, ela decolou da Estação da Força Espacial de Cabo Canaveral, na Flórida, por volta de 12h11, pelo horário de Brasília.

articles.title: Pésimas noticias si querías un Galaxy S26: Samsung sube sus precios desde hoy
Small Electronics Manufacturers Save Big on ERP - EE Times
articles.text:
Instead of spending large sums and years implementing a traditional ERP system, small and medium-sized electronics manufacturers are finding that modern, SME-focused manufacturing software can provide the functionality they need at a fraction of the cost and implementation effort.
Cost-effective and easy to use
MRPeasy is a manufacturing ERP system designed specifically for small and medium-sized manufacturers. This focus sets it apart from systems that originated as accounting or inventory applications, as well as large enterprise ERP platforms that can require extensive consulting, customization, and IT resources.
For smaller electronics manufacturers, the difference in implementation effort can be substantial.
Poweronics, a power electronics manufacturer producing gate drivers for high-power applications, needed to manage around 1,200 components across its product portfolio. Managing Director Colin Hart self-implemented MRPeasy after starting a free trial.
“The implementation was very straightforward—setting up MRPeasy only took me about three hours,” Hart says. The setup included around 1,500 SKU lines as well as existing bills of materials and sales, purchase, and manufacturing orders.
Britannia 2000 Holdings, which manufactures mission computers, displays, airborne video recorders, and other electronics for the aerospace and defense industry, also implemented the system internally.
“I set it up myself and it was that easy,” says Director Ralph Jones.
Cost is often another major consideration.
Exacta Technologies currently uses MRPeasy across dozens of users and integrates it with systems including Xero and Grafana. Managing Director Chris Landen says the software continues to provide good value even as the company has grown.
“MRPeasy does a lot for what it costs,” he says. “There are systems that cost far more and don’t give you meaningfully better functionality.”
The functionality electronics manufacturers actually need
Affordability only matters if the system can handle the realities of electronics manufacturing.
Electronics companies commonly need to manage large numbers of components, multi-level BOMs and subassemblies, product revisions, long supplier lead times, subcontracted operations, serial and lot traceability, and rapidly changing material costs. Even relatively small manufacturers can therefore have highly complex operations.
Poweronics is a good example. Its approximately 1,200 components need to be coordinated across purchasing, inventory, BOMs, manufacturing orders, and customer demand. After implementing MRPeasy, the company gained much tighter control over inventory.
“We’ve never had a shortage after adopting MRPeasy,” Hart says.
This is particularly important in electronics manufacturing because one missing low-cost component can prevent an expensive finished product from being completed. Reliable inventory records combined with material requirements planning help manufacturers see what they have, what upcoming production will consume, and what needs to be purchased.
For Exacta Technologies, which manufactures custom hardware platforms and high-performance servers, product complexity has increased significantly as the company has grown. MRPeasy is used to manage multi-level and configurable BOMs together with revision and engineering change control, inventory, purchasing, and production planning.
“Our product set is large and complex,” Landen says. MRPeasy enables the company to manage complex BOMs, including their revisions and engineering changes.
Traceability is another key requirement for many electronics companies.
Britannia 2000 operates in aerospace and defense, where the ability to track materials and components through the production process is particularly important.
“With the software, I’m able to track components and achieve traceability throughout the order chain,” Founder Ralph Jones says.
For manufacturers combining internal production with outsourced processes, ERP also provides a way to keep subcontracting within the same production plan.
US-based Technodynamics manufactures explosion-proof LED lighting systems for hazardous environments. Its manufacturing processes involve BOMs, routings, inventory, subcontracting, material tracking, and production costing. The company uses MRPeasy to keep internal and outsourced operations within one manufacturing workflow.
“The more complicated your manufacturing process gets, the more MRPeasy makes sense,” says Senior Production Engineer Alfred Neufeld.
Better control without enterprise-level overhead
The attraction of SME-focused ERP is therefore not simply that it costs less. The goal is to provide enough manufacturing functionality to replace spreadsheets and disconnected tools without introducing another layer of unnecessary complexity.
For electronics manufacturers, this can mean having one system connecting:
- Complex bills of materials and product revisions
- Inventory and component availability
- Material requirements and purchasing
- Production planning and scheduling
- Manufacturing orders and shop-floor reporting
- Lot and serial number traceability
- Routings and subcontracted operations
- Production costs and product pricing
- Customer orders, quoting, and delivery dates
Having this information connected becomes increasingly valuable as a manufacturer grows.
Exacta Technologies originally moved away from a combination of accounting software and spreadsheets because manual processes were becoming difficult to scale. Today, MRPeasy provides the operational backbone for a substantially larger company.
“Since we started using MRPeasy, we have achieved over 100% growth in revenue,” Landen says. “And we have almost tripled our employee count from 25 to 70 without adding the same proportion of administrative overhead.”
This illustrates an important point for growing electronics SMEs: an ERP investment does not necessarily need to come after a company becomes large. Putting proper manufacturing processes in place earlier can make it easier to grow without continually adding spreadsheets, manual coordination, and administrative staff.
Survey shows significant improvements after implementation
MRPeasy’s latest customer survey shows that these individual electronics manufacturing experiences reflect broader trends among its manufacturing customers.
Respondents reported average improvements of:
- 58% in inventory tracking accuracy
- 46% in operational efficiency
- 46% in cost control
- 37% in on-time deliveries
- 28% in overall business growth
And importantly for SMEs, gaining that level of control no longer necessarily requires an enterprise-sized ERP project.
As KCL Manufacturing’s VP of Operations and Manufacturing, Jonathan Greenwald, puts it, MRPeasy provides “robust, value-driven ERP capabilities typically reserved for larger enterprises” while remaining suited to a growing manufacturer.
The experiences of Poweronics, Exacta Technologies, Britannia 2000, Technodynamics, and other electronics manufacturers point to the same conclusion: smaller companies can now access serious manufacturing ERP functionality without taking on the cost and complexity traditionally associated with enterprise systems.
To learn more, please visit mrpeasy.com

articles.title: Some Pixel owners can't unlock their phones after the latest update
articles.text:
What we know so far: A growing number of Pixel owners say the September 2026 update has left them unable to unlock their phones, even when they enter the correct PIN or pattern. The problem appears to be in the lock screen itself. Some users say their pattern resets after they connect one or two dots, making it impossible to finish the gesture. Others report that the phone reads the first digit of a PIN as a complete entry, then immediately says the PIN is wrong. The result is the same in both cases: owners are locked out of their phones.
Reports have surfaced from users of the Pixel 10 Pro XL, Pixel 8a and Pixel 8 Pro, along with other models in Google's Pixel lineup. The mix of newer and older phones suggests the issue may be tied to software shared across the devices, rather than a hardware problem in one model.
That is what makes the bug more serious than a routine update problem. The lock screen is not just another part of the interface. It controls access to the phone and the data stored on it. If Android cannot properly register a PIN or unlock pattern, users may be shut out of photos, messages, files, apps and other information stored on the device.
One Pixel 10 Pro XL owner tried several ways to regain access. They restarted the phone, entered Safe Mode, cleaned the screen, connected a USB mouse and reinstalled the same Android build. None of those steps worked. The phone was eventually factory reset.
A reset may get the phone working again, but it comes with an obvious downside: it erases local data. That makes it a last resort, especially for people who do not have recent backups. Photos, downloads, app data and other files could be lost if they are not stored in the cloud or copied to another device.
Pixel 10 Pro XL – Can't unlock phone after September update (pattern resets after 2 dots)
by u/go6ka in GooglePixel
The reports also show why lock-screen bugs are difficult to troubleshoot. A phone might appear to be working normally in every other way. The display may respond to taps, and the user may know the correct PIN or pattern. But if the software handling the input is broken, the device may never receive the full credential in the form needed to unlock it.
Safe Mode can be useful when a third-party app is causing trouble, but it is less likely to help if the issue is part of the system update. Reinstalling the same build may not change anything either if the defect is in that version of Android. Using a mouse can help rule out a damaged display or touch-input problem, but it will not fix a lock-screen process that is misreading valid entries.
Google has not publicly confirmed the problem or announced a fix. It is also not clear how many users are affected, whether the issue is tied to a specific version of the update, or whether it appears only under certain security settings or device conditions.
For now, affected users should avoid a factory reset until they have checked for backups on another device or through their Google account. Contacting Google Pixel Support before wiping the phone may also be worthwhile, particularly if the company is gathering reports from users to identify the cause.

articles.title: The IKEA x Xbox gaming furniture collab is actually genius — take a look at the full range
articles.text:
Hear me out, the IKEA x Xbox collab is actually genius — take a look at the full range, from thumbstick stool to wall-mountable display boxes to show off your controllers
Playful touches and hidden storage galore
Swedish homeware titan IKEA has joined forces with Xbox to create what might be the perfect gaming collection. The YXSTABY range is quirky and playful, but doesn't forget the practical considerations of gamer furniture. Many of the pieces are on castors so they can be wheeled into place when needed and tucked away when not, and plenty have hidden pockets, slings and compartments to stash your gaming gear neatly.
If you'd rather make a feature of your kit, the wall-mountable, mirrored display boxes will show your controllers off from every angle. I'm a particular fan of the storage unit that doubles as a side table — again on castors for easy wheeling. You can slide the casing to reveal your gaming gear or hide it away.
To create the collection, the designers drew inspiration from the Xbox controller. The D-pad features in a lap cushion and on a decorative platter, and — less subtly — the thumbstick has been transformed into a stool. (TechRadar's James Pickard had a chance to sit on one when the collection was unveiled at Gamescom and insists that despite being completely absurd, it's "more comfortable than it looks".)
The YXSTABY range is finally available to buy today — scroll down to check out the full collection.

articles.title: Test du Samsung Galaxy S26 FE : un Galaxy S25 FE en plus cher et un poil plus puissant
articles.text:
C’est une tradition chez Samsung. À la rentrée, pour redonner un peu de vigueur à sa série de smartphones haut de gamme présentée fin février, le constructeur coréen lance une « Fan Edition » de son Galaxy S26+. Il faut donc voir le Galaxy S26 FE comme une sorte de « sous-Galaxy S26+ », ou de « Galaxy S26+ Light ».
Il a un écran de même taille que le Galaxy S26+ sorti en début d’année, mais un équipement un peu moins performant. Samsung peut ainsi le vendre moins cher, avec un meilleur rapport performances / prix.
Le Galaxy S26 FE succède au Galaxy S25 FE, avec lequel il a beaucoup de points communs. Trop, diront certains :
- Même écran
- Même équipement photo
- Même batterie
- Mêmes options de recharge
Le Galaxy S26 FE ne diffère vraiment de son prédécesseur que sur deux points : le design de son bloc optique et un processeur Samsung Exynos plus véloce. S’y ajoutent Android 17 et un capteur selfie au cadrage un peu plus large.
Compte tenu de son prix (relativement) abordable, ce nouveau smartphone haut de gamme est-il une alternative convaincante au Galaxy S26+ ? Voici notre avis complet.
    Pour aller plus loin
            Quel est le meilleur smartphone à moins de 800 € en 2026 ?
            
Fiche technique
| Modèle | Samsung Galaxy S26 FE | 
|---|---|
| Dimensions | 76,9 mm x 161,6 mm x 7,4 mm | 
| Interface constructeur | One UI | 
| Taille de l’écran | 6,7 pouces | 
| Définition | 2340 x 1080 pixels | 
| Densité de pixels | 385 ppp | 
| Technologie | AMOLED | 
| SoC | Samsung Exynos 2500 | 
| Puce graphique | Samsung Xclipse 950 | 
| Stockage interne | 128, 256 Go | 
| Appareil photo (dorsal) | Capteur 1 : 50 Capteur 2 : 12 Capteur 3 : 8 Mp | 
| Capteur photo frontal | 12 Mp | 
| Définition enregistrement vidéo | 8K@30fps | 
| Wi-fi | Wi-Fi 6 (ax) | 
| 5G | Oui | 
| NFC | Oui | 
| Capteur d’empreintes | Sous l’écran | 
| Type de connecteur | USB Type-C | 
| Capacité de la batterie | 4900 mAh | 
| Poids | 193 g | 
| Couleurs | Bleu, Vert, Gris | 
|  | Fiche produit | 
Design
Puisque Samsung a modifié le design de ses Galaxy S version 2026, par rapport aux modèles de 2025, il devait logiquement en faire de même pour le Galaxy S26 FE.
Le bloc optique du nouvel appareil a donc été redessiné. On passe de trois objectifs indépendants (il n’y avait donc pas vraiment de bloc optique sur le Galaxy S25 FE), à trois objectifs regroupés derrière une plaque de verre.
Cela ne change pas grand-chose, mais cela permet au constructeur d’affirmer que le Galaxy S26 FE arbore un nouveau design. Samsung explique aussi que ce bloc empêche la poussière de se glisser entre les objectifs. Ce design est-il plus séduisant ? Cela dépend bien sûr des goûts de chacun.
À part ça, on retrouve les formes des Galaxy S26 : dos plat en verre, sur lequel on repère assez bien les empreintes digitales ; bords plats ; armature en aluminium ; bordures noires très fines autour de l’image ; écran plat protégé des rayures par un verre Gorilla Glass Victus+.
Cette année, les trois coloris proposés sont le graphite, le vert d’eau et le bleu. L’ensemble a de la classe et se tient bien en main, avec le lecteur d’empreintes digitales placé au bas de l’écran.
Le poids et l’épaisseur du Galaxy S26 FE sont quasiment inchangés par rapport au modèle précédent : 193 grammes (contre 190 grammes) et 7,4 millimètres d’épaisseur. Le Galaxy S26+ est à peine plus léger et plus fin (190 grammes et 7,3 millimètres).
Enfin, smartphone haut de gamme oblige, la certification IP68 est de mise. Le smartphone résiste donc à la pluie, à la poussière et à une immersion jusqu’à 1,5 mètre d’eau douce pendant 30 minutes. Samsung déconseille toutefois de l’utiliser à la plage ou à la piscine.
Écran
L’écran du Galaxy S26 FE exploite une dalle OLED de 6,7 pouces, comme son grand frère. Toutefois, là où le Galaxy S26+ affiche une définition QHD+ (3120 x 1440 pixels), le Galaxy S26 FE se limite au Full HD+ (2340 x 1080 pixels).
Autre différence, les deux écrans montent à 120 Hz, mais celui du Galaxy S26 FE n’utilise pas la technologie LTPO. Son taux de rafraîchissement ne peut donc pas être géré aussi finement que sur le Galaxy S26+. Il est juste possible de sélectionner le mode adaptatif (jusqu’à 120 Hz) ou le mode 60 Hz.
Enfin, la luminosité de l’écran du Galaxy S26 FE, quoique élevée, l’est moins que sur le Galaxy S26+. Ainsi, la luminosité maximale que nous avons mesurée est de 1100 nits, en activant le mode Luminosité automatique. De quoi obtenir une bonne lisibilité lorsqu’on se trouve dans un environnement très éclairé (en extérieur, en plein soleil, par exemple).
Celle-ci peut même grimper jusqu’à 1839 nits, en HDR, selon les mesures réalisées à l’aide de notre sonde Calibrite Display Pro HL et du logiciel CalMAN Ultimate de Portrait Displays.
Seul bémol, la colorimétrie de l’écran n’est pas extraordinaire : le Delta E moyen est de 4,6 avec le profil colorimétrique appelé Vif ; la température moyenne des couleurs est de 6676 K (proche de la référence de 6500 K) ; et la reproduction du gamut DCI-P3 ne s’effectue qu’à hauteur de 76 % (51 % pour le gamut BT.2020).
Bref, même si l’écran du Galaxy S26+ est plus lumineux, celui du Galaxy S26 FE l’est suffisamment pour offrir un affichage de qualité, en toutes circonstances.
Performances
Alors que le processeur Samsung Exynos 2400 équipe le Galaxy S25 FE et que c’est l’Exynos 2600 que l’on trouve dans le Galaxy S26, Samsung a retenu sa puce Exynos 2500 pour ce Galaxy S26 FE. Elle est assistée de 8 Go de mémoire.
Cette puce exploite dix cœurs, dont un cadencé à 3,3 GHz. Si on se fie aux résultats obtenus avec les principaux benchmarks (Geekbench, AnTuTu, 3DMark), ses performances sont excellentes, supérieures à celles obtenues avec le Galaxy S25 FE.
Quelques smartphones concurrents, vendus aux alentours de 800 €, sont moins performants :
- Le Oppo Reno 16 Pro et son processeur MediaTek Dimensity 8550 Super.
- Le Xiaomi 17T et sa puce MediaTek Dimensity 8500 Ultra.
Bien sûr, l’Exynos 2500 est moins véloce que l’Exynos 2600 des Galaxy S26 et Galaxy S26+. Il est également moins performant que les smartphones équipés des puces Snapdragon 8 Elite (Honor 600 Pro) et Dimensity 9500 (Xiaomi 17T Pro).
Son GPU est en revanche particulièrement efficace. On peut jouer à Fortnite dans les meilleures conditions possibles, à 120 images par seconde et en qualité graphique Épique.
Sa température reste contenue, même après une demi-heure de jeu. En revanche, son processeur chauffe suffisament pour brider assez durement ses performances, conservant 67 % de ses performances maximales pendant les longues tâches intensives.
Logiciel
Le Samsung Galaxy S26 FE fonctionne sous Android 17, avec l’interface et les fonctions de One UI 9. Pour rassurer ceux qui gardent longtemps leur smartphone, le constructeur garantit sept versions majeures d’Android et sept ans de correctifs de sécurité, jusqu’en septembre 2033.
À l’instar des autres smartphones de la série Galaxy S, le Galaxy S26 FE dispose de la panoplie complète des fonctions Galaxy AI :
- Des assistants pour la traduction automatique et l’aide à la rédaction.
- Des assistants pour l’analyse des enregistrements audio et des pages Web.
- Des fonctions de retouche / création graphiques, et d’optimisation des vidéos (Ma Cam suivi, Gomme audio).
- Now Brief
- Now Nudge
En revanche, lorsqu’il s’agit de retoucher ses photos, on est susceptible de plus souvent faire appel aux fonctions boostées à l’IA :
- Effacer des objets ou des personnes.
- Déplacer des éléments de l’image.
- Créer : ajout d’éléments en les décrivant par écrit, par oral ou en les dessinant directement à l’écran.
- Style : modification des photos, grâce à divers effets visuels, comme le dessin 3D, l’aquarelle, le rendu au crayon, la BD, etc. Le style Sci-Fi est particulièrement amusant, puisqu’il place la personne photographiée dans un décor futuriste. Cerise sur le gâteau, ces styles peuvent être superposés.
Photo
Le Galaxy S26 FE reprend le même équipement photo que le Galaxy S25 FE, et quasiment celui du Galaxy S26+ (la seule différence réside dans la définition du capteur associé au téléobjectif). Il est donc composé de quatre couples objectif / capteur :
- Grand-angle : focale de 23 mm et ouverture de f/1.8, capteur de 50 mégapixels avec stabilisation optique.
- Ultra grand-angle : ouverture de f/2.2 et capteur de 12 mégapixels.
- Téléobjectif : focale de 75 mm (zoom optique 3x), ouverture de f/2.4 et capteur de 8 mégapixels avec stabilisation optique (contre 10 mégapixels pour celui du Galaxy S26+).
- Objectif frontal, pour les selfies : focale de 30 mm, ou 23 mm en plan large, et capteur de 12 mégapixels.
Grand-angle
Si les photos générées par le capteur grand-angle ont une définition de 12 mégapixels par défaut, le mode 50 mégapixels peut être activé. Rappelons que certains concurrents récents exploitent un capteur grand-angle de 200 mégapixels, comme l’Oppo Reno 16 Pro ou le Honor 600 Pro.
Quoi qu’il en soit, le Galaxy S26 FE capture de superbes photos dans ce mode, quelles que soient les conditions d’éclairage.
De nuit, la technologie quad pixel binning montre son efficacité, sans pour autant trop modifier la colorimétrie réelle de la scène. Les photos sont particulièrement convaincantes, si on les regarde à l’écran du smartphone (moins sur un grand écran).
Ultra grand-angle
En mode ultra grand-angle, les résultats sont très satisfaisants, même si, comme souvent, la précision est plus grande au centre de l’image que sur les bords.
De nuit, il devient compliqué d’obtenir des photos exploitables. Si les sources lumineuses ne sont pas trop éloignées, on obtient des images de qualité passable, au mieux.
Zoom
Le téléobjectif du Galaxy S26 FE offre une focale de 75 mm, soit un zoom optique 3x. Les Oppo Reno 16 Pro et Honor 600 Pro font toutefois légèrement mieux, avec une focale de 80 mm (zoom optique 3,5x), alors que les Xiaomi 17T et 17T Pro sont dotés d’un téléobjectif 5x (115 mm).
Comme on peut le voir sur les exemples ci-dessous, les images sont impeccables entre 2x et 3x, et encore correctes jusqu’à 10x.
2x
3x
De nuit, même avec un petit zoom, 2x (recadrage du capteur principal) ou 3x (optique), le piqué des images est rarement au rendez-vous, sauf si on est entouré de multiples éclairages.
10x
Avec le zoom numérique 10x, les images commencent à perdre en précision, ce qui se voit surtout si on les consulte sur un moniteur.
20x
Le phénomène s’amplifie, c’est bien normal, dès que l’on dépasse cinq fois le zoom optique du téléobjectif, soit 15x.
Les images sont trop dégradées pour être satisfaisantes. Les algorithmes d’amélioration d’image de Samsung, qui interpolent massivement, deviennent contre-productifs.
Toutefois, la perte de qualité n’est pas trop visible sur le petit écran d’un smartphone.
30x
Il est préférable de ne faire appel au zoom numérique maximum qu’en cas d’absolue nécessité, tant les images générées deviennent approximatives.
Selfie
Les selfies bénéficient d’une excellente précision (ils sont capturés en 4000 x 3000 pixels), si les conditions d’éclairage sont optimales. Tous les détails de la peau sont parfaitement discernables.
Ils sont réalisés avec une focale de 30 mm, ou en plan large, en 23 mm. Ce dernier est d’ailleurs un peu plus large que sur le Galaxy S25 FE (26 mm).
En revanche, les photos sont légèrement moins bien définies dans un environnement moins favorable, comme en intérieur. Elles demeurent néanmoins satisfaisantes.
De nuit, bien que l’écran éclaire notre visage (mais pas aussi fortement qu’avec les smartphones Xiaomi), les selfies offrent une précision très moyenne. Les clichés font toutefois illusion sur le petit écran.
Vidéo
Le Galaxy S26 FE assure des captations vidéo de grande qualité (4K, 60 images par seconde, mode HDR), avec le capteur dorsal mais aussi celui qui est placé en haut de l’écran. Le capteur arrière peut même filmer en 8K, avec 30 images par seconde.
Pour la stabilisation des vidéos, deux options sont disponibles, en mode QHD avec 60 images par seconde : super stabilité avec verrouillage horizontal, ou stabilisation sans ce verrouillage.
On voit mal pourquoi choisir la seconde option, tant le verrouillage de l’horizon est efficace. En effet, dès la première seconde de captation vidéo, le smartphone verrouille l’horizon et le conserve par la suite, même si on fait pivoter le smartphone, plus ou moins violemment. Dès lors, les enregistrements réalisés lorsqu’on est en mouvement bénéficient d’une stabilité à toute épreuve.
Audio
Les deux haut-parleurs du Galaxy S26 FE s’en sortent bien, dans l’ensemble. Une fois n’est pas coutume, le déséquilibre entre celui qui est situé en haut de l’écran et celui placé près du port USB-C n’est pas aussi flagrant que sur d’autres smartphones.
De plus, la puissance maximale est satisfaisante et les différentes plages de fréquences sont assez bien audibles, même les basses. C’est d’autant plus appréciable qu’il n’y a aucun moyen de modifier le rendu audio (pas d’égaliseur).
Réseau et communication
Le Galaxy S26 FE accepte deux cartes nano SIM, une nano SIM et une eSIM, ou deux eSIM.
Comme sur la plupart des smartphones haut de gamme, aucun de ces emplacements n’accepte de carte microSD, ce qui est bien dommage.
Enfin, le Wi-Fi 6E et le Bluetooth 5.4 sont pris en charge (contre Wi-Fi 7 et Bluetooth 6 sur le Galaxy S26+). Le port USB-C se contente de l’USB 2.0, là où le Galaxy S26+ passe à l’USB 3.2.
Batterie
La batterie du Samsung Galaxy S26 FE a une capacité de 4900 mAh, comme celles du Galaxy S25 FE et du Galaxy S26+. Samsung n’est toujours pas passé aux batteries lithium-ion silicium-carbone (Si/C) sur ses Galaxy S, contrairement à ses modèles pliants, les Z Flip 8, Z Fold 8 Ultra et Z Fold 8, qui n’offrent pourtant pas de très grandes capacités.
Les concurrents chinois du coréen, comme Honor, Oppo ou Xiaomi, ont pour leur part franchi le pas et embarquent des batteries de très grande capacité (6000 à 7000 mAh), grâce à cette nouvelle technologie.
Sur sa fiche officielle, Samsung annonce une durée de vie minimale de 1 200 cycles de charge pour la batterie du Galaxy S26 FE, contre 2 000 cycles pour celle du Galaxy S25 FE. La capacité ne bouge pas, mais le constructeur s’engage sur une longévité nettement moindre.
Nous avons mesuré l’autonomie offerte par le Galaxy S26 FE dans différents cas de figure, avec une luminosité toujours ajustée à 250 nits.
Ainsi, dans un premier temps, nous avons évalué l’autonomie bureautique / multimédia, grâce au test intégré à l’application PCMark, avec la fréquence adaptative utilisée par défaut. Il a fallu 11 heures et 40 minutes pour que le niveau de la batterie passe de 100 % à 20 %.
Le même test, réalisé cette fois-ci avec un taux de rafraîchissement fixe de 60 Hz, a tenu à peine une heure de plus, soit 12 heures et 45 minutes.
Ces deux résultats sont moyens et devraient permettre d’envisager une à deux journées d’utilisation. Ils sont largement inférieurs à ceux du Honor 600 Pro ou du Xiaomi 17T Pro, avantagés par leurs plus grosses batteries.
En streaming vidéo (à 60 Hz), l’autonomie atteint environ 21 heures : la batterie a perdu 38 % de sa charge après 8 heures de lecture sur Netflix. Ce résultat se situe, encore une fois, dans la moyenne basse, loin des 29 heures de lecture vidéo annoncées par Samsung (mesurées en lecture locale, et non en streaming).
Pour recharger la batterie, on peut utiliser un adaptateur secteur filaire. Dans ce cas, l’opération se déroule exactement de la même façon qu’avec le Galaxy S25 FE, puisque la puissance maximale est toujours de 45 watts. C’est aussi la puissance de recharge filaire du Galaxy S26+, et c’est mieux que le Galaxy S26 (25 watts).
Sur le papier, ce n’est pas très rapide : d’autres smartphones de la même gamme de prix se rechargent à 80 ou 100 watts.
Heureusement, en pratique, la recharge filaire n’est pas si lente, si on dispose de l’adaptateur Samsung de 45 watts, vendu séparément :
- 70 % en 30 minutes
- 91 % en 45 minutes
- 98 % en 55 minutes
Toutefois, on ne peut s’empêcher de penser qu’elle pourrait être plus rapide.
Idem pour la recharge sans fil, qui plafonne toujours à 15 watts, comme sur le Galaxy S25 FE. Certains modèles concurrents font bien mieux (50 watts pour le Honor 600 Pro et le Xiaomi 17T Pro).
Prix et disponibilité
Présenté le 27 août, le Galaxy S26 FE est en vente en France depuis le 4 septembre.
Il est proposé en deux versions :
- 799 €, avec 8 Go de mémoire et 128 Go d’espace de stockage,
- 899 €, avec 8 Go et 256 Go de stockage.
Cela représente une hausse de 50 € pour la version 128 Go, et de 90 € pour la version 256 Go, par rapport au Galaxy S25 FE à son lancement (749 € et 809 €).
Heureusement, sur le site du constructeur, un code promo permet, au moment où nous écrivons ces lignes, d’obtenir une réduction immédiate de 100 €, cumulable avec une autre réduction de 50 € si le paiement passe par PayPal.
La facture finale peut donc descendre, tant que cette promotion dure, à 649 € (128 Go) ou 749 € (256 Go), ce qui est nettement plus intéressant.
Car le Galaxy S26, lancé à 999 € en février dernier avec 12 Go de mémoire et 256 Go de stockage, se trouve aussi autour de 799 € chez certains revendeurs. Il est toutefois plus petit, avec son écran de 6,3 pouces. Pour avoir un affichage de grande taille, il faut se tourner vers le Galaxy S26+. Là, l’addition est nettement plus salée : 1369 € actuellement chez Samsung (il a pris 100 euros depuis son lancement) ou 1100 euros chez des revendeurs (Fnac, Darty)
Pour un propriétaire de Galaxy S25 FE, le Galaxy S26 FE n’a guère d’intérêt : l’écran, la batterie et la recharge ne changent pas, et seul le processeur progresse. Pour les autres, il devient intéressant en promotion, à 649 €.
Face aux Xiaomi 17T Pro et Honor 600 Pro, en revanche, hors promotion il est battu. Ces derniers offrent plus de puissance, plus d’autonomie et 512 Go de stockage pour environ 800 €.

articles.title: Scaling cloud migrations with agentic AI on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Scaling cloud migrations with agentic AI on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
October 2026: This post was reviewed and updated for accuracy.
Scaling cloud migrations with agentic AI on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore raises a practical question. Which parts of a large migration program belong to a managed service, and which parts need custom automation? One enterprise program answered that question across 300+ applications and a fixed fiscal year deadline. The four-agent pattern in this post reduced infrastructure as code (IaC) development time from 3 to 4 weeks per application to minutes, based on internal project tracking data.
This pattern runs alongside AWS Transform rather than in place of it, as a hybrid that adds custom agents where your program requires them. AWS Transform covers the migration and modernization work, and AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) covers the database tier. The agents in this post attach to those services and carry one further requirement: sources and destinations reached through Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools that your organization builds and maintains.
AWS Professional Services builds a suite of purpose-built AI agents for programs with that requirement. The agents use the Strands Agents SDK and run on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. Each agent reaches its sources and destinations through MCP tools exposed by AgentCore Gateway.
In this post, you explore the architecture of a four-agent pattern for MCP-connected environments. You also see the code that defines an agent, connects it to its tools, and applies responsible AI controls. The pattern includes four agents:
- The Intake Agent, which reads migration inputs from document and collaboration systems through MCP tools.
- The IaC Agent, which generates IaC that composes your approved internal modules.
- The Migration Intelligence and Governance Agent, which reports and governs inside your own program tools.
- The Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) Agent for operations after cutover.
To follow along, you need an AWS account with access to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore and to Amazon Bedrock foundation models. You also need familiarity with the Strands Agents SDK and MCP server patterns, plus the IaC tooling used by your organization. Confirm first that an AWS managed service does not already cover your migration path.
When this pattern applies
AWS Transform covers migration and modernization for server, network, mainframe, .NET, and application code workloads as a managed service, and AWS DMS covers databases. This pattern adds agents for the requirements that stay specific to your organization.
On the program described here, three conditions held together.
- MCP-connected sources and destinations: The systems holding the migration inputs, and the systems receiving the outputs, were reached through MCP tools that the delivery team built and maintained. They included an internal wiki holding security standards, a ticketing system, a collaboration platform, and an in-house provisioning API.
- Organization-specific IaC composition: Generated infrastructure code had to compose an internal module library that the security office reviews and approves. Writing that composition by hand took 3 to 4 weeks per application, which across a 300+ application portfolio translates to years of engineering effort.
- Work continuing past cutover: Program scope included operations after handover, which sits outside the migration services.
Architecture overview
This pattern uses four purpose-built agents. The architecture attaches to a migration program at three points: the systems holding migration inputs, IaC composition, and operations after cutover. The pattern applies security at each of those points. The following diagram shows how the agents, tools, and AWS services connect.
The pattern organizes agents into two journeys. The migration journey agents handle discovery through deployment. The operations journey agent handles post-migration monitoring.
Migration journey agents:
- Intake Agent (Phase 1): Reads architecture documents, questionnaires, and dependency records through MCP tools, then defines target state architecture.
- IaC Agent (Phase 2): Generates IaC that composes your approved internal modules for each application.
- Migration Intelligence and Governance Agent: Provides automated portfolio reporting, well-architected assessments, and governance across Jira, Confluence, and Webex.
Operations journey agents:
- SRE Agent (Phase 3): Provides monitoring and automated remediation after cutover.
AWS managed services carry the migration and complement the custom agents:
- AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS): Generative AI-assisted schema conversion and automated cutover for database migration.
- AWS Transform: Discovery, wave planning, landing zone creation, network conversion, rehost or replatform execution, and modernization for mainframe, virtualized, and .NET workloads.
How the components connect
This section describes how the framework components interact at runtime.
Each agent is a Strands agent, defined by a foundation model, a system prompt, and a set of tools. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime hosts them in a serverless environment with session isolation and multi-agent orchestration. Amazon Bedrock foundation models power the reasoning that interprets documents, generates code, and drives multi-step workflows. For model availability by AWS Region, refer to Supported foundation models in Amazon Bedrock.
Each agent calls MCP tools scoped to its function through AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, which converts your APIs, AWS Lambda functions, and existing services into MCP-compatible tools. AgentCore Identity, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, authenticates each call through scoped AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles and your identity provider.
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore memory stores agent session state and shared context. Agents use this shared context to persist outputs and track migration progress across over 300 applications. When the Intake Agent completes discovery, it writes the target architecture and dependency mappings to AgentCore memory. The IaC Agent reads this shared context to begin code generation without manual handoff.
Defining an agent in code
The following Python example defines the IaC Agent and prepares it for Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime. The agent reaches your MCP tools through AgentCore Gateway, and it calls a foundation model through Amazon Bedrock with an Amazon Bedrock Guardrails policy attached.
The entrypoint returns the generated IaC together with the policy set version that shaped it, so a reviewer traces the output back to a signed-off standard. AgentCore Runtime handles session isolation and scaling. For deployable examples, see the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore samples repository and the Strands Agents samples repository on GitHub. For the deployment steps, refer to Getting started with AgentCore runtime.
Phase 1: Intake Agent for automated discovery
The Intake Agent reads the migration inputs that live in your document and collaboration systems. On this program, those systems were reachable through MCP tools the delivery team built and maintained.
The agent ingests architecture documentation, application inventory lists, intake questionnaires, and dependency records through those tools. It then produces a target AWS architecture with a recommended migration pattern, resource sizing specifications, and a compliance validation report.
The output feeds directly into the IaC Agent, creating an automated handoff from intake to infrastructure provisioning.
Phase 2: IaC Agent for automated infrastructure code generation
AWS Professional Services deployed the IaC Agent first in the portfolio, and it delivers the most immediately measurable impact. It generates IaC code adhering to your security best practices and standards.
How it works
The agent workflow proceeds through five steps:
Step 1: Ingest the steering document. The agent reads the steering document from the wave team. It extracts deployment scope, compliance constraints, and Security Office-approved wave-specific overrides.
Step 2: Interpret the target state architecture diagram. Using the Intake Agent’s output, the IaC Agent identifies infrastructure components, their relationships, and dependencies.
Step 3: Generate IaC. Based on this interpretation, the agent generates IaC using your defined and established patterns. It populates configurations with wave-specific parameters and configures remote state management. It then applies mandatory tagging and adds monitoring configurations required by organizational standards.
Step 4: Validate through Policy in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Before execution, Policy in AgentCore evaluates each tool call against Cedar rules. It calculates the scope of potential change, checks dependency conflicts with concurrent waves, and confirms compliance window validity.
Step 5: Execute and report. The centralized execution plane triggers the IaC, monitors deployment, and reports outcomes through AgentCore Observability, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Post-deployment validation runs automatically and compliance metrics update in real time.
Custom MCP tools: The security foundation
Each action passes through custom MCP tools exposed by Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway and governed by AgentCore Identity and Policy in AgentCore. AgentCore Identity authenticates each agent action through scoped IAM roles with least-privilege access. The framework validates inputs against defined schemas and rejects malformed inputs at the boundary.
No credentials or sensitive values pass through agent context, because AgentCore Identity resolves secrets at runtime from a centralized credential provider. AgentCore Observability and AWS CloudTrail write each agent action to an immutable, centralized audit trail. Policy in AgentCore enforces Cedar rules that help prevent a single operation from affecting more than a defined threshold.
Curated organizational policies as MCP tools
The security office curates the policy set, not the agent. A versioned document holds each rule, the resource types it covers, a machine-checkable assertion, and the approval record. The following example shows three policies and one wave exception.
An AWS Lambda function serves that document, and AgentCore Gateway exposes the function as an MCP tool named get_policies. The IaC Agent requests only the policies in scope for the resource types in the wave it generates.
The response carries the policy set version, so generated code records which rules produced it and a reviewer traces a resource back to a signed-off standard. Waived policies travel in their own field rather than disappearing, and the compliance report lists them for the wave. Each exception carries an expiry date, so a lapsed waiver stops applying without manual cleanup.
Two policy layers operate here, and they answer different questions. AgentCore Policy evaluates Cedar rules to decide whether an agent calls a tool at all. The curated policy set decides what the generated infrastructure satisfies.
IaC generation based on your patterns
The IaC Agent generates infrastructure code based on your defined and established patterns. These patterns encode organizational standards into reusable constructs. They include network configurations, security group rules, IAM roles, Amazon CloudWatch alarms, Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) configurations, Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) layouts, and mandatory tagging.
This approach provides consistency across waves, speed for wave teams who don’t write infrastructure code from scratch, and governance where security updates propagate to consumers on their next deployment cycle.
Output artifacts
The agent produces IaC code, automated test cases, compliance reports, and deployment runbooks for each application.
The IaC Agent pushes generated code directly to your code repository (such as AWS CodeCommit, GitLab, or Bitbucket). From there, it enters your existing review and deployment pipeline without requiring changes to your existing toolchain.
Migration Intelligence and Governance Agent: Portfolio-wide visibility
A 300+ application portfolio needs status reporting, progress tracking, follow-up actions, and well-architected validation. On this program, that work ran inside the customer’s own Jira, Confluence, and Webex. Performing it by hand creates significant overhead for project managers and delivery leads.
The Migration Intelligence and Governance Agent addresses this with automated, on-demand intelligence and governance across the portfolio. It aggregates data from three sources through AgentCore Gateway. Jira provides sprint progress and impediments. Confluence provides architecture documentation and runbooks. Webex provides meeting notes and action items.
The agent provides well-architected assessments across migrated workloads, compliance and governance validation, and architecture pattern adherence tracking.
Automated actions include updating Confluence pages with latest migration status, creating Jira tasks for identified action items, and generating ServiceNow tickets for escalations. These actions require explicit human approval before execution. This approval-gated architecture is a core design principle across the four agents. Agents support human decision-making rather than replacing it.
On-demand reporting across the 300+ application portfolio replaces manual aggregation, based on internal project tracking data. Your results might vary based on portfolio size and tool integrations.
Phase 3: SRE Agent for proactive post-migration operations
The SRE Agent covers the phase after handover. The migration services complete at cutover. After applications run on AWS, the SRE Agent shifts the team from reactive response to proactive improvement.
The agent monitors Amazon CloudWatch metrics, application performance data, and historical patterns. It raises alerts before issues affect production. The agent also publishes automated remediation playbooks for common failure patterns and recommends efficiency improvements.
Target areas (with human-in-the-loop approval) include database cluster right-sizing, performance tuning, storage tiering, and compute scaling and efficiency improvements.
The SRE Agent extends the pattern past migration. Applications don’t land on AWS and stop there. They continuously improve over time.
Data migration with AWS DMS
Alongside the custom AI agents, two AWS managed services handle the data and application modernization, server and network migration layer.
DMS Schema Conversion with generative AI reduces manual schema mapping effort. It converts code objects that rules-based conversion leaves unfinished, such as stored procedures, functions, and triggers. This capability is generally available in a subset of AWS Regions, so confirm Region support during wave planning. AWS DMS then shortens the cutover window with automated migration tasks. The service integrates directly into the agent pipeline. The IaC Agent provisions target infrastructure, then AWS DMS migrates the data.
AWS Transform covers the server, network, and code layers of the same program. The AWS Transform User Guide lists the current capabilities by workload type.
Security and compliance: Embedded, not bolted on
This architecture embeds security from the start, not as an afterthought, applying it at each phase of the migration lifecycle. Key controls across the agent suite:
- Security standards enforcement: The IaC Agent pulls your security office standards directly from Confluence and applies them across generated IaC using custom MCP tools.
- Landing zone validation: The framework validates generated infrastructure against the enterprise’s landing zone compliance requirements before deployment.
- Human-in-the-loop approval gates: Automated actions across all agents in the suite require explicit human approval before execution. No agent acts autonomously on production systems.
- AgentCore Gateway coordination: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway coordinates context and security controls across agents, maintaining consistent policy application throughout the migration lifecycle.
- Continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) integration: The framework integrates security controls into the CI/CD pipeline, with automated test cases generated alongside IaC to catch compliance issues before they reach production.
- Responsible AI controls at the inference layer: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails applies content filters, denied topics, sensitive information filters, and contextual grounding checks to each prompt and each model response. An agent acts only on output that clears the guardrail. Guardrail traces flow into AgentCore Observability alongside the tool-call audit trail.
This approach aligns with the AWS shared responsibility model. AWS provides security of the underlying infrastructure, while you’re responsible for security in the cloud. The agents automate your configuration responsibilities while maintaining human oversight for approval decisions.
In this implementation, the pattern maintained enterprise security standards across the over 300 application portfolio at speeds manual processes could not match. Your results might vary based on your security requirements and organizational standards.
Measurable impact
Across the migration program, this framework delivered the following results. These metrics reflect this specific implementation. Your results might vary based on application complexity, team size, and organizational requirements.
- IaC development time reduced from weeks to minutes: from 3–4 weeks per application to minutes of automated generation (based on internal project tracking data).
- Pattern consistency applied across waves: no wave can deviate from the approved IaC patterns baseline.
- Security compliance: verified automatically at each deployment, with a complete audit trail requiring zero manual effort.
- Architecture-to-deployment fidelity improved: the agent interprets the diagram, and the IaC realizes it as designed.
- On-demand portfolio reporting across over 300 applications with precise metrics and zero manual aggregation.
- Wave team onboarding improved: teams upload documents and the agents produce the IaC and the reports.
Cost considerations
Running this pattern adds cost in a few predictable places. Foundation model tokens usually dominate, because intake and IaC generation push documents, policies, and architecture context through a model and return generated code. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore bills on consumption. Runtime charges per second for the CPU and memory a session uses, and CPU scales to zero while an agent waits on a model response or a human approval. Gateway, Memory, Policy, and Guardrails each bill per unit of use, and Observability telemetry bills at Amazon CloudWatch rates.
Across a 300+ application portfolio the agents run for the length of the migration program rather than as a single job, so treat this as a running cost that tracks wave activity. Token volume follows document size and tool-call count more than application count, so a pilot wave gives you a per-application baseline. On the AWS Transform side, the assessment and the migration agents for virtualized, Windows, and mainframe workloads are available at no cost. The resources a migration creates bill normally, and custom transformations are priced per agent minute. For current rates, refer to Amazon Bedrock pricing, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore pricing, AWS Transform pricing, Amazon CloudWatch pricing, and the AWS Pricing Calculator.
Clean up resources
To avoid ongoing charges after you finish testing the framework, remove the resources that you created:
- Delete the agents from AgentCore runtime, then remove the Gateway targets and the Gateway.
- Delete the AgentCore memory resources that hold session state and shared context.
- Delete the guardrail, the Policy in AgentCore definitions, and the IAM roles created for the agents.
- Delete the CloudWatch log groups that AgentCore Observability wrote to, if you no longer need the history.
- Delete any AWS DMS replication instances and endpoints provisioned for test migrations.
Confirm in the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore console that no agent sessions remain active.
Conclusion
Migrating 300+ applications to AWS on an aggressive timeline needs more than added engineers. Managed services carry most of that work. Where a requirement falls outside them, an agent pattern can close the gap while humans keep decisions, approvals, and strategy.
This pattern delivered measurable results on one program whose sources and destinations sat behind MCP tools. Purpose-built Strands agents addressed those specific requirements, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore applied security structurally, and human-in-the-loop design kept automation supporting decision-making rather than replacing it. Use AWS Transform and AWS DMS for the migration, and run these agents with them where MCP-connected sources and destinations call for it.
Next steps
Based on your use case, consider these paths:
- Planning a migration? Connect AWS Transform to your favorite AI code companion and get started with server, network, and code migration and modernizations, and AWS DMS for database.
- Sources and destinations behind MCP tools? Evaluate this pattern. See Amazon Bedrock AgentCore to learn how to build and deploy agents.
- Internal module library to honor? Evaluate the IaC Agent. IaC development time dropped from weeks to minutes against a manual baseline on this program.
- Governance inside your own program tools? Consider the Migration Intelligence and Governance Agent for status reporting and well-architected assessments. Learn more about Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Memory for agent state management.
- Post-migration? Explore the SRE Agent pattern to shift from reactive operations to proactive improvement. Use Amazon CloudWatch for monitoring and automated alerting.
- Building your own agents? Start with the Strands Agents SDK and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, using MCP servers tailored to your migration bottlenecks. Open the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore console to get started, read Deploying Strands Agents to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime.
To explore the services used in this post:
- Amazon Bedrock AgentCore: Deploy and operate AI agents securely at scale.
- AWS Transform: Migrate and modernize infrastructure, applications, and code.
- Strands Agents SDK: Build AI agents with a model, a prompt, and tools.
- AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS): Migrate databases to AWS.
- AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM): Manage access to AWS services.
- Amazon CloudWatch: Monitor AWS resources and applications.
- Amazon Bedrock AgentCore documentation: Runtime, Gateway, Memory, Identity, and Observability.
For background on the services and SDKs used here, read these AWS posts:
- Introducing Amazon Bedrock AgentCore: Securely deploy and operate AI agents at any scale.
- Introducing Strands Agents, an open source AI agents SDK.
- Accelerate database modernization with agentic AI on AWS DMS Schema Conversion.

articles.title: Il déchiffre une lettre de 217 ans adressée à un général de Napoléon grâce à l’IA
articles.text:
Une archive numérisée peut être accessible à tous et tout de même conserver ses secrets. Mais cette lettre vieille de plus de deux siècles, destinée au général Marmont, l’un des commandants de Napoléon, vient de livrer les siens.
Dans un fil publié sur X ce mercredi 30 septembre, l’ingénieur en IA Carter Church raconte comment il l’a déchiffrée avec GPT-6 Astra, un modèle d’intelligence artificielle conçu par OpenAI. Selon lui, environ six heures de travail ont suffi à l’IA. Son compte rendu détaillé, mis en ligne le 18 septembre, retrace les étapes de cette enquête, de la lecture des symboles manuscrits à la reconstitution du message.
Tout part d’une reproduction du courrier, parue dans un article du lieutenant-colonel J. Vilcoq publié en 1969 dans la Revue historique des Armées et désormais accessible sur Persée, une bibliothèque numérique française. L’auteur y étudiait les procédés de chiffrement du Premier Empire, employés notamment pour empêcher qu’un courrier intercepté révèle les ordres et les positions des troupes.
Avant de casser le code, il faut lire les signes
La lettre commence par une phrase en français, suivie de 24 lignes mêlant chiffres, lettres et symboles inventés. Selon Carter Church, Astra a découpé le scan en lignes pour les transcrire. Le relevé final compte 1 300 éléments chiffrés, correspondant à 155 signes distincts.
Une première difficulté tient à l’écriture manuscrite : un même signe peut changer légèrement de forme selon la manière dont il a été tracé. L’IA doit reconnaître ces variations pour éviter de traiter comme deux symboles différents ce qui n’en est qu’un. Astra a d’abord relevé 175 tracés différents, puis les a ramenés à 155 signes.
Il faut ensuite comprendre ce que chaque signe représente. Le courrier utilise un chiffrement dit « homophonique » : plusieurs symboles peuvent remplacer une même lettre.
L’intérêt est de masquer les lettres les plus fréquentes. En français, le « e » revient souvent : s’il était toujours remplacé par un triangle, ce triangle apparaîtrait fréquemment et pourrait mettre sur la piste. En utilisant tantôt un triangle, tantôt un cercle ou un autre signe, on rend son repérage plus difficile. Dans la lettre à Marmont, le « e » dispose ainsi de neuf signes différents.
Pour avancer, Astra s’est appuyé sur des travaux existants. Selon Carter Church, l’IA a retrouvé un tableau de Daniel Tant, historien français de la cryptographie, consacré à ce code et qui donnait déjà la signification de 33 symboles. Ces signes revenant plusieurs fois dans le courrier, ils permettaient déjà de lire environ un tiers du message. Il restait à trouver les correspondances manquantes.
Comment l’IA a recherché les correspondances manquantes
Pour la suite, Astra s’est servi de son propre programme de déchiffrement, selon le récit de l’ingénieur. Celui-ci utilise le « recuit simulé », une méthode qui permet d’explorer différentes clés possibles.
Le programme attribue des lettres aux symboles, puis évalue le texte obtenu à partir des enchaînements de lettres habituels en français. Plus le résultat ressemble à la langue recherchée, meilleur est son score. Il modifie ensuite les correspondances et recommence.
La particularité du recuit simulé est d’accepter parfois un résultat temporairement moins bon. Cela permet de sortir d’une piste qui semblait prometteuse, mais qui ne mène pas à la solution. Au fil de la recherche, certains signes sont également identifiés comme des mots entiers, plutôt que comme des lettres.
Cette méthode existait avant les IA génératives. En 2019, le chercheur Nils Kopal, de l’université de Siegen, présentait déjà un outil intégré au logiciel libre CrypTool 2 pour attaquer les chiffrements homophoniques, automatiquement ou avec une intervention humaine. Ici, l’apport d’Astra tient à sa capacité à passer de la lecture du manuscrit à l’utilisation d’un programme pour le déchiffrer.
Un courrier militaire et une date corrigée
Le message retrouvé détaille notamment les positions et les effectifs des forces françaises et alliées face à l’Autriche. Carter Church le rapproche d’un ordre de Napoléon à Eugène de Beauharnais, vice-roi d’Italie, lui demandant, le 16 mars 1809, d’envoyer ces informations au général Marmont « dans une lettre chiffrée et par un officier intelligent ». Ces recoupements situent le courrier dans les derniers jours de mars 1809, deux semaines avant l’invasion de la Bavière par l’Autriche, et non en 1807 comme il était auparavant daté.
Le résultat a aussi été examiné par un spécialiste. Selon Carter Church, Satoshi Tomokiyo, qui anime le site de cryptographie historique Cryptiana, a confirmé le déchiffrement. La lettre y figure désormais parmi les énigmes résolues, avec sa datation corrigée.
Church reconnaît lui-même qu’un cryptographe aurait pu casser ce code avec suffisamment de temps. Ce qui l’a surpris, c’est le travail accompli par Astra à partir d’une image et d’une consigne : transcrire les signes, retrouver une clé partielle, compléter le déchiffrement et vérifier le contexte historique. Il a publié la clé et le programme utilisés pour permettre à d’autres d’examiner le résultat.
