articles.title: Container Apps Express Reaches GA on a Newly Generally Available Sandbox Layer
articles.text:
Microsoft recently made Azure Container Apps Express generally available, a deployment model that removes the environment provisioning step and replaces most configuration with opinionated defaults. It ships alongside the general availability of Azure Container Apps Sandboxes, the isolated compute layer Express runs on. The pairing follows the same shape Google shipped in Kubernetes Engine this year.
Express takes a container image, a region, and whatever configuration the app needs, then provisions the compute, ingress, and scaling itself. Apps run on consumption CPU with per-second billing, scale to zero when idle, and carry no environment provisioning fee. Microsoft describes Express as developer-first and agent-first, and makes the second part explicit:
AI-assisted workflows can create and update apps far faster than anyone can configure infrastructure by hand.
The speed comes from underneath. Microsoft's documentation states that Express is built entirely on Container Apps Sandboxes, a platform primitive that provisions from prewarmed pools for subsecond startup, isolates each workload in its own hardware-isolated microVM boundary, and bursts to thousands of concurrent sandboxes. Sandboxes also support suspend and resume, snapshotting full state including memory and disk, with sub-second restore.
Developers can use Sandboxes directly rather than through Express, which Microsoft positions for agent platforms and secure code-execution services. The top-level ARM resource is Microsoft.App/SandboxGroups, described as a management boundary for sandboxes sharing configuration, comparable to a Container Apps environment.
Reaction on Reddit suggests the primitive was in use well before the announcement. Commenter MuhBlockchain offered a detail Microsoft's own material does not state:
ACA Sandboxes actually underpin a lot of core Azure services including Foundry Hosted Agents.
Others described their own deployments. Commenter tankerkiller125real wrote that his team uses them for Python sandboxes for a customer facing agent harness. Commenter Minute_Passion_8077 described deploying them for clients through Bicep:
Just point it to an image and off you go. Dont need it? Scale to 0.
Asked how Sandboxes differ from Container Apps jobs, commenter brianveldman drew the line at lifecycle:
ACA Jobs are designed for run to completion tasks and batch processing (start to run to complete), while Sandboxes provide programmable, isolated compute environments with lifecycle control.
Not everyone was convinced by the isolation claim. Commenter RustOnTheEdge responded to the hardware-isolated microVM description with open skepticism, though without elaborating. One question went unanswered: commenter HgnX asked whether the same capability is available in Azure Kubernetes Service, noting that his team runs AKS because of requirements Container Apps does not meet.
That combination is recognizable. Google Kubernetes Engine pairs Pod snapshots, which checkpoint CPU and GPU memory through gVisor, with GKE Agent Sandbox for running untrusted agent code. Microsoft now pairs microVM isolation with snapshot-based suspend and resume, aimed at the same workloads. Both vendors are answering the same question: how to give an agent an isolated environment that costs nothing while idle and returns in under a second.
Express itself is the opinionated application layer on top, offering a focused subset of Container Apps capabilities: scale to zero, multiple replicas, HTTP ingress on a Microsoft-managed domain, environment variables, manual secrets, IP restrictions, log streaming, and autoscaling on HTTP, CPU, or memory rules.
The exclusions define where it stops. Express does not support custom domains, zone redundancy, Key Vault secret references, Easy Auth, OpenTelemetry, Dapr, jobs, workload profiles, GPU workloads, multiple revisions and traffic splitting, or system-assigned managed identities. Service discovery is absent, so apps communicate through their public URLs, and ingress is HTTP only. Microsoft's documentation carries the full list, along with constraints on outbound subnets, which cannot be changed once set, and on per-replica storage.
Microsoft is direct about the boundary, advising a standard environment where teams need greater control over networking, GPU compute, advanced configuration, or environment-level capabilities such as Dapr. The documentation nonetheless also lists rapid prototyping as a case where teams build quickly and then keep running in production without replatforming. For a workload needing a custom domain, zone redundancy, or Key Vault-backed secrets, those two statements pull in different directions.
Access is also narrower than standard Container Apps. Express requires a Microsoft Entra ID-backed account, and personal Microsoft accounts are not supported. Management happens through specialist interfaces rather than the Azure portal: containerapps.azure.com for Container Apps and sandboxes.azure.com for Sandboxes. Asked whether those replace the portal, MuhBlockchain said they do not:
It's just a separate view, though with a lot more detail. You'll still be able to manage them through the regular portal experience to.
Teams already running standard environments have a migration path, and a nudge. Self-migration works through archive and restore: archive the existing environment, then restore it as an Express environment. Microsoft says the process preserves app and environment configuration, takes about 15 minutes, and does not change the consumption-free grant. The FAQ also mentions an opt-out form in the migration notice for organizations needing additional approval or coordination, and notes that inactive environments, meaning those with no running apps or jobs and no recent activity, may be archived and put to sleep.
At general availability, Express reaches more than 40 Azure regions, covering almost every public region where Container Apps is offered. Microsoft says thousands of Express apps were created during public preview, and that customer feedback set the priorities for this release.

articles.title: Fall Into 25 New Games on GeForce NOW This October
articles.text:
Spooky season is streaming in. Alongside falling leaves, pumpkin spice and everything nice, 25 new games are joining GeForce NOW throughout October, including six ready to play this week.
From a new CONTROL Resonant reward for Performance and Ultimate members to The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt – Remastered joining the cloud, this GFN Thursday is packed with fresh reasons to play.
Claim Rewards
CONTROL Resonant is streaming from the cloud for GeForce NOW Performance and Ultimate members. Explore a warped Manhattan on the brink of paranatural annihilation as Dylan Faden harnesses extraordinary powers to battle the Hiss, the Mold and other reality-bending threats while searching for his sister, Federal Bureau of CONTROL Director Jesse Faden.
Performance and Ultimate members can claim the Third Ice Baseball Cap reward for CONTROL Resonant. After claiming the reward code, launch the Steam or Epic Games Store version of CONTROL Resonant, select “Options” from the main menu, navigate to “Gameplay” and choose “Enter Redeem Code.” The reward can be equipped after completing Act 1.
Cap it off: Claim the reward from Thursday, Oct. 1, through Sunday, Nov. 1, at 11:59 p.m. PT, before it slips into another dimension.

articles.title: Citrix NetScaler Post-Exploitation Payload Creates Superuser, Maps Web Shell to CSS-Like URLs
articles.text:
Threat actors have been observed exploiting a critical pre-authentication command injection vulnerability in Citrix NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway to drop web shells and attempt theft of configuration data.
LevelBlue's Threat Hunt Operations & Research (THOR) team, which analyzed the exploitation activity across multiple customer environments, said it identified malicious NetScaler authentication events containing attacker-controlled usernames designed to weaponize CVE-2026-88771.
CVE-2026-88771 (CVSS score: 9.5) is an improper input validation vulnerability that could allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary commands.
The security flaw, along with CVE-2026-88772, was disclosed last week after reports that the Dutch National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC-NL) reportedly sent a pre-notification to organizations in the Netherlands that urged organizations to shut their appliances down, citing active exploitation. As of writing, there are currently no details about who is behind these efforts.
"One of the most consistent characteristics across the identified events was attacker-controlled authentication data containing variations of the pitboss and NSPPE strings associated with exploitation of CVE-2026-88771," LevelBlue said.
Other attempts have been observed using curl or wget to fetch additional payloads from external servers, or extract NetScaler configuration data -
- 64.94.85[.]67:443/update_c08937.pl
- 31.56.197[.]72:9090/lula
- 23.27.143[.]20:9000/main.py
"Taken together, the observed commands demonstrate activity extending beyond basic vulnerability validation," LevelBlue said. "The attempts included payload retrieval and execution as well as collection and staging of NetScaler configuration data."
Notable among the second-stage payloads is a Python script ("main.py") that's designed to establish a reverse shell to "45.141.21[.]130" over TCP port 443. It also searches for running processes associated with "/var/python/bin/customsnmpd" and forcefully terminates them by issuing a "kill -9" command.
Another second-stage payload, "update_c08937.pl," is a Perl script with several post-exploitation capabilities -
- Modify "/flash/nsconfig/ns.conf" to create a local account named sec_monitor and assign it the superuser role.
- Archive the "/flash/nsconfig" directory into "/tmp/update_result_3567cs.tgz" and upload the resulting archive containing NetScaler configuration data to "64.94.85[.]67:443." The script then deletes the archive and erases itself to reduce the forensic footprint on disk.
- Change the permissions of "/bin/sh" to 6555 and deploy a PHP web shell at "/var/netscaler/logon/LogonPoint/.local_journal" for remote command execution and file upload and download.
- Modify "/etc/httpd.conf" to enable PHP execution and map the web shell to URLs resembling legitimate NetScaler CSS resources, corroborating activity observed by GreyNoise.
"While some attempts used commands such as whoami to test command execution, others attempted to retrieve additional payloads, collect NetScaler configuration data, establish reverse shells, create privileged accounts, and deploy web shells," LevelBlue said.
The disclosure comes a day after Mandiant Consulting and Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said dozens of organizations have been impacted by attacks exploiting CVE-2026-88772 to deliver PHP web shells, like WHIPSHOT, and a Python tunneler dubbed SLAPSHOT.

articles.title: The Download: AI “mind-reading” and creative uses for small batteries
articles.text:
The Download: AI “mind-reading” and creative uses for small batteries
Plus: the Pentagon has tapped Elon Musk to co-lead a future warfare project.
This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
An AI “mind-reading” tool can reconstruct what you’re looking at based on a brain scan
A new AI tool can guess what you’re looking at just by analyzing your brain scans—and recreate that image with remarkable precision. It can go the other way too, and predict a person’s brain activity based on what they’re looking at.
The researchers hope the “mindreading” tool could reveal more about how the brain works. It could also help locked-in people communicate and, incredibly, maybe even allow scientists to recreate the content of dreams.
But other scientists warn that a similar approach could reveal people’s inner thoughts and mental imagery, potentially without their consent.
Here’s how AI is getting closer to reading images from the brain.
—Jessica Hamzelou
How smaller, distributed batteries could help the grid
Large, utility-scale battery installations are coming online quickly around the world. But there’s been pushback from communities, especially population-dense ones like NYC, because of concerns about relatively rare but high-profile battery fires.
Faced with those obstacles, some startups are getting creative, finding ways to use relatively small batteries in unexpected places, from induction stovetops to food carts. By deploying these more consumer-focused batteries, the companies are helping people directly, cutting pollution or power bills.
These units are small on their own, but could add up to a lot of capacity. And as batteries get cheaper, they could find their way into more corners of our lives.
—Casey Crownhart
This story is from The Spark, our weekly climate tech newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Wednesday.
The must-reads
I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.

Project Meridian will examine battlefields from underground to space. (CNBC)
+ Musk will be joined by Palmer Luckey and Newt Gingrich (Guardian)

+ The Pentagon wants an AI-powered lie detector. (MIT Technology Review)
2 Chinese hackers impersonated ex-US officials to spy on American AI
The email campaign also impersonated an Anthropic employee. (CNN)
+ They targeted experts in military AI and export controls. (Reuters $)
+ OpenAI has accused China’s Moonshot AI of copying its models. (CNBC)
+ China’s DeepSeek and Huawei have teamed up on chip software. (NYT $)
+ Could China win the AI race? (MIT Technology Review)
3 After months of delays, Google has unveiled Gemini 4 Argon
The new model aims to re-establish Google at the frontier of AI. (Reuters $)
+ Google says the model beats OpenAI’s Astra on many benchmarks. (VB)
+ But some Google employees are skeptical about its coding performance. (Bloomberg $)
+ Google is testing paying publishers for AI search results. (Information $)
4 The FTC is investigating OpenAI, Anthropic, and other AI labs
The regulator will probe potential consumer harms from AI agents. (Axios)
+ It’s the first official US enforcement action on rogue agents. (Guardian)
+ Who’s liable when AI agents go rogue? (MIT Technology Review)
5 Scientists could soon create “mirror life” that evades nature’s defenses
Biologists in Singapore have called for new safeguards. (Economist $)
+ Synthetic mirror life could threaten life on Earth. (MIT Technology Review)
6 California has legalized balcony solar for renters and homeowners
The move could give plug-in solar a huge new market. (LA Times $)
+ The balcony solar boom is coming to the US. (MIT Technology Review)
7 Apple is planning a major push into the smart-home market this month
The new hub is expected to launch on October 13. (Bloomberg $)
+ New CEO John Ternus wants more product releases and fewer staff. (Quartz)
8 A new implant network uses body tissue as its wiring
It could connect tiny sensors and medical devices. (Ars Technica)
9 A modified parasite drug could be a breakthrough for endometriosis
It targets disease-causing cells and reduced lesions in mice. (Nature)
10 Singapore has a new answer to low birth rates: a government dating app
A Nobel-winning algorithm matches participants to one date at a time. (BBC)
Quote of the day
“I’ve spent my summer begging, borrowing, and stealing chips… I don’t want to say steal. Begging and borrowing!”
—Logitech CEO Hanneke Faber tells the Wall Street Journal that she’s scoured the globe for chips amid an AI-driven shortage, which she says won't ease for 12 to 18 months.
One more thing
Inside the hunt for the most dangerous asteroid ever
As asteroid 2024 YR4 hurtled toward Earth, astronomers determined that this massive rock posed a higher risk of impact than any object of its size in recorded history. Then, just as quickly as history was made, experts declared that the danger had passed.
This is the inside story of the network of global scientists who found, followed, planned for, and finally dismissed the most dangerous asteroid ever found—all under the tightest of timelines and with the highest of stakes. Find out how they did it.
—Robin George Andrews

articles.title: Inside Microsoft’s big Copilot rethink
articles.text:
Last week, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella hosted an intimate, invite-only event for leaders from some of its key enterprise customers. Instead of a flashy media event, Nadella outlined the future of Copilot directly to the customers Microsoft really cares about, pitching its latest rethink of the AI assistant as the “OS for work.”
Inside Microsoft’s big Copilot rethink
Copilot is now being positioned as the ‘OS for work.’
Microsoft is adding coding and agent capabilities directly into Copilot, as well as bringing the full power of Office into Copilot for the first time. Nadella is betting that AI will change the way people work in the same way that Microsoft Office did in the ’80s and ’90s.
“How did a multinational company do a forecast in 1981? You had interoffice memos and faxes and all of these artifacts that then just disappeared and you suddenly had an Excel spreadsheet in an email,” said Nadella. “We are the architects of a new frontier of work, using these new tools and capabilities.”
Microsoft has spent the past few months fusing together its consumer and enterprise Copilot apps into a single unified user interface, with a goal to make Copilot as influential as Office once was. The result is a big departure from the Copilot consumer design that Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman launched two years ago. That design was heavily influenced by the work Inflection AI had done with the Pi personal AI assistant, after Microsoft hired many of the Inflection AI team just months prior.
The new Copilot app now looks a lot more like the commercial one, with separate tabs for chat, coding, and the new Autopilot AI agent. There are some small nods to the consumer UI that was available before, but overall it looks like the type of enterprise app you’d associate with Microsoft.
“There’s a really important reason why we decided to do this,” said Copilot chief Jacob Andreou at Microsoft’s customer-only event last week. “The bar for enterprise software is higher than it has ever been before. The expectations we have of the tools we adopt at work are set by the things we use after hours and at the weekends at home. What this means is that consumer UX and care needs to make its way into the workplace.”
Andreou joined Microsoft AI last year, focused on product and growth. In March, Nadella appointed him as the single boss of Copilot across both commercial and consumer, reporting directly to the Microsoft CEO. He’s now responsible for the design, engineering, and growth of Copilot.
Sources familiar with Microsoft’s Copilot plans tell me that redesigning Copilot over the last six months hasn’t been easy. There have been tensions between the team under Andreou, and those working for Charles Lamanna on the Copilot, Agents, and Platform (CAP) team. Lamanna’s team has been building Microsoft Scout, an always-on personal agent built on top of OpenClaw. Microsoft announced Scout at its Build developer conference in June, with just a desktop preview app. Less than six months later, I understand that the app has been put into maintenance mode, with Microsoft focusing on the cloud version, which has been rebranded to Autopilot.
I’m told the rebrand was driven in part by legal concerns around the Scout name, as Yahoo uses “Yahoo Scout” branding for its own AI-powered features. Sources tell me Microsoft had even considered using Mico, the Clippy-like character from the consumer Copilot, to replace Scout. Nadella favored Autopilot instead, allowing Microsoft to present its AI agent in a more enterprise-friendly way, instead of a bouncing blob.
Some of Microsoft’s caution around making Autopilot too cute comes at a time when rogue AI agents are hacking into businesses. Nadella addressed these concerns last week, laying out Microsoft’s design goals for Copilot. “[It’s] about organizations having control of their firms in an age of AI, where AI by definition is a learning machine,” said Nadella. “It can’t be about leaking the core of what your firm is about.”
Andreou also admitted that agents “have been almost impossible to bring into the enterprise,” due to them needing the autonomy and flexibility that businesses usually balk at. “It is their superpower, and it’s the same thing that makes them absolutely terrifying to an IT admin.”
Microsoft thinks it has solved the AI agent problem for businesses with its “OS for work,” but it also seems to be leaving the door open for competitors like Meta and OpenAI to build the “OS for life.” In a world where 1.2 billion people use ChatGPT every week, Microsoft is playing to its traditional business-focused strengths instead of trying to compete with consumer-friendly Muse and Dots agents.
Andreou isn’t giving up on Copilot for consumers just yet, however, and he seems to want to hone in on those that want the power of enterprise apps at home. “Microsoft consumers are a little bit special. There’s almost 90 million folks that pay for Microsoft 365 out of their own pocket,” said Andreou. “These are people who value the use of things like PowerPoint and Excel so much in their personal lives that they actually go ahead and pay for it themselves.”
With Office baked into Copilot, you’ll soon be able to create and edit inside Microsoft’s AI assistant instead of having to switch to Office apps like Word and PowerPoint. There’s a full ribbon interface, and it essentially looks like the web version of Office directly inside Copilot. I think this is Microsoft’s first real acknowledgement that we’re heading to a future where AI can create a lot of the documents that people used to rely on Office for. Microsoft’s move to bring Office into Copilot has the potential to fundamentally reshape the future of Word, Excel, and PowerPoint.
Nadella is now positioning Copilot as the platform for this new AI era of work, instead of just cramming AI features into Office itself. Microsoft has tried to sell business on Copilot in Office multiple times in recent years, but the response to a $30 per month, per user Copilot subscription was lukewarm two years ago.
Nadella still thinks Microsoft will nail AI at work, and in turn convince businesses to pay for it. “The way we think of Copilot is not just the product itself changing, it’s the contours of work inside the enterprise changing,” said Nadella. [It’s] the dance between the shape of the product and the organizational structural change to work.”
The pad
- Microsoft refreshes its smaller Surface Pro and Laptop with Qualcomm’s X2 Plus. Microsoft is keeping the same design and hardware features of its existing Surface Pro 12-inch and Surface Laptop 13-inch devices, but it’s upgrading them with Qualcomm’s latest Snapdragon X2 Plus chips. That should mean better performance and battery life, but thanks to RAMageddon, it also means higher price points. Microsoft is also bringing back the black color option for both of these smaller Surface devices, with platinum silver or violet colors available too. Both of these refreshed Surface devices will be available on October 13th, with the 12-inch Surface Pro starting at $1,149.99 and the 13-inch Surface Laptop starting at $1,199.99.
- Microsoft’s new Surface Mouse has haptic feedback and a customizable action button. Microsoft’s smaller refreshed Surface devices might not be all that exciting, but the company also announced a refresh to the Surface Mouse for the first time in 10 years. The new model includes haptic feedback support and has a customizable action button for the first time. It’s nice to see more mice with haptic feedback, which works through subtle vibrations during things like clicks, drags, and alignment in Windows 11.
- Microsoft Ink Canvas is an AI-powered digital sketchpad. Microsoft is launching a new digital sketchpad app for Windows next month. Microsoft Ink Canvas will be available first on the new Surface Pro 12-inch, and other supported devices on October 13th. It supports sketching with pen or touch, and includes AI image generation and summaries. It’s essentially an AI-powered version of the various digital whiteboard apps Microsoft has created over the years.
- Microsoft puts Brad Smith in charge of communications. Microsoft is moving its communications group out of marketing and into its Corporate, External, and Legal Affairs (CELA) organization. The surprise change will see Microsoft vice chair and president Brad Smith oversee communications, while the company searches for a replacement for Frank Shaw, chief communications officer, who is departing later this year. This move seems to position Microsoft PR to be more like how AI startups operate, allowing researchers to lead demos and write blogs. Microsoft is still chasing Google, Anthropic, and OpenAI to become a top AI model lab, and Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella says he’s “excited about the opportunity to help our engineers, sellers, partners, and others closest to our products and customers become an even bigger part of how we tell our story.”
- Bill Gates says regulate AI, because it’s powerful enough to cause a billion deaths. While Microsoft is pushing ahead with its new Copilot app, Microsoft cofounder Bill Gates wants AI regulations. In an interview with NBC News, Gates says that AI is “certainly powerful enough to drive events that, you know, cause a billion deaths.” He wants politicians and law enforcement to “get into the discussion about what safeguards and monitoring look like.”
- Microsoft is killing off the “Copilot Plus PC” brand. When Microsoft announced its Surface Laptop Ultra in May, there was no Copilot Plus PC branding to be found. Even though the new 12-inch Microsoft Surface Pro and 13-inch Surface Laptop technically meet the system requirements for a Copilot Plus PC, Microsoft is not calling them by that name anymore. There doesn’t appear to be a direct replacement after two and a half years of Copilot Plus PCs, but Microsoft does have a Windows event next week, so maybe we’ll hear about a new brand for its AI-focused PCs.
- Human workers are reviewing prompts and images sent to Microsoft Copilot. Human contractors are reviewing Copilot users’ prompts and uploaded images, according to a new report from 404 Media. The publication reports that some contractors working on Copilot have described seeing disturbing requests and potentially illegal images. “Faces are always uncensored, and many of the prompts are sexual in nature and dubiously consensual,” says one person who reportedly works on the Copilot prompts.
- Xbox’s Mythic Achievements are here, and they’re just like PlayStation Platinum trophies. Microsoft has officially announced its new Xbox Mythic Achievements, and they’re already available for Xbox Insiders to test. Mythic Achievements work a lot like Sony’s PlayStation Platinum trophies and are unlocked once you’ve earned every original achievement for a game. Mythic Achievements leaked as part of an Xbox PC app last week, complete with a unique unlock sound. Mythic Achievements are now in testing just weeks after Xbox CEO Asha Sharma revealed that Xbox would be getting a platinum trophy equivalent later this year.
- Windows 11’s 2026 update is now available. Microsoft is rolling out Windows 11 version 26H2, aka the Windows 11 2026 Update. It’s what Microsoft calls a “small enablement package,” allowing Windows 11 users to download and install the latest release quickly with a single restart. So what’s new? Well, due to the way Microsoft releases new Windows features these days, many of the same features that have been rolling out to version 25H2 will be part of 26H2.
- Gears of War: E-Day is a great game launching at a terrible time. My colleague Andrew Webster has been playing Gears of War: E-Day, and he’s impressed. “E-Day is reminiscent of a James Cameron film: Absolutely every element is in service to creating a thrilling sci-fi spectacle,” says Webster. “It’s as close to a playable Aliens as you’re bound to find.”
- Xbox’s Gears of War pizza cutter sold out in hours. Speaking of Gears of War, Xbox has teamed up with Prince St. Pizza to launch a pizza cutter to mark the launch of E-Day. The $60 cutter is built in the shape of the Prototype Lancer weapon from the game, and also includes an in-game pizza emblem. Unfortunately for Gears of War fans, the cutter sold out within hours of going on sale. Still, Prince St. Pizza will also be selling an “Emergence Pie” pizza with a spicy vodka sauce, so if you’re lucky they might even carve it up for you with the Lancer cutter.
- “Xbox is not for sale” says Microsoft’s gaming chief. Xbox CEO Asha Sharma has denied reports that Microsoft is considering selling off its Xbox business. “Xbox is not for sale,” says Sharma in an interview with The New York Times. “We will do whatever it takes to set the company up for success, and we will look at the right partnerships, the right operating model and everything needed to achieve that.” The Information reported in June that Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella and CFO Amy Hood had been considering spinning out Xbox entirely, and then reported earlier this month that both execs have “more recently supported Sharma’s plans to overhaul the unit.” The overhaul includes moving Halo, Sea of Thieves, and Age of Empires under Activision, as well as selling off smaller Xbox studios. The recent changes look geared toward making Xbox a wholly owned subsidiary like Microsoft has done with LinkedIn.
Note: I’m traveling to San Francisco next week for the Windows and Surface event on October 7th, so Notepad might not arrive on time.
I’m always keen to hear from readers, so please drop a comment here, or you can reach me at notepad@theverge.com if you want to discuss anything else. If you’ve heard about any of Microsoft’s secret projects, you can reach me via email at notepad@theverge.com or speak to me confidentially on the Signal messaging app, where I’m tomwarren.01. I’m also tomwarren on Telegram, if you’d prefer to chat there.

articles.title: Google lanza su primer satélite para llevarse los centros de datos al espacio
articles.text:
Google lanza su primer satélite para llevarse los centros de datos al espacio
La empresa investiga cómo crear servidores en la órbita terrestre. SpaceX y otras empresas le llevan cuerpos de ventaja
Un cohete Falcon 9 ha despegado este jueves desde California con el primer satélite del proyecto Suncatcher, una iniciativa a largo plazo de la tecnológica Google para explorar cómo enviar al espacio centros de datos con una capacidad similar a los terrestres. El lanzamiento se ha producido alrededor de las ocho y media de la tarde, hora peninsular española.
Las grandes compañías tecnológicas aspiran a que el espacio sea un lugar privilegiado donde desplegar grandes servidores, en parte para escapar de los impactos sociales y ambientales que estas grandes infraestructuras generan en tierra.
Elon Musk, de SpaceX, Sam Altman, de OpenAI, Jeff Bezos, de Amazon, y Jensen Huang, de Nvidia, están de acuerdo en que el futuro está en llevar los servidores a la órbita terrestre, aunque hoy por hoy se trata de un objetivo aún lejano; y en ningún caso se replicará en el espacio lo que ya existe en la superficie terrestre.
Con el lanzamiento de este jueves, Google se convierte en la primera gran tecnológica en empezar un proyecto de este tipo. No es, sin embargo, la primera empresa que lleva al espacio servidores en miniatura para explorar la viabilidad del proyecto. Por ejemplo, la compañía Starcloud lanzó en noviembre de 2025 su primer satélite con una unidad de procesamiento gráfico (GPU) del gigante de los chips Nvidia, y tiene previsto un segundo en octubre.
La gran diferencia es que Google manda al espacio una tecnología propia compuesta por cuatro chips denominados unidades de procesamiento de tensor (TPU), el ladrillo básico en el que se sustenta toda su inteligencia artificial (IA). Este primer prototipo es equiparable en potencia a solo una de las miles de unidades de procesamiento que en la actualidad componen los grandes centros de datos.
El gran objetivo del lanzamiento de este jueves es entender si los chips de la compañía resisten las condiciones del espacio exterior sin fallar, especialmente si les azota una tormenta solar. Si todo va bien, la empresa planea lanzar otros dos artefactos similares al espacio en 2027 para comenzar a probar su sistema de comunicación.
La idea que persiguen las tecnológicas no es replicar estos enormes centros de datos en el espacio, lo que sería prácticamente inviable con la tecnología actual y además muy caro. En su lugar, se planea crear redes de cientos de satélites comunicados por láser, de forma que puedan hacer grandes tareas de computación, archivar datos de máximo secreto o ser una red de seguridad si se caen los servidores terrestres. En el mejor de los casos, esta capa de servidores espaciales sería un complemento a la de los terrestres, pero no un sustituto.
El proyecto plantea aún muchos retos tecnológicos difíciles de resolver, como los fallos en los chips causados por la radiación espacial, la rápida obsolescencia de los procesadores y, sobre todo, el coste de enviar una gran flotilla de satélites de IA al espacio.
Google considera que su proyecto de investigación puede llevar unos 15 años, que es lo que han tardado en desarrollar coches sin conductor, desde los inicios en 2009, al medio millón de pasajeros a la semana que tiene en la actualidad su filial Waymo.
Competidores espaciales
Uno de los grandes limitadores de este futuro es el coste de llevar cualquier cosa al espacio. En la actualidad, gracias a los cohetes reutilizables, dominados por SpaceX, es de unos 3.000 dólares por kilo. Para que los centros de datos espaciales sean rentables, habría que reducir ese corte hasta una décima parte. Es algo que Google no espera que ocurra hasta mediados de la próxima década.
El gran favorito para conseguir esa caída de precios radical es Elon Musk con el cohete más potente de la historia, el Starship. Si algún día consigue ir y volver al espacio sin fallos, y ser completamente reutilizable, podría bajar los precios hasta apenas 100 euros por kilo, según el magnate. Su principal empresa, SpaceX, sería la mayor beneficiaria, y también la mejor situada para desplegar servidores de IA, para la que aprovecharía parte de la tecnología ya existente de su red de satélites Starlink, cuyos dispositivos ya se comunican usando haces de luz láser.
El conglomerado empresarial de Musk ha pedido ya permiso para lanzar un millón de satélites para un “centro de datos en órbita” para el que no maneja fechas. La empresa Blue Origin de Jeff Bezos ha pedido licencia para una constelación de 51.600 satélites para su propio centro de datos espacial. Pero aún no han lanzado prototipos al espacio.
Este primer satélite de Google, creado en colaboración con la empresa espacial Planet Labs, tendrá una vida útil de un año. Seguirá una órbita en la que sus paneles mirarán siempre al Sol, clave para aproximar al máximo la energía disponible. Aún así, este primer artefacto solo generará una energía equivalente a la que usa un microondas. Los chips a bordo podrán realizar operaciones sencillas y comunicarse con la IA terrena de Google, Gemini, durante unos 15 minutos cada vez.
Una gran baza de los servidores espaciales es que no necesitarían las ingentes cantidades de agua que emplean en Tierra para refrigerarse, porque la temperatura media es de menos de 100 grados bajo cero. Pero el vacío hace que el calor generado por la computación no se disipe, lo que implica dotar a los satélites con sistemas adicionales para radiar el calor, y limita por ahora la capacidad de computación en órbita.

articles.title: South African startup Exten AI helps non-technical founders build full-stack apps in plain language - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
South African startup Exten AI has developed an AI-native platform that lets entrepreneurs with no coding skills build working software applications just by describing them in everyday language.
Launched earlier this year by Luncedo Simelane, Exten AI turns natural-language prompts into production-ready apps. Unlike many “text-to-code” tools, it goes beyond the frontend, providing a robust underlying infrastructure layer for every generated application, and instantly provisioning a full backend that includes an isolated database, file storage, secure user authentication infrastructure, and the runtimes required to host and run autonomous AI agents.
“It is basically a digital tech co-founder to a non-technical entrepreneur with a great software idea, delivering a production-ready stack in under 30 minutes,” Simelane told Disrupt Africa.
Simelane taught himself coding before leaving his LLB studies to focus on software architecture full-time.
“I realised that tech infrastructure gaps were the single biggest bottleneck holding back African innovation,” he said, adding that the key gap in the market is what he calls the “plumbing problem”.
“Global text-to-code platforms primarily serve existing developers to make them code faster, or stop at creating superficial visual frontends,” he said. “Solo builders and small business merchants hit a brick wall because they don’t know how to deploy backend systems, structure relational databases, or handle security authentication. Exten AI solves this exact problem by acting as an automated technical partner.”
On competition, Simelane said: “We sit between global frontend prompt tools, which skip the database entirely, and complex enterprise low-code systems like Microsoft Power Apps, which are far too expensive and rigid for emerging market creators.”
The startup is fully bootstrapped. An early proof of concept was endorsed on Sunday Sessions by Professor Mamokgethi Phakeng, former vice-chancellor of the University of Cape Town, and Exten AI is launching a pilot at the end of September with the University of Fort Hare’s Centre of Entrepreneurship and Rapid Incubator. Student founders there will use the platform to build MVPs for their businesses.
“Demand immediately outpaced our initial server capabilities,” Simelane said. The first public release drew over 100 signups, and Exten AI moved into a closed-cohort testing phase to keep its infrastructure stable. Early users have already launched live apps, including LedgerAI for accounting automation, EduAgent for teachers’ lesson planning, and LuminaAI, a custom communication dashboard.
Exten AI uses a tiered SaaS subscription model.
“While generating and testing apps is frictionless, users pay a predictable monthly subscription once their apps go live to the public,” Simelane said. Pricing scales with server load, database storage, and AI agent usage. “Because we’ve prioritised architecture optimisation during our closed-cohort phase to perfect our user unit economics, early revenues have been minimal.”
Scaling has been the biggest challenge.
“Having dozens of users simultaneously asking an AI engine to map out, provision, and launch complex database schemas live on the cloud caused massive infrastructure queues early on,” Simelane said. “It required weeks of deep-dive architecture rewrites to isolate and stream these automated builds.”
Exten AI is now raising a ZAR1.5 million (US$90,000) investment round to scale its server layers and support thousands of concurrent builds. The startup is currently focused on South African SMEs and solo founders, but plans to expand to tech hubs and university incubators across Sub-Saharan Africa.
“Emerging markets are experiencing a severe software developer shortage alongside an explosion of young entrepreneurs who need localised digital tooling to survive and scale,” Simelane said.

articles.title: Simple Energy bets Rs 1,750 Cr fundraise on clearing delivery backlog, scaling across India
articles.text:
Simple Energy bets Rs 1,750 Cr fundraise on clearing delivery backlog, scaling across India
Shreshth Mishra, Co-founder of Simple Energy, an electric two-wheeler maker, explains how the company’s recent Rs 1,750 crore Series C funding will help address past delivery delays and working capital bottlenecks.
Electric two-wheeler maker Simple Energy on Wednesday raised Rs 1,750 crore in its Series C funding round, taking its total funding to more than Rs 2,530 crore.
The equity round was led by Dr. Arokiaswamy Velumani Family Office alongside co-founders Suhas Rajkumar and Ankit Gupta, with participation from Bengaluru-based HNI Amit Mishra and the Haran Family Office.
The round is among the largest equity raises in the EV two-wheeler space. For Shreshth Mishra, Co-founder of Simple Energy, however, the immediate priority is less about the size of the fundraise and more about what it allows the company to execute.
“This latest round isn’t just about capital—it’s about scale,” Mishra told YourStory.
Founded in 2019 by Suhas Rajkumar and later joined by Mishra and Ankit Gupta as co-founders, Simple Energy develops electric two-wheelers with much of the vehicle architecture developed in-house, including the chassis, battery pack, motor, and software.
The Bengaluru-based company has also built its own powertrain, from development through manufacturing. That approach, Mishra says, has become particularly important as the company has dealt with supply chain disruptions and sought greater control over critical components.
“When you’re building a hardware and manufacturing business, it is incredibly capital-intensive," he said.
In its early years, Simple Energy faced notable hurdles, from supply chain bottlenecks to delayed delivery timelines that tested customer patience.
“As a startup, you’re always trying to extract the absolute maximum out of every minimal input,” Mishra said.
“Now, this capital allows us to fix those working capital cycles, clear our backlogs, and scale faster to deliver on our promises,” he added.
Scaling existing capacity
Rather than acquiring new land, Simple Energy is focusing on expansion on its existing Krishnagiri campus, where it plans to ramp up production over the next 10 to 24 months.
The company’s in-house engineering capabilities are also intended to reduce its exposure to some external supply shocks.
“We didn’t lose a single day of production line output because of rare-earth magnet shortages,” Mishra shared, pointing out that Simple Energy became the first Indian OEM to commercially deploy heavy rare-earth-free motors, with nearly 15,000 units on the road.
The company has similarly sought to keep control over other parts of its product development, including its chassis, battery, and software. It claims to have developed its electric two-wheelers around factors such as range, charging time, and affordability.
The fresh funds will also drive an aggressive retail rollout. Building beyond its current network of over 80 outlets across 60-plus cities, Simple Energy is targeting Tier II and Tier III markets across northern, central, and eastern India, leveraging its models like the Simple One, Simple Wave, and Simple Ultra.
But Mishra stresses that expanding reach means more than just opening showrooms. “It’s not just about the sales experience; after-sales support is critical,” he said, noting that every new retail outlet will be paired with a dedicated service centre.
Reducing supply-chain risks
Looking ahead, the company is preparing to de-risk its supply chain by partnering with emerging domestic cell manufacturers while navigating ongoing global dependencies for semiconductors.
Charging infrastructure is another area where the company is opting to work with existing networks rather than build an entire proprietary system. By partnering with operators like Bolt, Simple Energy allows riders to tap into existing public infrastructure.
“Our goal is to make sure we’re self-sustainable in the coming period,” Mishra said, setting the stage for Simple Energy's eventual path toward the public market.

articles.title: Face aux Meta Ray-Ban, Rokid débarque officiellement en France avec 2 paires de lunettes intelligentes
articles.text:
Face aux Meta Ray-Ban, Rokid débarque officiellement en France avec 2 paires de lunettes intelligentes
Après l'Allemagne, Rokid, le spécialiste chinois de la réalité augmentée, poursuit sa percée européenne en s'attaquant au marché français.
Le marché des lunettes connectées compte un acteur de plus dans l'Hexagone. Rokid, qui s'est fait un nom dans la réalité augmentée et l'intelligence artificielle, a profité du Mondial de l'Optique de Villepinte pour dévoiler son offre française. Au programme, deux modèles et un allié inattendu pour les distribuer.
“La France est un marché qui structure la présence de Rokid en Europe, alors que nous poursuivons le développement de notre présence à l’international”, explique Zoro Shao, Global General Manager de la marque, qui confirme au passage un partenariat avec le réseau Krys Opticiens, d'abord à Paris, puis dans plusieurs boutiques ailleurs sur le territoire, sans plus de précisions.
Rokid AI Glasses et Style Pack : deux modèles de lunettes aux philosophies distinctes
Le lancement s'articule autour de deux produits bien distincts. Les Rokid AI Glasses, d'abord, misent sur un affichage en réalité augmentée binoculaire et concernent plutôt les usages professionnels. Motorisées par la plateforme Qualcomm AR1, elles embarquent des fonctions de traduction et de transcription en temps réel, ainsi qu'un assistant IA multi-LLM, compatible notamment avec GPT et Gemini. Le tout tient dans un format pesant 49 g, ce qui reste très raisonnable pour des lunettes censées afficher de l'information devant vos yeux toute la journée. L'idée, vous l'aurez compris, est de permettre à l'utilisateur d'accéder à ses données et de communiquer dans plusieurs langues sans jamais sortir son smartphone de sa poche.
Le second modèle, baptisé Rokid AI Glasses Style Pack, fait l'impasse sur l'écran. Tout passe ici par l'interaction vocale avec une prise en charge de 12 langues à l'oral et 86 pour la traduction. Rokid positionne ce modèle comme un compagnon du quotidien, pensé pour les voyages et la création de contenus plutôt que pour la productivité en entreprise. Il vient se placer en concurrence frontale avec la flopée de lunettes Meta Ray-Ban.
Open AI Ecosystem : l'atout logiciel de Rokid face à la concurrence
Côté logiciel, Rokid a décidé de prendre à contre-pied un marché où chaque constructeur tend à verrouiller son environnement. Son Open AI Ecosystem est ainsi présenté comme la première plateforme permettant à des lunettes intelligentes d'exploiter plusieurs grands modèles de langage, sans enfermer l'utilisateur dans un écosystème propriétaire.
Pour les développeurs, la marque propose AIUI Studio, un outil accessible directement depuis un navigateur et qui ne réclame aucune expérience en programmation. Il suffit de décrire son idée en langage naturel pour que l'outil génère l'application correspondante. En revanche, la tarification à terme de cette fonctionnalité reste floue. La communauté de développeurs de la marque revendique en tout cas près de 35 000 inscrits. Plus de 500 agents sont même d'ores et déjà disponibles sur son Agent Store.
Prix, disponibilité et partenariat avec Krys Opticiens en France
Pour toucher le grand public, Rokid a choisi de s'appuyer sur un réseau bien implanté plutôt que sur les seuls circuits high-tech. Krys Opticiens proposera les lunettes connectées de la marque dans une dizaine de ses magasins. Un choix de distribution qui en dit long sur l'ambition de Rokid de faire passer ses lunettes du rayon gadget au rayon optique.
Reste la question des prix. Les Rokid AI Glasses avec affichage sont proposées seules à 699 €, tandis que le Style Pack sans écran s'affiche à 499 €. Pour le lancement, deux offres groupées sont mises en avant. Le Rokid AI Glasses Travel Set, qui ajoute une boîte de chargement, des verres solaires, un concentrateur audio et des accessoires de voyage, est proposé à 649 € en précommande du 25 septembre au 22 octobre.
Le Rokid Style Travel Set, avec boîte de chargement et verres photochromiques, descend quant à lui à 449 €. Ces packs sont disponibles en précommande sur la boutique officielle jusqu'au 22 octobre pour des expéditions à partir du 25 octobre.

articles.title: WhatsApp renforce son contrôle parental pour les ados
articles.text:
Superviser l’utilisation que font vos ados de leur compte WhatsApp sans pour autant s’immiscer dans leur vie privée est un difficile équilibre. Pour vous permettre de guider votre progéniture dans l’utilisation de la messagerie, WhatsApp introduit de nouvelles options dans son contrôle parental.
Ces nouvelles options, spécifiquement destinées à la supervision des comptes des adolescents, visent à encourager le dialogue familial en permettant aux parents d’avoir une visibilité adaptée à l’utilisation que fait leur enfant mineur de l’application.
Des options pour mieux accompagner l’ado dans l’usage de WhatsApp
Ces nouvelles options intégrées au contrôle parental, totalement facultatives, viennent s’ajouter aux protections déjà existantes au sein de l’application. Elles ont pour but principal d’aider les parents à accompagner leurs ados dans l’utilisation qu’ils ont de la messagerie. Pour fonctionner, il est donc nécessaire de relier le compte du parent à celui de l’ado.
Mais le champ d’action des parents est suffisamment restrictif pour ne pas empiéter sur l’intimité de leur progéniture. Les parents peuvent ainsi définir les paramètres de confidentialité de leur ado, notamment pour ce qui est de choisir qui a le droit de voir sa photo de profil et ses informations personnelles, ou de l’ajouter à des groupes.
Dans le cas où l’ado souhaiterait assouplir les règles mises en place dans les paramètres de confidentialité de son appli, toute modification de ces paramètres devra être validée par un parent qui devra saisir un code PIN parental.
Les parents seront informés par des notifications lors de certains événements. Ce sera par exemple le cas quand l’ado rejoint ou quitte un groupe, si un groupe dans lequel votre ado se trouve s’agrandit significativement ou encore lors de l’ajout d’un nouveau contact.
Certaines fonctionnalités de WhatsApp seront par ailleurs encadrées. Les parents pourront ainsi choisir qui est autorisé à voir les Statuts de leur ado, mais aussi quels Status ces derniers sont autorisés à consulter. Il en sera de même pour ce qui est de l’accès aux Chaînes WhatsApp.
Contrôler l’activité sans bafouer l’intimité
Trouver la juste limite entre un contrôle parental strict et trop permissif peut sembler délicat. Si la question ne se pose pas pour les ados de moins de 13 ans, pour les plus vieux, la question de préserver leur intimité est indispensable. Si toutes les conversations (messages et appels) restent chiffrées de bout en bout avec le contrôle parental activé, la confidentialité des échanges des ados est elle aussi préservée.
Car personne en dehors de la discussion, pas même les parents superviseurs, n’est en mesure de lire le contenu des conversations, d’écouter les appels ou d’accéder aux contenus échangés par l’ado. Surtout, les adolescents sont automatiquement informés de ce qu’implique la mise en place du contrôle parental sur leur compte WhatsApp.
WhatsApp précise que le déploiement de ces nouvelles options de contrôle parental est en cours et se fera de manière progressive. Il est donc probable que vous ne voyiez pas ces nouveautés immédiatement dans votre application.

articles.title: Kpop Demon Hunter 2 va voir très grand avec un gros virage de la part de Netflix
articles.text:
Netflix sortait déjà des films en salles (plus de 30 l’an dernier selon Ted Sarandos, le co-CEO de Netflix), mais avec des dispositifs limités et faits sur mesure. Pour sa plus grosse licence familiale, la plateforme change d’échelle. Lors de la conférence Bloomberg Screentime, ce mercredi 30 septembre à Los Angeles, Ted Sarandos a promis « une très large sortie en salles » pour la suite du film d’animation, avec une sortie « grande, large et mondiale » pour Kpop Demon Hunter 2.
La suite, de nouveau réalisée par Maggie Kang et Chris Appelhans, est attendue pour 2029 selon Deadline, mais Netflix n’a pas encore fixé de date. Ted Sarandos n’a précisé ni les pays concernés, ni la durée d’exclusivité en salles, si c’est bien de cela qu’il s’agit.
Les exploitants de salles reprochaient depuis longtemps à Netflix de refuser une exclusivité de 45 jours au cinéma. La chaîne américaine AMC, qui boycottait la plateforme pour cette raison, avait même boudé la première sortie de Kpop Demon Hunters en août 2025.
Un carton sur Netflix pour Kpop Demon Hunter, puis un succès surprise en salles
Le premier film Kpop Demon Hunter est devenu le film le plus vu de l’histoire de Netflix, devant Red Notice, avec 325,1 millions de vues en 91 jours. KPop Demon Hunters suit un groupe de popstars qui chassent les démons la nuit.
En août 2025, la plateforme tente un coup d’essai timide en projetant le film pendant seulement 48 heures dans 1 700 salles nord-américaines. Plus de 1 000 séances ont affiché complet, selon Netflix, et le film a rapporté entre 18 et 20 millions de dollars en deux jours. Le film est revenu en salles pour le week-end d’Halloween, du 31 octobre au 2 novembre 2025, aux États-Unis et dans une douzaine d’autres pays, dont le Royaume-Uni, l’Espagne et l’Allemagne, mais pas la France.
Pour Ted Sarandos, les fans les plus passionnés voient le film en salle en premier, et ceux qui le découvrent ensuite sur Netflix sont surtout des spectateurs occasionnels. Il admet aussi qu’un film qui marche au cinéma ne cartonne pas forcément sur la plateforme.
IMAX, fenêtres de 50 jours, Netflix élargit sa place au cinéma
Ce virage vers les salles obscures ne s’arrête pas aux chasseuses de démons. KPop Demon Hunters 2 s’inscrit dans une nouvelle stratégie où Netflix se sert du cinéma pour faire monter l’attente autour de ses gros films, sans en attendre de grosses recettes.
Pendant des années, Netflix a tenu la salle à distance. Ted Sarandos qualifiait même la fenêtre d’exclusivité au cinéma de « concept dépassé », rappelle Variety. L’entreprise admet aujourd’hui qu’une sortie en salles peut faire grandir une licence avant son arrivée sur la plateforme. Ted Sarandos présente pourtant ce choix comme sélectif : les sorties larges iront aux films familiaux que le public revoit en boucle, quand les films d’auteur suivront un autre parcours.
