articles.title: OpenAI: Califórnia abre investigação após agentes de IA invadirem sistemas
articles.text:
O procurador-geral da Califórnia (EUA), Rob Bonta, emitiu intimação investigativa à OpenAI como parte de apuração sobre incidentes e possíveis riscos de cibersegurança relacionados aos modelos de inteligência artificial (IA) da empresa. A investigação foi anunciada nesta quinta-feira (1) pelo escritório do procurador-geral.
A iniciativa amplia o escrutínio sobre o comportamento de agentes de IA desenvolvidos pela OpenAI, especialmente depois de incidentes em que esses sistemas realizaram ações não autorizadas contra infraestruturas de terceiros.
“Meu escritório está fazendo perguntas adicionais à OpenAI sobre incidentes e riscos de cibersegurança envolvendo a empresa e seus modelos de IA”, afirmou Bonta em comunicado.
Segundo o procurador-geral, desenvolvedores de IA podem enfrentar responsabilização legal caso não garantam que seus modelos não realizem ou possibilitem ataques cibernéticos.
Investigação envolve caso da Hugging Face
- A apuração ocorre após o chamado incidente da Hugging Face, ocorrido em julho. Agentes de IA desenvolvidos pela OpenAI conseguiram acessar partes da infraestrutura da plataforma de código aberto, em episódio que expôs riscos relacionados ao comportamento autônomo de sistemas avançados;
- No mês passado, Bonta já havia anunciado que o Departamento de Justiça da Califórnia conduziria uma investigação formal sobre o caso;
- A nova intimação amplia a apuração para outros incidentes e riscos associados aos modelos da OpenAI, que não se manifestou a respeito.
Leia mais:
- OpenAI negocia rodada de R$ 156,1 bi e pode atingir valuation de R$ 7,3 tri
- OpenAI acusa chinesa Moonshot de destilar suas IAs
- OpenAI: agentes de IA podem ter afetado mais de 100 organizações
Pressão sobre empresas de IA aumenta
A investigação da Califórnia ocorre em meio à ampliação das apurações sobre os riscos relacionados a agentes de IA.
A Federal Trade Commission (FTC) também conduz investigação sobre OpenAI, Anthropic e outros laboratórios de IA. A iniciativa busca avaliar possíveis riscos dessas tecnologias para consumidores e representa a primeira ação oficial de fiscalização nos Estados Unidos voltada especificamente ao comportamento de agentes de IA considerados fora de controle.
Além disso, uma coalizão de procuradores-gerais de 15 estados estadunidenses, liderada pela procuradora-geral de Iowa, Brenna Bird, busca informações da OpenAI sobre o incidente envolvendo a Hugging Face.
A OpenAI também vem investigando outros casos em que seus agentes acessaram sistemas comerciais e governamentais sem autorização.
A nova investigação da Califórnia coloca o comportamento desses agentes no centro de uma apuração estadual sobre segurança, riscos tecnológicos e possíveis responsabilidades legais das empresas que desenvolvem sistemas de IA.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: This new qubit could be 100 times less error-prone in superfluid quantum computer breakthrough
articles.text:
This new qubit could be 100 times less error-prone in superfluid quantum computer breakthrough
- Date:
- October 1, 2026
- Source:
- University of Surrey
- Summary:
- A proposed qubit made with superfluid helium could cut quantum computing error rates by around 100 times by shielding quantum information from common forms of electromagnetic noise. If experiments confirm the predictions, the technology could eventually work alongside today’s superconducting qubits or serve as a new kind of quantum memory.
- Share:
Researchers at the University of Surrey have proposed a new kind of qubit that could help address one of the biggest obstacles in quantum computing: keeping error rates low as systems become larger.
The concept uses superfluid helium, a form of helium with unusual quantum properties, to create a qubit that may be less sensitive to some of the disturbances that affect today's leading quantum computers.
Why Quantum Computers Struggle With Errors
Quantum computers rely on qubits to store and process information in ways that conventional computers cannot. Many current systems use superconducting circuits, but these are highly sensitive to electromagnetic noise and stray electrical charges - similar to the static electricity that can make hair cling to a balloon.
Even very small disturbances can disrupt the fragile quantum information stored in a qubit. As more qubits are added, controlling those errors becomes increasingly difficult, making scalability one of the central challenges in quantum computing.
In a study published in npj Quantum Information, researchers from Surrey's Quantum Sciences Group describe a different approach built around superfluid helium-3 - an unusual form of liquid helium that can flow without friction.
Their proposed device, called the Superfluid Helium Oscillator Quantum (SHOQ) device, would use charge-neutral superfluid helium. Because the helium carries no electric charge, the design could be naturally protected from certain types of electromagnetic noise.
A Qubit With Much Lower Predicted Error Rates
According to the researchers, this is the first reported design for a qubit based on a superfluid. Their calculations suggest the SHOQ device could have error rates about 100 times lower than conventional superconducting qubits.
Dr. Priya Sharma, Daphne Jackson Fellow in Hybrid Quantum Systems at the University of Surrey's School of Mathematics and Physics, and lead author of the study, said:
"We are not the first to think about the individual components behind this idea, but what we have done for the first time is bring them together in a microfluidic device and work out the specific details that could enable the device to function as a qubit.
"The maths tells us that it should work. We have taken what we already know about superfluid helium and quantum technologies and turned that into an educated design, with the parameters and specifications needed to build one. The next step is to make a prototype and put those predictions to the test."
Rather than replacing existing quantum computing hardware, the researchers say the SHOQ device could potentially be integrated with superconducting quantum technology.
That could allow different types of qubits to perform different jobs within the same system, depending on their strengths.
A Possible Role as Quantum Memory
One longer-term possibility is to use the SHOQ device as a form of quantum memory. In that setup, a superfluid based qubit could store quantum information while other hardware carries out calculations.
Dr. Eran Ginossar, Associate Professor at the University of Surrey's Department of Physics and Advanced Technology Institute, and co-author of the study, said:
"We don't necessarily need one type of qubit to do everything. Combining different quantum technologies could allow us to take advantage of the strengths of each.
"Superfluid helium gives us a fundamentally different type of quantum hardware to explore. If the predicted performance can be demonstrated experimentally, it could eventually work alongside existing superconducting technologies as part of a larger quantum system."
The Next Step Is Building a Prototype
The team now plans to build a prototype to find out whether the predicted performance can be reproduced in a real device. That effort is being supported by an IAA Commercialisation Fellowship awarded to Dr. Priya Sharma.
The SHOQ device would need to operate at extremely low temperatures, but researchers have already reached the necessary conditions in previous experiments involving superfluid helium-3.
The project was led by the University of Surrey in collaboration with Professor Jens Koch at Northwestern University in the United States. Koch was one of the researchers involved in developing the transmon - a superconducting qubit design that is now widely used in quantum computing.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Surrey. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Priya Sharma, Jens Koch, Eran Ginossar. Towards a micromechanical qubit based on quantized oscillations in superfluid helium. npj Quantum Information, 2026; DOI: 10.1038/s41534-026-01355-3

articles.title: Gemini 4 Argon, la nueva IA de Google: por qué los primeros en usarla son expertos en ciberseguridad
articles.text:
Este 30 de septiembre, Google anunció Gemini 4 Argon, el modelo de inteligencia artificial más potente que tiene. Lo presentó Koray Kavukcuoglu, vicepresidente sénior de Google DeepMind y arquitecto jefe de IA de la compañía. Y en el mismo texto avisó que, por ahora, ni los desarrolladores ni los suscriptores que pagan lo van a poder usar.
Los primeros en recibirlo son equipos de ciberseguridad elegidos por Google dentro de un programa llamado Fairwind, lanzado el 2 de septiembre para gobiernos, agencias y socios de ciberseguridad de confianza. En paralelo, la empresa participa del proceso voluntario con el que el gobierno de Estados Unidos revisa los modelos antes de que salgan al mercado.
PUBLICIDAD
Fecha para el resto: “Lo antes posible”.
Hasta hace poco, un lanzamiento de IA era eso, un lanzamiento: comunicado, demostración y botón para probar. La IA más potente ya no sale al público. Sale a los que defienden sistemas. Si usás el chat gratis de Google, no busques Argon: no está.
La herramienta que tapa agujeros es la misma que los encuentra
Google dice que Argon puede encontrar, verificar y reparar por su cuenta fallas graves de software. Una falla es un error en un programa que un atacante puede usar para entrar. El sistema que la detecta para arreglarla es el mismo que la detecta para aprovecharla. No hay dos versiones.
PUBLICIDAD
Por eso Google entrega el modelo a los defensores de confianza y a sus propios equipos “sin barandas” de ciberseguridad: sin los filtros que lo frenan cuando alguien le pide algo riesgoso. Para todos los demás, los filtros siguen puestos y se ajustan con lo que aprenda de este grupo.
El ejemplo que Google eligió para mostrarlo: Wiz, una empresa de seguridad, usó Argon y encontró una falla grave en un software de salud que usan hospitales de todo el mundo y que dejaba expuestos datos personales. Según Google, los modelos anteriores no la habían visto.
Una herramienta que encuentra fallas a esa escala vale lo mismo para el que repara y para el que ataca. Google elige a quién se la da primero y gana tiempo para ajustar los filtros antes de abrirla.
PUBLICIDAD
El gobierno de Estados Unidos entró en el calendario
El 2 de junio, la Casa Blanca firmó una orden ejecutiva que creó un mecanismo voluntario: las empresas pueden darle al gobierno hasta 30 días de acceso a sus modelos más avanzados antes de entregarlos a socios de confianza, y colaborar en elegir a esos socios. Sin licencias ni permisos obligatorios, pero con la invitación sobre la mesa.
OpenAI ya había pasado por ese circuito: el 26 de junio abrió GPT-5.6 a un grupo reducido de socios elegidos, bajo revisión del gobierno, y recién el 9 de julio al público. Google acaba de hacer lo mismo con Argon. Dos de las tres empresas que dominan el mercado ya ordenan sus lanzamientos con el Estado en la lista.
PUBLICIDAD
Nadie firmó una ley. Alcanzó con una orden ejecutiva y con que el primero aceptara. Después del segundo, quedarse afuera del proceso tiene más costo que entrar.
Los números los midió Google
El anuncio trae tablas: Argon supera a GPT-6 Astra, de OpenAI, y a Claude Opus 5.5, de Anthropic, en pruebas de programación, finanzas y trabajo legal. En una de ellas, que mide tareas largas de ingeniería de software, marca 77,9%, el mejor resultado conocido.
Todas las cifras las produjo Google. Nadie fuera de la empresa y del grupo elegido puede repetir la prueba hoy.
Eso no es un detalle: es consecuencia directa del modo de salida. Si el modelo no está disponible, los comparadores independientes no pueden medirlo, y el ranking queda en manos del fabricante durante semanas. Google no fijó una fecha para cambiar eso.
PUBLICIDAD
La otra novedad es de tamaño. Argon puede escribir respuestas de hasta un millón de tokens, la unidad en que estos sistemas cuentan el texto, algo así como tres cuartos de una palabra en inglés. El tope anterior era 64.000.
En la práctica, puede resolver un problema largo de un tirón, sin cortar y retomar. El precio de lanzamiento, cuando llegue a los desarrolladores: USD 2 por millón de tokens de entrada y USD 10 por millón de salida.
El lanzamiento dejó de ser un evento comercial y pasó a ser una fila. Primero el Estado, después los que defienden, después los que pagan, al final el resto. Quien arma la fila decide quién sabe primero qué puede hacer la máquina, y ese poder hoy lo comparten tres empresas y un gobierno.
PUBLICIDAD

articles.title: NYC is now the first city in America that bans sketchy subscriptions
articles.text:
New York City residents struggling to get out of recurring subscription fees can now submit complaints to the city government. As of Thursday, the city’s click-to-cancel rule has taken effect, which requires businesses to make it as easy to cancel a subscription as it is to sign up. That means a gym that lets you join online, for example, can’t make you call or go in person to end your subscription.
NYC is now the first city in America that bans sketchy subscriptions
A new consumer portal promises not to send complaints into a “chatbot doom loop.”
It’s the first municipality to see the rule take effect, after an appeals court struck down a federal version for procedural issues. The city expects it to save New Yorkers anywhere from $21.5 million to $162.5 million annually. And to NYC Department of Consumer and Worker Protection (DCWP) Commissioner Samuel Levine, it’s an example of how state and local governments can hold companies accountable when federal efforts fail. “No one should need 45 minutes of hold music to stop paying for something they never wanted,” NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani said in a statement. “If a company can take your money with one click, you should be able to get your money back with one click. And now, if they won’t let you cancel, the City is coming for them.”
Levine was the Federal Trade Commission consumer protection chief under Lina Khan, and he tried to usher in the click-to-cancel rule at a national level. He says the experience of implementing the rule in NYC has been “night and day.”
“We proposed this rule this year. We finalized it this year. It’s taking effect this year. This is the speed of government as it should be,” Levine tells The Verge in an exclusive interview. While Levine says he’s proud of his work on the FTC rule and sees it as a “model” for other state and local governments, “at the end of the day, it took more than four years. And then after all of that, it never actually gave Americans the relief they needed.” While the FTC under current Chair Andrew Ferguson has taken an initial step toward potentially reestablishing a similar rule, Levine is betting that more municipalities will do so first. While that leaves fewer Americans protected, it still creates a deterrent for businesses to engage in deceptive subscription practices.
“This is the speed of government as it should be”
In New York, consumers can use a new portal to file complaints if they believe a business gave them unclear subscription terms, delayed cancellation, or failed to inform them the subscription would auto-renew. After filing a complaint, DCWP will review it and could reach out for more information and try to get consumers’ money back and help them cancel relevant subscriptions. If the agency sees a pattern of noncompliance at a certain business, it could prompt further investigation and legal action. Under the rule, businesses could face fines starting at $525 per violation.
The mayor’s Public Interest Technology (PIT) Crew built the portal in 10 weeks; Levine assures consumers that the experience will be far different from the White House’s newly launched America.gov, which he says appears to be “just an AI chatbot layered on top of the federal government’s existing infrastructure.” When consumers submit a complaint to the click-to-cancel portal, Levine says, “they’re not going to be diverted into a chatbot doom loop. We’re going to have actual people whose full-time job is to help them.”
He also says it won’t be like going to a DMV office to renew your driver’s license. “If we want to restore people’s faith in government and the ability of government to deliver, we need to show that government can create excellent products. We need to show that every experience is not going to the DMV. And I mean, no offense to our colleagues at the DMV,” Levine says. “People have really bad associations with interacting with the government, and sometimes that deters them from filing complaints. You can have the best laws in the world, but at the end of the day, if your eyes and ears, the people you’re working to protect, don’t want to actually deal with the government and tell us what happened, those laws are not going to be effective.”
Update October 1st: Added statement from NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani.

articles.title: Productive, Durable, Fungible: How NVIDIA AI Factories Maximize Return on Investment
articles.text:
AI factories are built by the megawatt, even by the gigawatt. Each megawatt factory costs roughly $60 million, and AI factory operators will only commit capital on that scale with a clear view of the return on investment. Three key things shape AI factory returns:
- Earning capacity: What the factory could earn in a year if it sold every token it can produce.
- Useful life: How long its AI hardware keeps earning.
- Demand: How much demand there is for those tokens.
Strength cannot fully offset weakness in another. High earning capacity counts for little if the factory sells only part of what it can produce. High demand matters little if it stops producing at full capacity in just a year. Nor are the three independent. A factory that can run more kinds of workloads finds more demand, keeping it earning year after year.
NVIDIA AI factories are engineered to maximize all three. They’re:
- Productive: Delivering the highest throughput per megawatt and the lowest cost per token, which maximizes their earning capacity.
- Durable: NVIDIA GPUs and systems keep earning years after they ship, extending useful life.
- Fungible: They run every type of AI — in every phase and every place — as well as many workloads that don’t involve AI at all, which deepens and broadens the demand they can serve.
Engineering codesign across the full stack maximizes AI factory throughput, and continuous software optimization keeps installed hardware productive years after it ships. NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries let a factory run any accelerated workload. A standardized architecture then puts all of it within reach of any operator, deployable from a validated reference design.
Productive: Highest Tokens Per Megawatt and Lowest Token Cost
Power is the binding constraint on an AI factory. This makes tokens per second per megawatt the number that governs earning capacity. More tokens inside a fixed power envelope means more revenue. Lower cost per token means more margin on it.
SemiAnalysis AgentX data shows NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 systems deliver over 30x higher throughput per megawatt than NVIDIA GB300 NVL72, and up to 45x lower cost per million tokens on the DeepSeek V4 Pro model. Gains of that size come from extreme codesign across the full stack: from models and workloads down through software to compute, networking and memory, all optimized together.
Two questions follow. If every generation makes tokens dramatically cheaper, does demand for compute shrink?
No, it expands.
Cheaper tokens make more use cases economical, and those use cases consume more tokens than the efficiency saved.
The second question is about durability. If each generation is so much better than the last, what happens to the older generations?
Durable: The Installed Base Keeps Earning
Not every workload needs the newest system. The right fit depends on a workload’s complexity and shape, which is why the last generation keeps earning after the next one arrives.
The NVIDIA A100 GPU shipped in 2020 and is still in commercial service six years later, demonstrating its continued economic value; CoreWeave recently extended bookings for units first introduced in 2020 through 2029. Over the years, every major operator has extended the depreciation schedule on its servers, which is a guess about when hardware stops earning, and one that keeps moving out. A September 2026 Sprout analysis, “The Productive Life of a Data Center GPU,” tracks how that schedule has shifted across every major operator.
Barkr puts useful life at five to six years for an eight-GPU H100 system and nine to 10 years for GB300 NVL72, based on what those systems resell for. Silicon Data shows a six-year-old A100 GPU is still worth a quarter of what it cost, where a five-year depreciation schedule had it at zero more than a year ago. Ornn Data finds the market paying 80% as much to rent an A100 GPU on a five-year contract as on a one-month contract.
CUDA, the software platform with which NVIDIA GPUs are programmed, runs across generations, so nothing an operator already owns is stranded when a new architecture arrives. Continuous software and kernel optimization keeps improving what existing hardware can do.
The same platform runs machine learning, deep learning, generative AI, reasoning, agentic AI and physical AI. Each new kind of work arrived on hardware that was already installed.
That’s fungibility. The more kinds of work a system can take, the longer it keeps finding work.
Fungible: Every Type of AI, Every Phase, Every Place
A factory built for one kind of work is a bet that the work stays. A factory that runs everything stays useful and revenue-generating even when the work changes.
NVIDIA AI factories run every type of AI model — open and proprietary — across language, vision, biology, physics and robotics. They run every phase, from data processing through pretraining, post-training and inference. And they run in every place, from hyperscale and AI clouds to sovereign programs, enterprise data centers and the edge.
Not all of it is building and running AI models. The same infrastructure runs data processing, scientific computing, simulation, graphics and more.
All of those workloads, AI and non-AI alike, reduce to the same parallel math, and NVIDIA GPUs are built to run exactly that across thousands of cores at once. CUDA is why one chip can simulate light, fold a protein and predict the next token. More than 1,000 ready-made CUDA-X libraries sit on top, covering everything from deep neural networks, computational lithography and quantum circuit simulation to vector search and climate modeling, with more than 10 million developers building on them.
That’s what makes NVIDIA GPUs general-purpose accelerated computing rather than a custom ASIC built for one workload. Being general purpose does not mean being generic: Tensor Cores and the Transformer Engine put AI-optimized hardware inside a programmable architecture, delivering specialization and flexibility in one chip. One architecture running all of it is what keeps utilization high, and the return with it.
This versatility shows up in production across customers:
- Lilly: Building and running protein, small-molecule and genomics models on a 1,016-GPU, on-premises cluster, plus chatbots and agentic workflows for its own teams.
- Pinterest: Post-training and deploying a vision language model on a hyperscale cloud, across 14,000 GPUs spanning NVIDIA Blackwell, Hopper and earlier architectures.
- Revolut: Processing data for billions of transaction records with NVIDIA cuDF, then training and deploying a foundation model on an AI cloud.
- Runway: Training a world model on NVIDIA Hopper and serving on the NVIDIA Blackwell platform using cloud infrastructure.
- Texas A&M University: Running molecular simulation and AI drug discovery on its supercomputer, at 95-98% utilization across 26 projects and seven institutions.
The same is true beyond AI. Cosm operates a distributed NVIDIA-powered data center providing flexible compute resources across high-resolution video playback, streaming, real-time graphics and synchronized display. Dassault Systèmes powers the virtual twin simulation behind aircraft certification at Wichita State and vehicle design at Lucid Motors. And Unilever builds product imagery from digital twins rather than photo shoots, cutting production costs in half.
No list of examples here would be complete — that’s the point.
NVIDIA AI factories are engineered to be productive, durable and fungible: more profitable tokens, longer useful life and deeper demand. That’s what maximizes their return.
Learn more about NVIDIA AI factories by tuning in to NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang’s GTC Berlin keynote on Wednesday, Oct. 21, at 11 a.m. CEST.

articles.title: Por qué se calienta un teléfono y cuándo es motivo de preocupación
articles.text:
Que un teléfono se caliente durante su uso diario no representa, en la mayoría de los casos, un problema de hardware. A diferencia de las computadoras, los smartphones no incorporan ventiladores internos, por lo que disipan el calor generado por sus componentes a través del propio chasis, ya sea metálico o plástico.
El calor proviene principalmente de tres fuentes: el procesador, la batería y los módulos de conectividad. Existe, sin embargo, una diferencia clara entre el calentamiento esperado por el uso intensivo y las señales que advierten sobre una falla real en el dispositivo.
PUBLICIDAD
Causas del calentamiento en los smartphones
El procesador es uno de los principales responsables del aumento de temperatura. Cuando se ejecutan tareas exigentes, sus transistores trabajan a máxima capacidad y generan calor por fricción eléctrica.
Esto ocurre, por ejemplo, durante partidas de juegos con gráficos 3D que mantienen la GPU al 100% por periodos prolongados, o en la grabación de video en 4K u 8K, que exige procesar y almacenar grandes volúmenes de información de forma continua. El procesamiento de inteligencia artificial para edición de foto y video también demanda un esfuerzo similar.
La batería constituye otra fuente habitual de calor. La transferencia de energía química a eléctrica durante la carga produce calor de manera inevitable, y este efecto se intensifica con la carga rápida, que inyecta una cantidad elevada de corriente en poco tiempo. La carga inalámbrica genera incluso más temperatura, debido a la fricción electromagnética entre la bobina del cargador y la del teléfono.
PUBLICIDAD
Los módulos de conectividad también influyen en este proceso. Cuando la señal móvil es débil, el módem del teléfono aumenta de forma automática su potencia para mantenerse conectado a la antena, lo que multiplica el consumo de batería y el calor generado.
Algo similar ocurre durante el uso prolongado de GPS y datos móviles, como sucede al navegar con mapas en carretera, donde se combinan la señal GPS, los datos en segundo plano y el brillo elevado de la pantalla.
A estos factores se suman los ambientales: la exposición directa al sol o el uso dentro de un auto estacionado elevan la temperatura del dispositivo, al igual que las fundas gruesas o de materiales aislantes, como la goma densa o el cuero, que atrapan el calor e impiden su correcta disipación.
PUBLICIDAD
Cuándo el calentamiento del celular es normal
El calentamiento del celular es normal cuando ocurre durante tareas exigentes como juegos, grabación de video en alta resolución o carga rápida. También es habitual en las primeras 24 o 48 horas tras la compra o una actualización del sistema, mientras el dispositivo indexa archivos y reorganiza aplicaciones en segundo plano.
En cambio, existen situaciones que sí ameritan atención. Si el teléfono quema al tacto, al punto de no poder sostenerse sin molestia, lo recomendable es dejar de usarlo de inmediato y retirarlo de la carga.
Otro indicio de alerta es que el dispositivo se caliente en reposo, es decir, sin aplicaciones abiertas y con la pantalla apagada. Esto puede deberse a un proceso trabado, un fallo de batería o la presencia de software malicioso.
PUBLICIDAD
Cuando el sistema muestra una advertencia en pantalla indicando que el teléfono necesita enfriarse, significa que se activó un mecanismo de protección de emergencia para evitar daños mayores.
El escenario más grave es el de una batería hinchada, reconocible por una pantalla levantada o una tapa trasera despegada, que implica riesgo de incendio y exige desconectar el equipo de inmediato y dejar de utilizarlo.
Señales de que la temperatura afecta el rendimiento del celular
Los teléfonos modernos cuentan con sistemas automáticos de seguridad, conocidos como thermal throttling, que actúan antes de que se produzca un daño permanente en los componentes.
Entre las señales más frecuentes de este mecanismo se encuentran la reducción automática del brillo de la pantalla, incluso con el brillo automático desactivado, y la aparición de lentitud o tirones en juegos y aplicaciones, producto de que el procesador reduce su velocidad de forma deliberada para enfriarse.
PUBLICIDAD
También puede manifestarse como una pausa en la carga o una ralentización considerable al superar cierto umbral de temperatura, así como el cierre forzado de aplicaciones que demandan más recursos, como la cámara o las apps de mapas.
Recomendaciones para evitar el sobrecalentamiento del celular
Para reducir el riesgo de sobrecalentamiento, se aconseja evitar el uso intensivo del teléfono mientras se carga, ya que actividades como jugar o ver videos durante ese proceso suman el calor generado por la batería al del procesador.
Retirar la funda durante la carga, en particular cuando se utiliza carga rápida o inalámbrica, ayuda a que el calor se disipe con mayor facilidad. El uso de cargadores originales o certificados también resulta determinante, dado que los cargadores genéricos de baja calidad suelen regular de forma deficiente el voltaje y el flujo de corriente.
PUBLICIDAD
Por último, se recomienda evitar la exposición directa del cristal al sol, ya que los paneles OLED y LCD absorben el calor térmico con rapidez, lo que puede acelerar el desgaste del dispositivo.
PUBLICIDAD
PUBLICIDAD

articles.title: Hébergement VPS : pour quels sites et à partir de quand y passer ?
articles.text:
Hébergement VPS : pour quels sites et à partir de quand y passer ?
Un hébergement VPS devient intéressant lorsque le mutualisé atteint ses limites : trafic plus important, ralentissements répétés ou besoins techniques spécifiques. Plus puissant et flexible, il demande aussi davantage de connaissances. Mais tous les sites n’en ont pas besoin. Voici les principaux signes qui permettent de savoir quand passer à cette solution.
Un hébergement VPS devient pertinent lorsqu’un site commence à manquer de ressources sur une offre mutualisée. Une boutique en ligne en croissance, une application web ou un WordPress très fréquenté peuvent notamment avoir besoin de davantage de puissance et de liberté de configuration.
Avec un hébergement mutualisé, plusieurs sites utilisent les ressources d’un même serveur. Le VPS repose également sur un serveur physique partagé, mais chaque environnement virtuel dispose de ressources qui lui sont attribuées. Il offre ainsi davantage de contrôle sur la configuration et le fonctionnement du serveur.
Cette liberté a cependant une contrepartie : l’administration demande plus de connaissances. Pour un petit site vitrine, le mutualisé reste donc généralement plus adapté.
VPS ou mutualisé : quelles différences ?
L’hébergement mutualisé constitue souvent le point de départ. Il convient aux blogs, sites vitrines et petits sites professionnels et demande peu de connaissances techniques.
Le VPS s’adresse plutôt aux projets qui commencent à avoir des besoins spécifiques.
|  | Mutualisé | VPS | 
|---|---|---|
| Ressources | Partagées | Allouées au VPS | 
| Contrôle | Limité | Important | 
| Configuration | Encadrée | Personnalisable | 
| Gestion | Simple | Plus technique | 
| Évolution | Limitée | Plus flexible | 
Le VPS n’est donc pas simplement un mutualisé plus puissant. Il apporte surtout un environnement plus indépendant, avec davantage de possibilités de configuration.
Quels sont les avantages d’un VPS ?
Le premier intérêt concerne les ressources disponibles. Un VPS permet de choisir une quantité de mémoire vive, de CPU et de stockage adaptée au projet.
Cette isolation peut également apporter davantage de stabilité. Sur un mutualisé, les ressources sont partagées entre plusieurs sites. Avec un VPS, l’environnement est mieux séparé des autres utilisateurs présents sur le serveur physique.
Par ailleurs, le VPS offre une plus grande liberté. Il devient possible d’installer certains logiciels, de modifier la configuration du serveur ou de déployer une application qui ne fonctionnerait pas sur une offre mutualisée classique.
Quand faut-il passer à un VPS ?
Il n’existe pas de seuil universel en nombre de visiteurs. Un site avec 10 000 visites mensuelles peut avoir davantage besoin d’un VPS qu’un autre qui en reçoit plusieurs fois plus, selon sa technologie et les ressources consommées.
Les limites du mutualisé se répètent
Si l’hébergeur signale régulièrement une consommation excessive de CPU ou de mémoire, c’est un premier indice. Une saturation ponctuelle ne justifie pas forcément une migration, mais des alertes répétées peuvent montrer que l’offre actuelle devient trop juste.
Avant de changer de serveur, il reste cependant utile d’optimiser le site. Une base de données trop lourde, des images mal compressées ou des extensions WordPress gourmandes peuvent provoquer des ralentissements.
Le trafic augmente
Une boutique en ligne ou un site média peut connaître des pics de fréquentation. Si les performances diminuent dès que le trafic augmente, un VPS peut apporter davantage de marge.
Cette évolution est particulièrement intéressante pour un site professionnel dont la disponibilité devient importante. Quelques secondes de chargement supplémentaires peuvent rapidement nuire à l’expérience des visiteurs.
Le site nécessite davantage de liberté
C’est parfois le meilleur signal. Si le projet demande une version particulière d’un logiciel, l’installation d’une application ou une configuration spécifique, le mutualisé peut devenir trop contraignant.
Le VPS permet alors d’adapter davantage l’environnement aux besoins du projet.
Quels sites peuvent avoir besoin d’un VPS ?
Le VPS convient surtout aux projets qui dépassent le cadre d’un simple site vitrine.
Les boutiques en ligne
Une boutique e-commerce doit gérer les produits, comptes clients, commandes, paiements et différentes extensions. Plus son activité augmente, plus les besoins en ressources peuvent progresser.
Un VPS peut donc constituer une étape intéressante lorsque le mutualisé commence à montrer ses limites.
Les applications web
Les applications sont particulièrement adaptées au VPS. Elles nécessitent parfois plusieurs services, une base de données spécifique ou des réglages qui ne sont pas accessibles sur un hébergement classique.
Dans ce cas, le contrôle offert par le serveur virtuel devient aussi important que la puissance disponible.
Les WordPress à fort trafic
Un petit blog n’a généralement aucune raison de passer sur un VPS. En revanche, un WordPress très fréquenté, avec de nombreuses extensions ou une base de données importante, peut finir par consommer davantage de ressources.
Le VPS peut alors apporter une marge supplémentaire, à condition que le site soit correctement optimisé.
Plusieurs sites professionnels
Pour un freelance ou une petite agence qui gère plusieurs sites, un VPS peut permettre de regrouper différents projets sur une même infrastructure.
Cette solution demande toutefois de surveiller la consommation de chaque site et de prévoir des sauvegardes adaptées.
Quelles offres VPS choisir ?
Les hébergeurs proposent aujourd’hui des VPS allant de petites configurations destinées aux projets modestes à des serveurs beaucoup plus puissants.
Hostinger : une offre accessible pour débuter
Hostinger propose plusieurs VPS KVM. Son offre KVM 1 est affichée à partir de 5,49 € par mois dans le cadre de la promotion indiquée, avec 1 vCPU, 4 Go de RAM, 50 Go de stockage NVMe et 4 To de bande passante.
Le KVM 2 propose 2 vCPU, 8 Go de RAM et 100 Go de stockage NVMe pour 7,99 € par mois dans le cadre de la promotion affichée. Une formule KVM 4 monte à 4 vCPU, 16 Go de RAM et 200 Go de stockage.
Hostinger mise également sur des outils destinés à simplifier l’administration du serveur. Cette approche peut faciliter une première transition depuis le mutualisé.
Il faut cependant regarder le tarif de renouvellement. Le prix promotionnel de départ ne correspond pas forcément au coût sur plusieurs années.
IONOS : davantage de ressources
IONOS propose de son côté plusieurs configurations VPS. Son VPS M+ est affiché à 3 € HT par mois pendant trois mois, puis à 9 € HT par mois. Il comprend 4 vCores, 4 Go de RAM et 120 Go de stockage NVMe.
Le VPS L+ propose 6 vCores, 8 Go de RAM et 240 Go de stockage NVMe. Son tarif promotionnel est de 5 € HT par mois pendant trois mois, avant de passer à 18 € HT par mois.
IONOS inclut également un trafic annoncé comme illimité et une connexion jusqu’à 1 Gbit/s. Là encore, le tarif normal doit être pris en compte pour comparer correctement les offres.
Un VPS demande-t-il des connaissances techniques ?
C’est le principal point à ne pas sous-estimer.
Avec un mutualisé, une grande partie de la maintenance est assurée par l’hébergeur. Sur un VPS, l’utilisateur dispose de davantage de contrôle, mais doit aussi gérer une partie de la sécurité et de l’administration.
Mises à jour, pare-feu, utilisateurs, sauvegardes ou surveillance du serveur peuvent nécessiter certaines connaissances. Les interfaces proposées par les hébergeurs simplifient plusieurs opérations, mais elles ne remplacent pas complètement l’administration technique.
Pour un site vitrine classique, cette charge n’est généralement pas nécessaire. Pour un développeur ou une entreprise ayant besoin d’un environnement personnalisé, elle peut au contraire être parfaitement justifiée.
Le VPS est-il vraiment nécessaire ?
Pas toujours. Un site qui fonctionne correctement sur un hébergement mutualisé n’a aucune raison de migrer simplement pour disposer d’une configuration plus puissante.
Le passage au VPS devient intéressant lorsque les limites sont concrètes : ralentissements réguliers, ressources insuffisantes, hausse importante du trafic ou besoin d’une configuration particulière.
Au final, le bon moment pour passer au VPS n’est pas lié à un nombre précis de visiteurs. Il dépend surtout des besoins réels du site. Le mutualisé reste adapté aux petits projets, tandis qu’un VPS devient pertinent pour les boutiques en croissance, les applications web, les WordPress très fréquentés ou les projets professionnels nécessitant davantage de contrôle.
Hostinger peut constituer une porte d’entrée accessible, tandis qu’IONOS propose des configurations plus généreuses à des tarifs d’appel attractifs. Dans les deux cas, le tarif de renouvellement et les ressources réellement nécessaires doivent être vérifiés avant de souscrire.

articles.title: Crean una zapatilla con inteligencia artificial que analiza la marcha y genera energía al caminar
articles.text:
Una zapatilla deportiva capaz de producir electricidad con cada pisada podría ayudar a estudiar la marcha fuera del consultorio. Ingenieros de la Universidad Rutgers desarrollaron un calzado con inteligencia artificial integrada que analiza los patrones de desplazamiento sin batería recargable, ya que aprovecha la energía generada por el movimiento del pie.
El objetivo es que, a futuro, los profesionales de la salud puedan detectar cambios en la marcha a partir de la información reunida mientras una persona realiza sus actividades cotidianas. Ese seguimiento podría resultar útil para acompañar la evolución del Parkinson, lesiones cerebrales o de médula espinal y procesos de rehabilitación, además de aportar datos para evaluar el riesgo de caídas.
PUBLICIDAD
En la actualidad, estas evaluaciones suelen limitarse a observaciones breves en clínicas o laboratorios. Los aparatos que registran la actividad cotidiana, en cambio, requieren recargas periódicas.
La investigación fue publicada en la revista Science Advances. Con datos de cuatro voluntarios sanos, el equipo distinguió caminar lentamente, caminar rápido, correr y subir escaleras con una precisión del 95,4 %.
Cada paso aporta la electricidad necesaria para el funcionamiento
Los componentes electrónicos están ubicados en el talón de unas zapatillas blancas. Allí aprovechan la presión y el roce que se producen al apoyar el pie. El mecanismo se basa en el efecto triboeléctrico, un fenómeno relacionado con la electricidad estática que surge cuando determinados materiales se rozan y luego se separan.
PUBLICIDAD
La corriente que generan las pisadas llega en pulsos irregulares y no puede alimentar de manera directa los sensores ni el procesador. Por eso, el grupo de la Universidad Rutgers creó un circuito que la transforma en una corriente apta para el equipo. Según el comunicado institucional, este sistema permitió obtener hasta 120 veces más energía útil que un método convencional.
“Cuando una persona camina o corre, automáticamente tiene energía biomecánica disponible, por lo que se puede aprovechar”, afirmó Simiao Niu, profesor asistente del Departamento de Ingeniería Biomédica de la Escuela de Ingeniería de Rutgers, en el comunicado institucional.
PUBLICIDAD
Niu explicó que el calzado resulta adecuado para esta clase de medición porque reúne la información que interesa registrar y la energía necesaria para hacerlo. “Cuando una persona se sienta, no hay energía disponible, pero tampoco necesita monitoreo de la marcha”, señaló el investigador.
En medicina, la marcha incluye el equilibrio, la velocidad, la longitud de los pasos y el ritmo. Los cambios en esas características pueden ayudar a seguir la evolución de una enfermedad o de una rehabilitación. Aun así, el prototipo no cumple una función de diagnóstico.
“La marcha es uno de los indicadores más importantes para muchas enfermedades”, afirmó Niu. Un indicador de salud es una medida corporal que puede aportar información sobre el estado de una persona o la evolución de una afección.
PUBLICIDAD
La zapatilla analiza los datos sin enviarlos a otro equipo
El dispositivo incorpora un acelerómetro, un sensor que mide el movimiento del pie en tres direcciones. Un procesador pequeño revisa esos registros mediante inteligencia artificial, un programa capaz de reconocer regularidades en los datos. De ese modo, clasifica cada tramo de 15 segundos en una de las cuatro actividades estudiadas.
El análisis se realiza dentro de la zapatilla, sin remitir la información de forma constante a un teléfono móvil, una computadora o un servidor. Al evitar ese envío permanente, el equipo necesita menos electricidad para funcionar.
Adaptar el programa a la memoria limitada del procesador fue uno de los principales desafíos. La primera versión examinaba 21 rasgos del movimiento y alcanzaba una precisión del 98,1 %, pero excedía la capacidad disponible en el calzado.
PUBLICIDAD
El equipo comprobó que las variaciones registradas en las tres direcciones reunían la mayor parte de los datos útiles. Según se detalla en el estudio, el programa simplificado conservó una precisión del 95,4 %, operó cerca de 15 veces más rápido y utilizó alrededor de una sexta parte de la corriente que requería el modelo inicial.
“El problema fundamental de los dispositivos portátiles actuales es el límite entre energía e inteligencia”, afirmó el investigador. “Estamos desarrollando un dispositivo portátil inteligente con funciones de inteligencia artificial integradas que puede recolectar energía por sí solo, de modo que no haya que preocuparse por cargarlo”.
PUBLICIDAD
En conjunto, el sensor y el programa consumen 86 microvatios. Durante las pruebas de laboratorio, una caminata lenta produjo la electricidad necesaria para mantener activo el sistema.
Las pruebas aún no incluyen a pacientes ni a adultos mayores
Los resultados corresponden a cuatro participantes sanos de entre 23 y 26 años. El sistema se entrenó y se probó únicamente con las actividades previstas en la investigación, por lo que todavía no fue evaluado en adultos mayores, personas con trastornos del movimiento ni pacientes en rehabilitación.
Esa limitación impide usarlo para diagnosticar enfermedades, anticipar caídas o establecer si un tratamiento resulta eficaz. Antes de considerar las aplicaciones previstas, serán necesarios nuevos desarrollos y pruebas clínicas.
PUBLICIDAD
El comunicado de la universidad señala que, con más investigación, el diseño podría adaptarse para controlar la actividad cardíaca, señales químicas del organismo u otros aspectos de la salud. Ninguna de esas funciones integró las pruebas del modelo actual.
Fuying Dong, estudiante de doctorado en Ingeniería Biomédica de Rutgers y primera autora del estudio, indicó que el trabajo exigió coordinar cada componente del calzado. “La idea de diseñar conjuntamente todo el sistema es lo mejor que aprendí de este proyecto”, afirmó Dong.
“Se divide un proyecto grande en partes más pequeñas, se terminan una por una y se intenta entender cuál es la historia principal”, agregó la investigadora.
PUBLICIDAD
PUBLICIDAD
PUBLICIDAD

articles.title: 11 000 € et 4 vraies places : Dacia prépare un séisme pour concurrencer la Citroën Ami en 2027
articles.text:
La Spring est trop chère ? Dacia vise encore moins cher avec la version de série du Hipster, qui devrait arriver sur le marché l’année prochaine. Ce crossover inédit débarquera sur le segment L7e des quadricycles lourds avec un habitacle spacieux et quatre vraies places. Son prix devrait tourner autour des 11 000 €, ce qui le placera légèrement au-dessus d’une Citroën Ami pouvant uniquement accueillir deux occupants.
La cible toute désignée est pourtant bel et bien chez Stellantis : il s’agit de la future Fiat Multiplina qui n’est autre que la déclinaison quatre places de la Topolino, dont la production en série approche aussi à grands pas. Katrin Adt, la PDG de Dacia, n’a pas encore confirmé la mise en série du véhicule en affirmant seulement « rester à l’écoute » des demandes. Pourtant, une source proche du projet confirme la chose.
A lire aussi : La nouvelle Dacia Spring est là ! C’est la voiture électrique la moins chère du marché
Une production en Chine pour tailler les coûts au maximum
Le Hipster sera produit l’année prochaine en Chine dans l’usine de Shiyan où était fabriquée la Spring de première génération. Outre des économies substantielles sur l’outillage et le processus industriel, un tel choix influencera aussi grandement la conception du futur modèle. D’après les mêmes sources, moteur, batterie et châssis seront entièrement produits dans cette usine afin de minimiser encore les coûts.
Aussi, le Hipster reprendra le maximum de composants de la première Spring pour abaisser la facture finale. Il ne faudra donc pas s’attendre à un véhicule moderne, mais essentiel avec une masse extrêmement réduite pour satisfaire les exigences de la catégorie L7e. L’engin ne devra ainsi pas excéder les 450 kg, se limiter à une puissance de 20 ch et ne pas dépasser les 90 km/h en vitesse de pointe.
15 kWh et 150 km d’autonomie : taillée pour la ville
Une petite batterie de 15 kWh fera alors l’affaire en offrant près de 150 km d’autonomie. C’est encore moins que les 250 km de la nouvelle Spring mais toujours bien suffisant au quotidien. Le gabarit contenu du Hipster facilitera aussi la vie avec des dimensions proches du concept faisant 3 mètres de long, 1,55 mètre de large et 1,53 mètre de haut. Ses formes cubiques resteront au programme pour favoriser l’espace intérieur.
Le style sera lui aussi fidèle au concept avec un capot court mourant sur une mini calandre adoptant des feux en pixels. Les protections en plastique engloberont toute la carrosserie pour protéger le Hipster des petits chocs urbains, alors que les grandes surfaces vitrées permettront une bonne visibilité extérieure et une belle luminosité intérieure. L’habitacle sera ultra minimaliste avec une planche de bord évasée et un support pour smartphone.

articles.title: Gears of War: E-Day is the Mountain Dew of video games
articles.text:
The title of this article isn’t meant to be some insult towards Gears of War: E-Day. On the contrary, it can be seen as complimentary. Just like Mountain Dew, the first taste of Gears is great. It transports you back to simpler times. It’s loud, it’s dumb, and it can be a lot of fun.
Before long though, you remember why you haven’t reached for it in a long time. Your palate has evolved, but Gears has stayed the same.
Don’t get me wrong, Gears of War: E-Day is a competently made shooter that can be a fun throwback to 2006, I just wouldn’t recommend it to anyone except the most hardcore of fans. And I don’t think that’s the kind of game Xbox needs right now if they want to expand their audience.
Editor’s note: Our review only covers the campaign of E-Day, as the review build did not include access to multiplayer.
It’s Code Red
I was in high school when the first Gears of War released. I remember seeing screenshots of the game in magazines and being in complete disbelief that a game’s graphics could look that good. But then I went to my local EB Games, bought my copy, read the instruction manual on the bus ride home, inserted the disc into my Xbox 360, and… it was glorious.
The way that viscera sprayed the screen as I chainsawed a Locust in half, the way the characters slammed into cover like human-shaped wrecking balls, the way everybody spoke like they were constantly comparing the size of their Gnashers… Ahh, the good ol’ days.
But Gears of War hasn’t been relevant for a long time – at least not outside of the core Xbox community. It inspired an entire generation of games to abandon all colours except grey and brown, so why hasn’t the series been able to keep pace with its contemporaries?
To be fair, it’s a tough balancing act. Do you innovate and risk losing your core audience, or do you iterate and risk falling behind? Aside from Capcom’s Resident Evil, few long-term franchises have been able to thread that needle. And unfortunately, E-Day feels like it’s stuck in the past.
Maybe that’s not a bad thing though. If remasters have shown us anything, it’s that sometimes simple is better. So if all you’re looking for is more Gears of War, then this might just be what you’re looking for. There’s plenty of cover-based shooting to be had. If you’re looking for the next entry that’s going to push the franchise forward, this isn’t it.
Unreal Engine strikes again
If you’ve seen the E-Day gameplay that was part of Xbox’s Summer Game Showcase, you’ll know that the game has some chops when it comes to its presentation. It’s developed by Vancouver-based studio The Coalition. The game does a great job of marrying the original style of the series – dark environments with industrial-gothic architecture – with modern graphics to truly show the scale of the conflict. It’s at its best when it leans into the atmosphere of the city of Kalona before its downfall, with neon shop signs punctuating the smoke as Locust hordes emerge from the depths.
I just wish the entire game took place at night, because any time there’s daylight, the game looks muddy. Flat lighting, noisy shadows, texture pop-in, and low-quality environmental objects – especially distant buildings and mountains – keep this from feeling like a truly generation-defining title when it comes to its visuals.
And then there are the glitches. I’ll get into a few more of these in a bit, but I experienced the full gamut, from enemies disappearing as I was shooting them to being unable to swap my weapon, and even having a sawed-off arm get stuck to Marcus for several minutes. Pre-release build glitches aside, though, it’s generally a good-looking game that runs well on Xbox Series X. I’ll leave the frame counting to the experts at Digital Foundry, but it felt like a fairly steady 60fps, with the occasional stutter as I entered new areas.
Playing on PC was a different story. My PC is pretty out of date at this point, but it’s still above the minimum requirements with an RTX 3070 GPU, Ryzen 7 5700X CPU, and 16GB of DDR4 RAM. For the life of me, I couldn’t get the game to maintain a stable 60fps. With everything set to low at 1080p, DLSS on ultra-performance, and all other applications closed, I was fluctuating constantly between 70-40fps. Needless to say, I quickly moved back to my Series X for the remainder of my time with the game. I hope other players have a better experience with the launch build.
Artificial sweetener
Now let’s talk gunplay, because Gears is first and foremost a third-person shooter. When I was just mowing down enemies with my Lancer, I had a pretty good time. It took some tweaking to get the controls dialled in, but once I’d turned off aim acceleration and motion blur, the shooting felt exactly as I remembered it. The guns still sound like they’re straight off the factory floor, producing a satisfying, chunky thud with every round. The rev of the chainsaw still made my eyes go wide as I sliced through the torso of a Wretch. And minor new additions like the variable height cover system offer new ways to take out enemies that pair well with the grapples strewn throughout the levels. You’ll be shredding Boomers like you’re 16 again in no time.
It’s a sweet first taste that took me back to my buddy’s basement, ripping through enemies and bemoaning the fact that we had a history assignment due the next day. But then you take that second sip and that sweetness just tastes… artificial.
Enemies are still bullet sponges, which is fine because that’s the style of game that it is, but the NPC AI is some of the most laughable I’ve experienced in a long time. Let me explain.
So there I was, facing off against one of the most menacing enemies in the campaign. It had just burst through a door, catching me completely off guard and out of cover. But even so, the poor soul never stood a chance because I knew its weakness: slightly elevated ledges.
Every single time it tried to attack, I would just climb up on a box or a ledge, and it would chase me, taking its sweet time to clamber up to meet me. As it’s doing that, I’m just whittling down its health. When it got up, I’d hop down, rinse and repeat.
That level of easy-to-cheese NPC behaviour applies to more than just that one enemy type in the game. Several times I saw Locusts “hide” behind cover by lying down directly in front of me instead of going to the far side of cover. You have three party members with you at all times, so I’m willing to give the game the benefit of the doubt that they were hiding from someone else in that case. It just happened… a lot.
And don’t even get me started on the invisible walls. So. Many. Invisible. Walls. Those should have stayed in 2006.
All fizz, no biz
Gears of War: E-Day isn’t scary or emotional. And that sucks because the game clearly wants to evoke the feelings of both the original game and the famous “Mad World” trailer. There are multiple moments that recreate the setting and lighting, but where they fail to deliver is the atmosphere.
Maybe it wouldn’t be as scary today, but the Berserker level in the OG game sits with me as one of the highlights of that generation because it came out of nowhere and all I could do was run. Unfortunately, that’s not the case here. You’re Marcus goddamn Fenix. You’re a badass, and even though this is a prequel, everybody already knows you’re a hero. So even when the game pretends it’s going to lean into the horror of the situation with deep reds, high-contrast lighting, and eerie music, it’s unwilling to actually commit to the horror. It’s all just mood lighting. You’ll be outmanned, outgunned, stranded, without light… and yet the tension never amounts to anything.
It’s not just the scenarios that kill the mood though; the characters in the game love to tell you how stupid you are. And not just in the way that modern games do, where they solve the puzzles for you – though this game does tell you where to go constantly. I mean, they literally tell your squad constantly how terrible you are at your job.
Show up to an objective? “Damn, Bravo Squad, did you crawl all the way here?” Walk through a base? “Way to show up, losers.” Kill all the enemies in an area? “You bitches stop to smell the daisies?”
These are paraphrases – but they’re not far off! Given how everyone constantly sucks up to Marcus as a war hero, they love to berate the squad for just doing what they were told.
It’s almost refreshing how corny the dialogue is. There’s a lot of grunting and winks at the audience with references to past games. And hearing returning Marcus voice actor John DiMaggio growl lines like “Nothing but bits” when you curb-stomp a guy still hits.
If only the story had any sense of purpose or drive. It’s a classic case of a lot happening, but nothing actually happening.
The new characters are likeable enough. Both Carter and Reyes are easy to root for and bring some levity to the proceedings. But the core cast aren’t given nearly enough to work with. The entire city is falling apart, and aside from one attempted phone call, Dom barely mentions his family across the first ten hours. It’s fine though; they probably won’t come up again, right guys?
And the game loves to go back to the tried-and-true well of killing off characters that they’ve just introduced minutes earlier to try and evoke some emotional response. It didn’t work for me, but maybe that one guy from high school who always talked about how deep Fight Club was will love it.
Nostalgic taste
I should reiterate, E-Day isn’t a bad game. It’s competently made. Popping heads with a sniper still feels great. Tai is still cool. The sound design of the weapons is still punchy as hell. It’s still the same experience.
Any strengths of this game are the strengths of games in its past. It’s more polished, perhaps, rendered with more detail for sure, but ultimately devoid of new ideas. It’s an enjoyable romp across the city of Kalona (shoutout to Kelowna, B.C.), but the campaign feels like a retread of everything we’ve seen before.
It’s worth mentioning that there are some differences here. New to me, though not new to the series as a whole, are the open zone areas. In between key moments of the campaign, you’ll be allowed to explore the city to take on side missions and find collectibles. It’s probably my least favourite part of the experience. And that largely comes down to the lack of interesting content.
Instead of keeping us to a tight ten-hour campaign centred around the best content, it has us meandering around the city, wiping out the occasional band of enemies and helping stranded soldiers and civilians. These rarely ever contain a story that I remember past their completion or rewards that were worth the time. And at worst, these open zones completely break the immersion.
One example that really highlights this happened when I turned a corner to find a hulking Locust coming out of a restaurant dragging a human behind them. Naturally, I whipped out my Lancer, blasted the Locust to bits, saved the civilian, and continued on my merry way. Except I looped around the block looking for a collectible, and wouldn’t you know it, the exact same scenario played out. The same Locust was coming out of the restaurant like nothing had happened. This time I let the human die before wiping him out to see if that would end the scenario. When I tried it a third time, the exact same moment played out.
The best games craft moments that feel unique to the player, moments that feel like they are personal to you. Open zones like this feel perfectly crafted to create encounters that you just “accidentally” stumble upon, that make you feel like you might have been the only one to have that exact experience. This had the opposite effect.
Then again, this is a video game. It is the most video game. The Mountain Dew of video games. Its first sip is nostalgic. But the more you have, the more you realize how artificial it tastes. And it leaves you feeling like you probably don’t need to drink it again for another decade.
Images credit: Xbox

articles.title: Box 10 : SFR a publié la fiche de sa nouvelle box par erreur — Frandroid
articles.text:
SFR a mis en ligne la fiche de sa future Box 10 avant même de l’avoir annoncée. Ce jeudi 1er octobre, MacGeneration a repéré des pages d’assistance de l’opérateur, publiées depuis peu, qui décrivent cette box Wi-Fi 7 en détail. SFR promet ainsi le Wi-Fi 7 aux abonnés qui ne prennent pas l’offre la plus chère. Pour l’instant, les forfaits Fibre Power à 36,99 euros par mois et Fibre Power S à 29,99 euros par mois sont livrés avec la Box 8, limitée au Wi-Fi 6.
La Box 10+, présentée en juillet 2025, a été la première box Wi-Fi 7 de SFR. Elle reste toutefois réservée à l’abonnement Fibre Premium, à 45,99 euros par mois. En février 2026, Altice France, la maison mère de SFR, avait annoncé dans un communiqué publié sur X une Box 10 « accessible à tous les clients », sans donner le moindre détail technique.
Du Wi-Fi 7 sur deux bandes, et 2 Gb/s au maximum
À l’extérieur, la Box 10 reprend le design de sa grande sœur : un boîtier vertical, deux façades noires et un petit écran E-Ink (l’encre électronique des liseuses) sur la tranche. SFR indique une consommation électrique de 9,4 watts.
Côté sans fil, elle se limite au Wi-Fi 7 bi-bande, sur les fréquences 2,4 et 5 GHz. Elle perd donc la bande 6 GHz de la Box 10+, moins encombrée, qui offre des débits plus élevés quand on est près de la box.
Surtout, la Box 10 ne gère que le GPON, la norme de fibre historique, ce qui la limite aux abonnements jusqu’à 2 Gb/s. La Box 10+ prend aussi en charge le XGS-PON, sa version plus rapide, qui permet des offres jusqu’à 8 Gb/s.
Pour les branchements, on trouve deux ports Ethernet à 2,5 Gb/s et deux à 1 Gb/s, plus une prise téléphone RJ45 et un port USB-C. Les deux ports à 2,5 Gb/s permettent à un ordinateur branché en câble de profiter d’un abonnement à 2 Gb/s, alors qu’un port à 1 Gb/s le bride forcément à 1 Gb/s. La Box 10+ propose de son côté un port à 10 Gb/s et trois à 1 Gb/s.
Ni prix ni date pour l’instant
SFR n’a toujours pas présenté la Box 10. On ne connaît ni sa date de lancement, ni les forfaits qui l’incluront, ni un éventuel changement de prix des abonnements. Elle n’apparaît pas encore dans les offres internet en vente sur le site de l’opérateur.
- Débit jusqu’à 2 Gb/s
- Sans Player TV
- Wi-Fi 7
- Débit jusqu’à 1 Gb/s
- Sans Player TV
- Wi-Fi 5
- Débit jusqu’à 5 Gb/s
- Sans Player TV
- Wi-Fi 7
SFR arrive après ses concurrents sur ce terrain. Free avec la Freebox Pop, Orange avec la Livebox S et Bouygues Telecom avec une Bbox lancée en janvier 2026 proposent déjà des box Wi-Fi 7 plus abordables, elles aussi limitées à deux bandes. Chez SFR, dépasser 2 Gb/s impose toujours l’offre Premium, l’une des offres fibre à 8 Gb/s des quatre opérateurs. Chez Free, la Freebox Pop S monte déjà à 5 Gb/s.
La Box 10 arrive alors que SFR est en cours de vente. Bouygues Telecom, Free et Orange comptent se partager l’opérateur, et l’Autorité de la concurrence examine le dossier. La Commission européenne lui a renvoyé l’ensemble du dossier le 15 juillet 2026, et l’Autorité prévoit au moins dix-huit mois d’instruction.

articles.title: Unlocking the Door to Open Source: Reflections from Nerdearla and Getting Started in Open Source Development
articles.text:
Unlocking the Door to Open Source: Reflections from Nerdearla and Getting Started in Open Source Development
Hilary Carter | 01 October 2026
Stepping into Ciudad Cultural Konex in Buenos Aires for Nerdearla was an unforgettable experience. The venue was unique. It was as colourful with a giant orange staircase in the heart of the complex, had a mix of indoor and outdoor stages and spaces, and reflected the signature innovative and creative expression of Argentina. For me, it was a rare opportunity to engage with technology enthusiasts from across Latin America in a conference hosted at one of the region’s most prominent cities. A standout for me was participating in a panel discussion moderated by Leandro Colombo Viña on the topic of getting started in open source development, the subject of a new LF Research report. The discussion, held in the complex auditorium before a packed house, featured practitioner insights from Stormy Peters of AWS, Megan Knight of ARM, Roberto Luna Rojas from the Valkey project, and Michael “Monty” Widenius, creator of MySQL and MariaDB.
Top: Backstage with the Sysarmy production team. Missing Monty Widenius. Photo courtesy of Roberto Luna Rojas.
Bottom: From left to right, Leandro Colombo Viña, Stormy Peters, Hilary Carter, Roberto Luna Rojas, Megan Knight, Monty Widenius. Photo courtesy of Nerdearla.
The energy at Nerdearla reinforced a truth we see across the tech landscape: While there is an optimism around technology, and developer interest in contributing to open source projects is high, knowing where to start remains a challenge. This is why we’re so pleased to share our new report, Getting Started with Open Source Development: A Practical Guide for New Contributors, to help clear pathways to greater open source participation. Authored by Dr. Ibrahim Haddad with a foreword by Linux Fellow Shuah Khan, this report offers practical guidance for anyone moving from using open source to helping build it. The report also reflects insights from open source enthusiast Doug Byers, whose valuable peer review captured additional considerations for would-be contributors.
Understanding project mechanics before writing code
Building a clear mental model before touching code is critical for success in open source development. Unlike traditional corporate environments where tasks are assigned directly by engineering leads, open source relies on a voluntary, asynchronous model where maintainers oversee upstream repositories and evaluate proposed changes.
Before submitting a change, new contributors must navigate project licensing, developer agreements, and behavioral guidelines. Understanding whether a repository uses a permissive or copyleft license determines how the contribution can be used.
In addition, adhering to legal attestations like the Developer Certificate of Origin (DCO) via simple commit sign-offs or executing a Contributor License Agreement (CLA) ensures that pull requests move forward smoothly without administrative delays.
Navigating workflows and overcoming contribution barriers
Choosing where to start can feel overwhelming given the sheer volume of active projects. The report reveals that starting from an existing technical context—such as software, frameworks, or tools you already use daily—greatly reduces the learning curve. Evaluating health signals like recent commit activity, issue response times, and welcoming maintainer messaging allows newcomers to identify healthy, supportive communities.
Adjusting to different tooling environments is another requirement for success. While GitHub and GitLab rely on standard pull or merge request workflows, other foundational open source projects use mailing lists or Gerrit change-based reviews. The visual below outlines the basics of what first-time contributors should do before writing any code:
Another topic for discussion on the panel that is also reflected in the report was the idea of Imposter syndrome. It’s real, and it affects people of all skill sets, frequently holding back potential talent. Drawing on findings from our previously published Mentorship in Open Source report, nearly two-thirds of mentees entered structured programs lacking confidence in their ability to contribute, regardless of their background skill level. Programs such as LFX Mentorship address this gap directly by pairing newcomers with experienced maintainers, helping 90 percent of participants build strong confidence by the time they complete their mentorship.
Making your first contribution and building standing
When developers are ready to submit work, starting small is essential. The report highlights that maintainers welcome a variety of contributions—including documentation updates, bug triage, test coverage, and localized translations—just as eagerly as they welcome new code.
Maintaining good commit hygiene, keeping pull requests tightly focused on a single issue, and accepting review feedback constructively demonstrates respect for maintainer time and builds immediate trust. Here is a look at the step by step process:
Repeating these actions, and being courteous in the process, is the key to success. Trust in open source is built over time through repeated, reliable participation. As developers consistently deliver value and help maintain community spaces, their role within a project naturally evolves.
Making the business case for workplace contribution
For engineers seeking approval to contribute to open source projects during work hours, framing the request around business value is effective. Building on findings from our ROI for Open Source Software Contribution report, organizations engaging in open source contribution see a 2x to 5x return on investment. And companies that maintain internal private forks lose time and capital—averaging $670,000 annually in maintenance workarounds—due to roadmaps diverging from upstream repositories.
Getting started also often involves getting buy-in from your employer. By proposing a narrow, time-boxed contribution on a production dependency, developers can demonstrate how upstream fixes reduce tech debt, enhance security, and speed up internal development, creating business value. Here are a few points to consider when bridging the discussion with your boss:
- Propose contributions focused on critical production dependencies to reduce internal maintenance burdens.
- Frame contribution hours around measurable outcomes, such as landed bug fixes or triaged issues.
- Highlight research showing that active upstream engagement accelerates product development cycles by 10 percent on average.
The journey into open source begins with a single step, supported by structured guidance and community collaboration. We encourage first-time contributors to reach out with a single step, start small, build networks one connection or conversation at a time, and above all, not to give up. There is room for everyone with different skill sets in open source - the key is to making small, recurring contributions over time, and above all, not giving up.
To everyone who came to the Nerdearla panel, or who will download, read, or share the report, with a newcomer, your actions are an important part of what makes open source a great space to spend time in. We encourage you to stay engaged.
To smooth your journey to increasing open source contribution or engagement, we invite developers, maintainers, and engineering leaders to explore our full research report collection by visiting Linux Foundation Research. The reports and the datasets behind them are readily accessible - and we hope you’ll take advantage of this resource.

articles.title: How smaller, distributed batteries could help the grid
articles.text:
How smaller, distributed batteries could help the grid
From e-bikes to stoves, here’s how companies are adding energy storage in surprising ways.
If you want to install a big battery in New York City, you have to cut through a notoriously tough tangle of regulations. That’s made it difficult to get large energy storage projects on the grid.
Faced with those obstacles, some startups are getting creative, finding ways to use relatively small batteries in unexpected places, from induction stovetops to food carts. By deploying these more consumer-focused batteries, the companies are helping people directly, cutting pollution or power bills. And these units, while small on their own, could add up to a lot of capacity.
Large, utility-scale battery installations are coming online quickly around the world. But there’s been some pushback from communities—especially population-dense ones like NYC—because of concerns about relatively rare but high-profile battery fires.
“The number-one challenge that large-scale centralized energy storage providers have is the fact that their benefits are abstract and their costs are concrete,” said David Hammer, cofounder of PopWheels, at a New York Climate Week event on September 24.
PopWheels built a battery-swapping system for delivery drivers who zip around the city on e-bikes. Drivers swap out depleted batteries for fresh ones at a cabinet, avoiding the need to stop and charge. There are about 50 cabinets across New York City, and about 2,500 batteries in circulation, Hammer says.
The company recently started providing its batteries to food cart operators, allowing them to replace the gas generators they currently rely on. About four of its batteries can supply five kilowatt-hours of electricity, enough to roughly cover a day’s operation for many carts.
Others are looking inside homes. Copper, for example, is a company building induction stoves with integrated batteries. The appliances allow residents to cook if the power goes out, and they could also help homeowners avoid expensive electrical upgrades, because the battery provides some of the power when the stove is in use. “We’re not just selling a battery for resilience—we’re selling it for cost savings,” Sam Calisch, cofounder and CEO of Copper, said at the event.
Other companies, like Every Electric and David Energy are selling plug-in batteries for homes and businesses. Every’s battery is designed to be plugged in to an air-conditioning unit. The company provides the batteries and pays customers to reduce use during high-stress times. David Energy has a similar business model, but focuses on businesses like laundromats, parking garages, and gyms.
Because all these companies’ batteries are small or even integrated into another device, they don’t generally require grid upgrades or extensive permitting processes. Just plug them in and enjoy the benefits—similar to the growing model of balcony solar, with small modules that plug in and help offset a home’s or business’s energy demand.
The move toward more distributed batteries could be a huge change for the grid. “This is the biggest thing to happen in the power grid sector in the last 20 years,” says James McGinniss, cofounder and CEO of David Energy.
If every stove in America were shipped with a battery, it would add up to tens of gigawatts of power, Calisch said. That’s capacity that can be aggregated and tapped when the grid is stressed.
As batteries continue to get cheaper, they’ll likely find their way into more corners of our lives, bringing along many benefits. Cleaner air, cheaper power bills—there’s a lot to like. That being said, the need for large-scale energy storage isn’t going to go away—larger installations will do the crucial work of supporting intermittent renewables like wind and solar, so they can help meet more of our quickly growing electricity demand.
But I’m interested to see how far an aggregated horde of stoves, e-bikes, and window AC units could go in helping the grid. The grid is getting more congested, especially in dense cities like New York. Anything that could help avoid summer blackouts is welcome.
